This research seeks to calculate the lifetime of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay events, which can be as short as 1.2 picoseconds. To achieve this, we developed a new method to measure the time at which the two kaons emerge from the decay, even though they travel at the same speed and their time of emergence is therefore the same. To account for possible deviations, we tested two different approaches using data from 1 billion $B^0_s$ production events obtained by analyzing 3 inverse picobarns of LHCb data. Our results show that $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ has a lifetime of 1.26 picoseconds, which is consistent with theoretical predictions made by the Standard Model. Additionally, we discovered that the time of the $B^0_s$ decay before the two kaons are produced is 1.43 picoseconds. This finding offers valuable insights into $B^0_s$ properties and may provide clues in identifying possible areas where the Standard Model may be incomplete. Furthermore, this research marks the first time the time of a single particle has been measured following a specific type of decay, known as a semi-leptonic decay, which occurs when a second particle, such as a muon, is produced in the process. This achievement paves the way for further studies of other semi-leptonic decays that could yield even more detailed information about the internal workings of particles. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. We observed a preferred direction first identified by the ANITA collaboration and reported here with enhanced statistical significance. This anisotropy persists even after accounting for magnetic deflection and the detection geometry of our observatory, suggesting a persistent source or accumulation area of these cosmic rays over ~79 million light-years. Furthermore, we found that cosmic rays originating from this direction have characteristics distinct from those from other areas, with a higher fraction being protons rather than heavier atomic nuclei. We also discovered that cosmic rays exhibiting anisotropy tendencies have more aligned and right ascension-dependent patterns, with certain preferred directions shifting about ~15 degrees from the initial direction reported by ANITA. These findings imply that components of the extremely energetic cosmic ray flux have specific spatial configurations rather than being randomly distributed, with some sources possibly being relatively small-scale. Additionally, we found that certain cosmic rays with aligned anisotropy tendencies tend to point towards regions of extreme star formation such as the Centaurus A galaxy, although we couldn't conclude any direct association with these specific sources. Overall, our study offers valuable insights into the high-energy interactions of cosmic rays with the cosmic microwave background and their potential connection to extreme astrophysical phenomena over vast intergalactic distances. Furthermore, we outline enhanced tests that could validate our findings and reveal more intimate relationships between these extremely energetic cosmic rays and their celestial sources. With the upcoming Pierre Auger Upgrade aimed at detecting even more finely detailed anisotropy patterns, we are confident that we will be able to draw more precise maps of the high-energy cosmic sky and gain a deeper understanding of the extreme astrophysical processes occurring within it. With this upgrade, we will be able to detect anisotropy patterns in specific areas of the sky with an accuracy many times more precise than the current standard, enabling us to identify potential sources or accumulation areas with a precision that is tens of times better. This will provide a more nuanced insight into the distribution of these extremely energetic cosmic rays and their potential association with certain celestial sources. In evaluating the potential of cancer therapies like immunotherapy, understanding the amount and infiltration location of tumor cells attacked by the immune system is crucial.  Automated detection of these cells in histopathology images can be very challenging.  To facilitate the learning of image categorization models by multiple contributors without the need to centralize image data, we introduce a novel application of federated learning.  Our approach, Federated Viola Jones (FFVJ), leverages federated learning to train a Viola Jones object detector for the identification of lymphocytes while maintaining the confidentiality of participant data.  Compared to a centralized approach using the same type of detector, FFVJ yields a notable improvement of 12% in precision and 15% in recall when evaluating the models' ability to correctly identify non-rare classes of lymphocytes.  The code for FFVJ is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghayabaka/FFVJ.  To facilitate the training process, we also provide a publicly accessible dataset of 5000 annotated H&E stained colon cancer images containing lymphocytes, which can be accessed through https://github.com/ghayabaka/Colon-FL.  This dataset serves as a representative example of how a large-scale pathology image dataset can be created through the participation of multiple contributors.  As part of this study, we also establish a precedent by openly discussing the difficulties encountered while annotating these images and the guidelines that were developed to standardize the annotation process.  These guidelines, along with our Open-Source Code and Contributer Agreement/Data Anonymization Guidelines can be found at https://github.com/ghayabaka/Colon-FL/tree/main/docs.  The accuracy of FFVJ was evaluated as part of a competition hosted by MICCAI 2022, where it outperformed six other participatory teams. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are frequently used for time series analysis tasks. TCNs use a network structure that repeatedly convolves and merges information across different time windows. However, as more channels are added, this structure can become less effective due to decreased information flow between extreme time windows. To address this, we propose a novel network structure optimization method called Trimming In Time (PIT). PIT systematically evaluates all possible channel trimming configurations and selects the most effective one through a combination of efficient forward propagation and score calculation. By integrating PIT into the training process, we significantly improve TCNs' performance across multiple metrics by up to +12.5% on certain tasks. Furthermore, our method substantially reduces model size by an average of 23.5% without compromising performance in other areas. We publicly release our code and source models at https://github.com/huang-128/PIT. Additionally, a simplified version of our method called Simplified Trimming In Time (STIT) has been accepted for presentation at the 31st International Conference on Artificial Intelligence (ICAI-2023). STIT achieves near-PIT levels of performance improvement but is even more lightweight and efficient. We hope our work inspires further research into optimized TCN structures that can handle temporal data more effectively. STIT has been included as an additional method in the updated code and model repository at https://github.com/huang-128/PIT. By applying our method to multiple public datasets, we have made numerous new discoveries that are summarized in the appendix of this paper. These findings highlight the general performance gains achievable through optimized TCN structures and may serve as benchmarks for future research in time series analysis. Moreover, we establish in this study that linear Lie and Zinbiel algebras exhibit similar properties, specifically that their representations share crucial aspects, including the same dimension, a common basis, and a parallelized structure. As a result, we conclude that the solvability of a finite-dimensional linear Lie algebra implies the solvability of its associated finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra, and vice versa. We also demonstrate that the nilpotency of a finite-dimensional linear Lie algebra implies the nilpotency of its finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra. Conversely, we observe that the nilpotency of a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra does not necessarily imply the nilpotency of its finite-dimensional linear Lie algebra. Additionally, we identify the minimal number of dimensions required for a finite-dimensional non-nilpotent Zinbiel algebra to exist, which is three. Our research analyzes the changes in flow angle and flow magnitude for various particle species in 5.02 TeV lead-lead collisions as observed by the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. We studied how these properties change depending on the centrality of the collisions and the kinetic momentum of the particles. Our findings reveal that the angle and magnitude of the flow exhibit distinct patterns of variation, with the angle showing a more pronounced dependence on kinetic momentum in more peripheral collisions and an only slightly varying dependence on centrality. Conversely, the magnitude displays a stronger dependence on centrality than on kinetic momentum. These results hold true for most measured particle species except protons, which exhibit unique behavior in both flow angle and magnitude. Specifically, the angle of the proton flow deviates from the trend in more peripheral collisions, while the magnitude of the proton flow shows a centrifugal shift compared to the other measured particles. These unique properties of protons may indicate a distinct interaction with the collective flow or an asymmetry in the strong interaction. Additionally, our research notes that in certain regions of kinetic momentum and centrality, the angle of the flow can exceed the expected range of $0.1$ radians, indicating a broader distribution than previously observed. Furthermore, we found that the average flow angle exhibits a higher value for particles with higher mass, demonstrating an increasing trend with increasing centrality up to mid-central collisions and a centrifugal shift with increasing kinetic momentum up to certain thresholds. On the other hand, the magnitude of the flow displays a larger variation with respect to centrality than with respect to kinetic momentum, but with a superposition dependence that smooths out at higher momentum levels, until reaching a minimum angular separation of approximately $0.1$ radians. A new econometric model has been developed for time-varying count data sequences, addressing a common issue with previous models. The traditional Poisson Autoregressive (PAR) model assumes constant data characteristics, but this new model adapts to changing conditions and offers a more precise fit to data. By incorporating time-varying parameters, the model provides a more nuanced understanding of complex data sequences. Specifically, the model includes a covariance function that reflects changes over time and a specific non-linear mechanism that explains how past values influence current counts. Estimation is achieved through a hybrid method combining maximum likelihood and the Nonlinear Least Squares technique, with an assessment of the model's performance through Monte Carlo simulations. The paper also explores real-world applications using annual crime rates in the United States and daily accident numbers in the United Kingdom. Results show that the Time-Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPAR) model outperforms other competing models according to various goodness-of-fit criteria and provides valuable insights into the underlying data processes. Nonetheless, future research is needed to fully explore the TVPAR model's capabilities and adaptations. Object recognition poses significant difficulties when objects are free to move within a 3D space. This research introduces a novel object representation called Neural Description Fields (NDFs). Based on the idea of Pioneering the Use of Riemannian Geometry in Deep Learning for 3D Object Recognition by Huang et al., NDFs are designed to represent objects as their intrinsic properties, using a geometry-inspired approach. Specifically, NDFs use a 3D manifold to map object poses to lower-dimensional embedded spaces, allowing for more distinct object identification. By incorporating the symmetry of the special Euclidean group (SE(3)) into their architecture, NDFs enable seamless pose normalization. To tackle real-world challenges, NDFs are integrated into a robust recognition framework that includes a non-linear reconstruction step and is designed to handle multiple objects per image. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through multiple experiments, including the rendering-based dataset generation challenge, where NDFs excel at recognizing objects under various poses, outperforming state-of-the-art competing methods. NDFs also exhibit strong performance in real-world scenarios, showing potential as a robust object representation method. Numerous applications in physics, chemistry, and materials science rely on molecular dynamics methods to solve complex problems. While Monte Carlo simulations offer a complementary alternative by generating configurational space samples, they can be less precise in their movements. To bridge the gap between these methods, we explore using Langevin Dynamics to derive a computationally efficient algorithm for sampling configurational space. By leveraging the advantages of both approaches – the local exploration of Monte Carlo methods and the global exploration of molecular dynamics – we develop a protocol that combines these features. Our method involves rewriting the Langevin Dynamics equation in a form that separates deterministic and stochastic components. We then design an importance sampling harmonic potential that facilitates local exploration. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method using three test cases: (1) a gyration radius test, where we show it outperforms conventional methods by a factor of over a hundred; (2) protein folding simulations, which indicate that our method can fold proteins in a feasible amount of time; and (3) grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations, which show our method excels at sampling configurational space when compared to conventional methods. These results suggest that our protocol can be an very useful tool for sampling configurational space. It has the potential to be more efficient than conventional methods, especially when employed in combination with harmonic potential techniques. We anticipate this algorithm will be an valuable resource for researchers utilizing molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo methods in research and development. This study seeks to offer a theoretical explanation for the fluid dynamic behavior of spheres moving through a confined space at medium speeds, specifically focusing on the partial sealing phenomenon that occurs when a sphere enters a liquid confine.  To achieve this understanding, we numerically analyzed intermediate-speed regime sphere movements using a method that incorporates Navier-Stokes equations and fluid kinetic energy criteria.  By extending previous research on the full-scale confinement case and incorporating the critical Reynolds numbers, we found a consistent flow pattern for 100 < Re < 10,000.  Additionally, we propose a dimensionless surface seal length (L*/d) model that reflects the complex interaction of sphere velocity and surface curvature at this speed range.  This model demonstrates a damped oscillatory pattern in response to increasing Reynolds numbers, providing a practical framework for designing optimal sphere shapes for optimal fluid dynamic behavior.  A critical review of the implications of this research within the context of its limitations is also presented. 
  This study is relevant to various industrial applications involving the movement of spheres through liquids, and both industrial and biological environments.  It is also the first step in investigating the more complex fluid dynamic behavior of spheres moving through a confined space at higher speeds.  Future research plans include numerically analyzing high-speed regime sphere movements and the interaction between a sphere and a confined liquid at the point of contact. 
  Regarding the latter topic, recent experiments have revealed a phenomenon in which the surface of a confined liquid reacts differently to the approach of a sphere moving at high speeds compared to its behavior at medium speeds; specifically, instead of sealing, the surface curves inward to form a cavity before the sphere moves through it.  This understanding has the potential to significantly impact the design of various industrial systems that involve the interaction between spheres and confined liquids, as well as our comprehension of certain biological processes, by providing a more precise mathematical framework that takes into account the critical factors of surface curvature and sphere velocity. 
  However, further research is needed to provide a complete theoretical explanation for the behavior of spheres moving through a confined liquid, particularly in regards to the sealing phenomenon at high speeds, as well as the formation of cavities and the generation of vibrations in this context.  A numerical model for high-speed regime sphere movements has been proposed but faces a significant hurdle in terms of numerical convergence.  Addressing this issue requires a comprehensive review and reassessment of the existing model, which is currently being conducted.  Once this matter is resolved, further experiments and a comprehensive analysis of the results will be performed.

The common approach to training universal models has been to use a fixed rule for all possible interactions between inputs and outputs. Yet, this method often leads to oversimplification, which can result in significant losses when the model is applied in real-world settings. To mitigate these limitations, we propose a new method for training models that allows for complex relationships between inputs and outputs by treating model predictions as the output of a program composed of multiple components. These program components can be the basic mathematical operations like summation or multiplication, but they can also be more sophisticated functions like polynomial invariants or bounded recurrent sequences. By doing so, we transform the task of training a universal model into a problem of finding the optimal parameters for these programs on a batch of data. This approach leads to a problem that can be solved using polynomial-time methods in a simplified case and involves using stochastic gradient descent on a web framework called Jax, which enables us to efficiently train a significant number of programs on a substantial dataset. I will also discuss the application of this approach to the problem of predicting polymer properties, where the task is to forecast certain molecular properties given a polymer structure, described in terms of its chemical formula and bond angles. By using this approach, we achieved a significant improvement in the accuracy of predictions on multiple datasets, outperforming even the native Jax implementations. We employ aggregate data from multiple well logs to model subsurface rock properties, utilizing a statistical method to handle uncertainties for real-time or updated geosteering applications. By aggregating attributes extracted from wells, we generate probability distributions to identify areas with optimal hydrocarbon accumulation probabilities, map reservoir boundaries with uncertainties, and estimate oil net present value (NPV) ranges. This approach has been effectively put into practice in the RoSE system for geosteering, and we provide case studies from the Halten Bank area in Norway. Through these examples, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in (1) accurately defining reservoir boundaries with uncertainties, (2) estimating uncertain oil volumes, and (3) evaluating the impact of logging data on oil NPV calculations. We also examine the influence of data quality on our approach and present strategies for handling data inputs, dealing with singular values, and visualizing complex probability distributions. Ultimately, our method represents a breakthrough in the use of real-time or updated data for geosteering decisions that consider uncertainty. By building on this work, operators and service companies can develop tailored decision-support tools that integrate multiple well logs to optimize hydrocarbon recovery. In addition, this research contributes to the development of advanced visualization tools and efficient uncertainty quantification methods for complex geosteering applications. Certain linear equations that generate a vector field's commutator also result in its vanishing, and fields that satisfy these equations have a key property - they maintain their form under commutation with a Lie derivative. We examine how these equations give rise to complicated phenomena in geometric field theory and provide a connection to integrability, discussing notable examples like the Euler-Poincaré equations and the Chern-Simons state equation in both two and three dimensions. We then go on to establish that most of these equations can be rewritten in a non-localized version, demonstrating this geometric aspect often leads to a field's time or space-averaged value being constant. Additionally, we discuss various methods for deriving these equations, including the use of a 'dual' field approach, and explore several of these approaches with simplified examples. To accelerate neural machine translation in low-resource languages, we propose a novel data-driven approach called Neural Machine Rendering. This method utilizes a pre-trained neural machine translation system for a high-resource language and leverages a monolingual translation archive in the target language to generate synthetic parallel data. By combining source sentence embedding with target sentence embedding, we can obtain a semi-synthetic parallel data set that significantly expands the original training data without introducing noise. In experiments, NMR outperforms other methods using both the full translation archive and a reduced version. Notably, it achieves +1.8 BLEU points improvement on low-frequency types in the NIST04 test set when using a reduced data set. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/NMR. For multi-domain settings, we introduce Neural Machine Rendering Ensemble (NMR-E), that directly accepts a translation archive for each domain. NMR-E attains a +2.5 BLEU points boost on the NIST04 test set compared to the baseline. These findings suggest that neural machine rendering can enhance translation performance in low-resource languages. Additionally, both NMR and NMR-E outperform other multi-domain models on the WMT14 test set. These models build upon the NMR-E base model reported in Table 5, using the same hyperparameters but increasing the number of ensemble members from 3 to 5. In particular, the 4-member ensemble achieves a +1.3 BLEU points improvement on the WMT14 test set. Moreover, our results indicate that both NMR and NMR-E are efficient methods, as they only incur a minimal additional training time compared to the baseline system. For example, the +1.8 BLEU points improvement of the 3-member NMR ensemble on NIST04 comes at the cost of approximately 7 hours of additional training. In contrast, deep learning-based approaches typically require substantial amounts of paired data and sophisticated architecture designs. In contrast, our proposed method relies on straightforward architecture designs and utilizes large amounts of monolingual data to boost translation performance. In particular, NMR and NMR-E need only a small amount of paired data (approximately 1500 sentences) to achieve these gains, making them highly cost-effective. In terms of implementation, both NMR and NMR-E can be integrated into existing neural machine translation systems with minimal modifications. Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential evidence for Hawking points in the CMB, however our findings were not statistically significant. We also discovered areas of low variance in the CMB, but these areas did not match the sizes predicted by the Hawking radiation model. Our work highlights the importance of further investigating these potential features of the CMB, and we make available a tool for other researchers to continue this study. Additionally, we explored the impact of irregularities in the CMB on our results, and found that they could be an alternative explanation for our findings, which in turn could be used to test the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. We also suggest using this model to make predictions about the distribution of quasars, which could be a more robust test of the model. We completed our analysis using Planck data before the release of the EB component, which is more relevant for detecting these features. We hope that future research will continue to investigate these potential features of the CMB, and we are willing to provide our analysis as a starting point for this investigation. In this research, we introduce a new concept called "prototypes" which represents a category's central characteristics. We believe that mastering these prototypes is key to successful recognition of that category. To effectively identify prototypes despite limited data, we propose a novel algorithm that leverages both explicit and implicit signals from data. This algorithm enables us to extract prototypes not just for images but also for other data types such as texts. To test the capabilities of our algorithm, we created a new evaluation protocol that assesses a model's ability to generalize across categories with limited data. Our results show that our algorithm significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in our evaluation protocol, and the learned prototypes are also verifiable through visualization techniques. This research provides a new framework for understanding how categories are represented, and our algorithm can be a valuable tool for domain experts to discover hidden patterns in data. Additionally, the prototypes extracted using our algorithm can be employed as labels for a limited set of data, thus eliminating the need for extensive annotation. Moreover, these prototypes can be used to transfer knowledge across domains with similar structure, thus enabling few-sample learning in new domains with only class-level data. And lastly, the prototypes extracted using our algorithm can be used to enhance the robustness of models against out-of-distribution samples. This research is relevant to various few-sample learning applications such as cross-domain classification, unsupervised classification, and open-set recognition. Cross-domain recommendation has been rising as a way to enhance recommendation accuracy across multiple areas of user preference. This approach involves mapping users from one domain to another based on their shared interests. However, a significant challenge arises when users' preferences are dispersed across various categories, making it difficult to activate the relevant latent factors. To tackle this issue, a new cooperative recommendation method is developed that improves user embedding by thoroughly learning their aspect preferences. This approach leverages both explicit and implicit feedback through a dual-branch embedding network, effectively capturing both short-term and long-term user interest. A multi-sparse-domain cooperative network is then proposed to enhance user embedding across multiple sparse domains by applying a feature alignment technique. This method is further enhanced with a aspect activation module that explicitly activates the latent factors associated with each user in each domain. A comprehensive set of multiple sparse domains user embedding methods is designed with state-of-the-art and baseline methods, leading to a thorough analysis of their differences, including strategies for handling explicit and implicit feedback, routing paths for feature extraction, and the scope of user interest capture. A wide range of experiments is conducted across three cross-domain recommendation tasks, demonstrating that the proposed method outperforms all existing multi-sparse-domain user embedding approaches. A detailed study of embedding space visualization and a practical application highlight the strengths of this method. The source code of the proposed method is released at https://github.com/ghhy127/MSCRE. With extensive experimental evaluation and thorough analysis, this work offers a clear framework for addressing the challenges of cross-domain recommendation in multi-sparse-domain scenarios. The escalating demand for advanced medical imaging modalities including MRI necessitates continuous quality control to avoid degrading performance.  Globally, a lack of standardized protocols exists for evaluating MRI systems.  The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)-compliant phantoms provide a universally accepted means of assessing MRI performance.  However, interpreting these performance metrics in a way that accounts for system variations is a complex task.  We frame this problem as a generalization issue in the presence of multiple distinct data sets, a problem that has not been extensively researched.  Initial experiments indicate that performing quality assurance based on IEC-compliant data alone is insufficient, while incorporating additional data sets leads to enhanced performance.  A key contribution of this paper involves presenting a new method for combining separate data sets and evaluating its application to the specific task of MRI performance assessment.  The proposed method demonstrates superior performance over a baseline method using conventional features.  Furthermore, it successfully generalizes across multiple distinct data sets, a characteristic that is typically absent in multi-dimensional features learned through deep learning techniques. Effective cooperation among agents in ongoing tasks like meetings relies heavily on the presence of suitable task assignments that align with their capabilities and interests. In reality, meetings involve numerous participants with varying levels of contribution and who are only motivated by personal satisfaction. To address this in a realistic scenario, a new framework has been developed that uses a recurrent model to assign tasks and incentivize cooperation among agents in a continuous manner. This approach ensures the sum of costs remains constant over time and is guaranteed by a cost function that is always non-negative. Moreover, this framework enables the generation of diverse and feasible action sequences that can be executed directly by agents in a data-driven manner. To facilitate learning among agents, a novel multi-agent recurrent model that incorporates drive-based and soft-max functions has been introduced. This model can learn from limited annotated data and achieves high levels of performance in a relatively short period of time. The effectiveness of this approach was verified through simulations using real-world meeting data. These simulations showed that the proposed framework produces results that are nearly as good as those found by optimal methods, and significantly better than existing approaches. Additionally, this framework's ability to generate action sequences that are highly similar to those observed in real meetings is a significant improvement. In fact, the action sequences produced by this framework were found to have an 86% similarity rate with the actual sequences observed during real meetings. This confirms the practical usefulness of this approach. Moreover, the action sequences generated by this framework were found to have a high level of diversity, which in turn led to higher levels of cooperation and satisfaction among agents. In fact, the action sequences produced by this framework resulted in an 11% increase in overall satisfaction and a 20% increase in cooperation among agents. This is a significant achievement as the existing state-of-the-art models have been known to decrease cooperation by as much as 5%. In conclusion, this proposed framework provides a more realistic and effective approach to modeling the continuous interactions that occur during real meetings. This approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in a more challenging scenario and highlights the importance of incorporating time-domain data into multi-agent recurrent models. This is an area that warrants further research in the field of natural language processing. Moreover, this proposed framework has the potential to be applied to a broader range of ongoing tasks like group projects, group discussions, and group decision-making processes. The foundation theorem in geometric combinatorics concerns a simplicial complex whose face hierarchy satisfies a specific pattern and inherent structure. It asserts that this complex can be explicitly defined through a set of implicit descriptions, effectively providing a clear, comprehensive framework. We employed a novel approach in which the distance modulus of Type Ia supernovae is corrected through a lensing amplification factor that accounts for the effects of weak gravitational lensing. By incorporating this amplification, we measured the product of the Hubble constant and the amplification factor, finding a value of 141.8 ± 8.2, and derived a value for the amplification factor of 1.204 ± 0.006, both in good agreement with previous estimates. Furthermore, our analysis identified a significant negative correlation between the amplification factor and the Hubble constant, indicating that future studies may need to model these parameters jointly. Our results for the Hubble constant and the deceleration parameter fell within previously reported ranges, while our estimate for the present-day cosmic density fraction fell slightly below the Planck-derived value. Our research paves the way for a data-driven approach to analyzing SN Ia and cosmic shear data, which can be incorporated into a comprehensive study of multiple probes. Nonetheless, our results necessitate a re-examination of the Hubble constant and the SN Ia distance ladder, with a special emphasis on the impact of weak lensing on these quantities. Additionally, we highlight the necessity to directly measure the amplification factor in future supernova surveys, with a recommended margin of error of 3.5%. Our study also illustrates the enhanced cosmological parameter estimation capabilities of future supernova surveys when combining data with a study of cosmic shear. Ultimately, a precise measurement of the amplification factor will serve as a crucial benchmark, influencing our comprehension of the SN Ia distance ladder and the overall cosmological parameter landscape. We begin by introducing the fundamental concepts of stochastic integration, both in its classical and rough path versions. Building on this foundation, we explore various types of SPDEs, including parabolic, hyperbolic, and semilinear equations, as well as their applications in fluid dynamics and stochastic geometry. A notable highlight is the discussion of the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations driven by the white noise and the rough path wind forcing. Ultimately, we delve into the existence and uniqueness of solutions for these equations, accompanied by illustrative examples from probability and analysis. A brief overview of key results and proof strategies is included for further exploration. These lecture notes are a compilation of the workshop's course materials, featuring input from P. Kaiser, G. Advanced computational techniques are employed to automatically extract radiology reports, indicating the presence or type of tumor. However, such software is susceptible to manipulation through the alteration of original scan images. This paper introduces various image manipulation methods used by malicious actors to deceive medical professionals and machine learning algorithms. A comprehensive analysis of commonly used image operations, including rotation, pixel modification, and removal, as well as more complex manipulations like inpainting and sketching, is presented. Our research highlights the inadequacy of current MRI tumor detection algorithms in handling these image distortions. To address this issue, a more comprehensive evaluation framework is proposed, covering both basic image operations and complex manipulations. This proposed framework can serve as a reference for developing robust MRI tumor detection algorithms capable of identifying tumors in both authentic and manipulated MRI scans. The analysis of molecular line data is crucial for studying the molecular process and gas dynamics in molecular clouds. However, observing these lines is complex due to their sensitive nature, often resulting in poor signal-to-noise ratios. To better understand such processes and retrieve more accurate information from data, researchers employ least-squares deconvolution (LSDF). The LSDF method involves guessing the molecular lines involved, which may not always be accurate due to limited information, leading to biased results. Consequently, the accuracy of the retrieved information is also biased, resulting in skewed conclusions. In this study, we investigate two approaches to line identification: a parametric model and a randomised model. The parametric model builds upon existing models such as GASOLINE and RASER, while the randomised model, inspired by the recent BAYES-LSDF algorithm, uses a random line pack to represent the molecular spectrum. We tested both approaches using mock data and real data from the Hubble Space Telescope, specifically observing how the choice of line pack affects the retrieval of line parameters, fluxes, and opacities. Our results show that the randomised model yields more stable and accurate line parameters and fluxes than the parametric model. This is likely due to the random model's ability to sample the molecular spectrum more comprehensively, reducing the bias associated with line selection. Notably, the randomised model performs comparably to the parametric model when the line pack is optimally selected, while producing more consistent results when no prior line selection is available. This study provides a foundation for further research on line selection and suggests that the randomised model offers a promising approach for tackling the uncertainty associated with line selection. It also highlights the importance of line selection and the associated bias that can arise from it, which may have implications for other applications of molecular line data. Ultimately, this study shows that the randomised model can deliver more accurate results than the parametric model and may be a more robust approach for retrieving line parameters and fluxes. Additionally, it raises questions about the optimal line selection and how it relates to the retrieval of line parameters and fluxes, providing a basis for further research into this topic. Finally, this study is significant for the broader field of molecular line data analysis, as it addresses a key challenge and provides a solution that may have implications for other applications of molecular line data. Context plays a crucial role in object detection, where understanding scene hierarchy is vital for identifying complex objects. Many studies have shown that increasing context through additional information can improve detection performance. However, the question remains whether this improvement stems from the enhanced context itself or other factors such as enhanced training or the use of next-generation object detectors? To answer this, we conduct a comprehensive context assessment for state-of-the-art object detectors in a multi-context framework, where the amount of context is systematically varied. Our findings indicate that only boundary-based objects are easily detected with minimal context by default, whereas inner-boundary objects require more complex context to be accurately identified. Interestingly, improving context often results in only a small improvement in detecting these inner objects. Notably, robust detection of these inner objects is still a significant challenge despite using the best object detectors and context. Moreover, our analysis also reveals that existing object detectors are not effective at capturing these inner objects' contexts, a problem that needs to be addressed in the future. Our study provides a thorough evaluation of object detectors in complex context settings, which will serve as a ground truth for future research. In particular, we issue a new research challenge: to develop a score-based method that can assess the quality of context for object detection tasks automatically. A possible approach using contrastive score learning is introduced and is shown to be effective in evaluating context quality, but it still needs further enhancement to handle diverse object detectors and contexts efficiently. We believe that solving this problem is crucial for enhancing the effectiveness of hyperparameter optimization, model ensembling, and generalization across different contexts. Finally, we hope that our work will inspire the community to address this challenge from a machine learning perspective, which is essential for making progress in complex object detection. Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize the Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. This provides a significant expansion of the Fontaine-Messing theory, as previous results were restricted to base fields. We also generalize the theory to include p-adic fields as base rings. Additional achievements include the demonstration that crystalline extensions are etale, and a description of the crystalline cohomology in this setting. Furthermore, this research outputs non-trivial results on the structure of crystalline tori. Beyond generalizing Fontaine-Messing theory, we also introduce an alternative approach to proving theorems in a broader context. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain results on the structure of perfect schemes hold universally. This has implications for the study of categories of coherent sheaves over such schemes. Finally, we explore connections between the structure of perfect schemes and the representation theory of the absolute Galois group through the Grothendieck-Langlands program. This involves generalizing the Fontaine-Messing theory in order to relate crystalline cohomology to \overline{Q}_p-cohomology directly. This direct connection would provide a path to studying the representation theory of the absolute Galois group through the geometry of schemes. This research achieves this direct connection for a base ring of the form $R$. This outcome holds promise for further results on the representation theory of the absolute Galois group arising from the geometry of schemes. Hawking discovered that the surface area of the event horizon in four-dimensional space-time remains constant, a phenomenon later explained through the use of holographic principles by Hawking himself. This discovery's broader implications were then explored across various dimensions. Building on previous work by B. C. Jenkins and A. R. King, as well as on the adaptation of these concepts to four-dimensional space-time by D. G. Epple, J. Krummenaker, N. Radinski, and P. Szybka, we have derived a similar, unchanging property for the surface area of the event horizon in d-dimensional space-time. This new property can be expressed in terms of the volume of the d-dimensional sphere, and it serves as a non-trivial check for the validity of our previous results obtained through the use of Fock's time-time metric transformation in the context of general relativity. Notably, this new property applies to both interior and exterior regions of the event horizon. Additionally, we have established that Hawking's original area formula in four-dimensional space-time can be derived from the application of Fock's transformation to the Schwarzschild metric, expanding our understanding of the underlying mathematical relationships between these concepts. As a result, we have shown that the surface area of the event horizon in four-dimensional space-time remains unchanged due to the specific geometric characteristics of the sphere, rather than any inherent dimensional variability. This finding further solidifies the relevance and usefulness of Fock's time-time metric transformation in the study of general relativity. Finally, we have also demonstrated that the application of this transformation to the de Sitter metric leads to a time-dependent horizon surface area, with implications for the dynamic variation of this quantity across time. This result, obtained through non-trivial mathematical derivation, confirms the fundamental consistency of the underlying theoretical framework of general relativity. Furthermore, it provides a precise, analytical expression for the temporal evolution of the event horizon surface area in expanding d-dimensional space-time, an outcome that arises from the inherent geometric properties of the d-dimensional sphere. As such, this study offers a valuable contribution to our current understanding of general relativity, especially in its implications for the behavior of event horizons in expanding space-times. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have been driven by massive lexical vector collections. These embeddings are often tested for their effectiveness in understanding the meanings and polarities of words. The assessments have been primarily limited to basic tasks such as analogous relationships and classification. A different approach is proposed in this paper to thoroughly examine the capabilities of these embeddings. It focuses on evaluating their ability to differentiate between the grammatical context of a word and its polarized form. Four leading embedding models are compared, and our results show that while they excel in polarized tasks, they struggle to distinguish the grammatical context from the polarized variations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that these models can be easily tricked into predicting incorrect polarities based on the surrounding words. Consequently, our findings suggest that relying solely on pre-trained lexical embeddings for classification may not be sufficient and that other factors such as semantic structure should also be considered. Additionally, our proposed framework can be employed to assess the validity of word embeddings in other multiple-class projects. In the case of the Loughran-McDonald dataset, our results indicate that the existing dataset is flawed and needs to be revised, and we have made our code publicly accessible to facilitate further research. Additionally, we have introduced a revised version of the dataset that addresses the issues we identified. It is available for download on GitHub at https://github.com/hubersat/LM_Broken_Dataset_Revisited. We have also submitted a new version of the dataset to the Harvard Dataverse for further review and approval. Once approved, it can be accessed under the identifier https://dataverse.harvard.edu.dataset/https://dataverse.harvard.edu/datasets/primary-dataset/hubersat/LM_Broken_Dataset_Revisited. It is essential to note that before utilizing any word embeddings in classification tasks, they should be validated through a context similar to the one we have demonstrated. Theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of BWf in achieving high data transfer rates and power transfer efficiency. The research can be seen as an early step towards developing real-world BWf protocols. This research introduces a hybrid interface tracking method that combines level-set and embedded boundary techniques to handle complex boundary dynamics, particularly in scenarios involving solidification and melting processes. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, we've developed a new interface representation which enables a more intuitive and coordinated treatment of advection, accumulation, and surface tension effects along the boundary. With a focus on resolving melting and solidification phenomena, we've chosen a conservative slope-limited third-order finite difference scheme to compute interface and node nudges. Implementing a novel'melting boundary' condition, we've successfully simulated various test cases including the interaction of multiple solids and fluids, Darcy-Boussinesq-like phenomena, and the solidification of a rotating fluid. Our study highlights the potential of this hybrid method to handle a wide range of boundary-related issues and suggests several future directions for its development. By leveraging modern high-performance computing capabilities, we expect this method to be highly effective in solving large-scale problems involving complex interface dynamics. One such problem of interest is simulating stellar solidification processes in the formation of large planets. With the ability to resolve internal boundary-driven fluid motions and melting/solidification processes, this method will be crucial in accurately modeling the planetary differentiation process. We investigate the problem of finding rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer games under various information exchanges between players. Our analysis considers three levels of private thinking, where players may have access to their own payoffs, those of a single other player, or the payoffs of all other players. We explore the complexity of detecting rationalizable equilibria in these scenarios and develop efficient algorithms for finding such equilibria under the latter two conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of multiple rationalizable equilibria and provide a systematic approach to ranking them based on their social welfare. Building on this, we develop an approximation algorithm to identify a high-welfare rationalizable equilibrium. Our study is complemented by a theoretical analysis and a computational experiment using a simulation of a multiagent version of the well-known Tragedy of the Commons game. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of our algorithms in practicing scenarios. This research contributes to the ongoing study of combining efficient computation with complete rationality in game theory and has implications for designing multiagent learning algorithms in dynamic settings. Our results are further linked to the problem of finding approximate best responses in multiplayer games. We introduce the concept of strongly rationalizable equilibria, which involves players selecting actions that are locally maximal with respect to a bounded computation, and provide a framework for analyzing this property in various computational models. Our work is a step towards a formal framework for modeling and studying the property of strong rationalizability in multiagent learning. Our study indicates that strong rationalizability is a more demanding property than rationalizability and may not be achievable in general. Additionally, we show that strong rationalizability is equivalent to the existence of an equilibria in a variant of the original game, where players have a different computation level for their action selection. Our analysis explores the computational models that support strong rationalizability and provides a rule for determining the computation level of a player's action. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of a nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold. It is demonstrated that a Cotton soliton on a non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, when it does not lie on the Reeb vector field, results in the manifold having a Kenmotsu structure. Furthermore, we show that a compact non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, equipped with a Cotton soliton whose direction is distinct from the Reeb vector field, cannot be complete. Additionally, we derive a Schur-type theorem for a nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, given that its Ricci tensor is an Einstein tensor, leading to the conclusion that the manifold is a Kenmotsu space. Building on earlier work by Ni and Wei, we prove that a compact non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, with a Cotton soliton whose direction is the Reeb vector field, has a certain integral property. This property leads to the conclusion that the manifold's potential function, obtained from the Reeb vector field and the Cotton soliton, meets a specific average value requirement, which in turn implies that the manifold's curvature has a specific characteristic. This characteristic, in turn, results in the manifold being conformally flat. This demonstration extends and provides a different proof for the result reached by Ni and Wei. To accelerate policy updates in continuous state reinforcement learning cases using experience replay, a widely adopted method is the replay buffer. However, the standard replay buffer suffers from performance issues due to its rigid structure. To address this, we propose a varying size replay buffer that adapts to the current policy by adjusting its size in relation to the variance of the data within. Specifically, we suggest setting the buffer size to be inversely proportional to the square of the variance of the cumulative distribution of state visitation frequencies. The resulting approach is theoretically justifiable and outperforms the standard replay buffer in multiple scenarios. Moreover, it requires minimal additional memory compared to a double replay buffer method. Our proposed method can be combined with both the multi-item experience replay and the neural network update methods, resulting in significant improvements in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, our proposed approach achieves comparable performance with significantly reduced memory usage. The source code of our proposed method is available at https://github.com/zwang84/VarREX. The key parameters of our proposed approach are easily interpretable and provide valuable insights into continuous state reinforcement learning. The variance of the data within the replay buffer is a critical factor that affects the performance of the policy update methods. I'd like to introduce libcommute, a C++11/14/17 template library that utilizes commute times to efficiently compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of sets of hermitian operators, tailored for use in molecular and nuclear physics. The accompanying pycommute Python wrapper leverages libcommute's extensive functionality to provide an intuitive, high-level interface for users. pycommute incorporates an innovative, generic diagonalization language that automatically generates optimized, specialized code for computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This customized approach leverages template metaprogramming to exploit the unique properties of commute times, forming a powerful toolkit that surpasses the capabilities of general-purpose diagonalization libraries. The libcommute/PARALIB hybrid parallelization framework, combining openMP and MPI, enables seamless transition between serial and concurrent execution. The comprehensive documentation and extensive example collection, hosted on the libcommute GitHub repository, serve as both a user guide and a framework for further development. Users are invited to contribute to the libcommute project via issues and pull requests on the GitHub platform. The libcommute suite of tools is designed to facilitate the development of custom, high-performance applications for computing spectral properties and the construction of linear operators, readily applicable to all common hermitian operator combinations encountered in molecular and nuclear physics. The library has already been employed in a published study, and we eagerly anticipate its use in future research projects. We introduce three new $N$-body simulation models for mimicking generic altered gravity scenarios. The models maintain the same Newtonian two-body dynamics while altering the behavior in multiple-body interactions. The "Conformal $\Lambda$CDM" model ignores the impact of $\Lambda$ on non-cosmological interactions, the "Conformal $\Lambda$-Zel'dovich" model alters the gravitational force's curvature, and the "Modified Kepler" model changes the force's linear aspect. We provide specific potentials and potentials per unit mass for these models and demonstrate their effectiveness in predicting cluster and galaxy distributions using $N$-body simulations. The simulations include $N=4096$ particles for two distinct generic altered gravity scenarios. We examine the dynamics of dark matter particles within a comoving dark matter halo at high resolution. Our simulations also account for dark energy's volume-filling effects, demonstrating an agreement with the modified models' predictions. We discover similar particle dynamics in our simulations, confirming the feasibility of these models for $N$-body simulations of altered gravity scenarios. Our work paves the way for investigating generic altered gravity scenarios using $N$-body simulations for cosmological applications. We make our simulation code, NBodySuite, publicly available for such studies. We further introduce a new "Altered Gravity Simulator" tool, allowing users to create customized simulation models from specified potentials. The suite's suite's dark matter simulation code is now openly sourced on the Code Repository at https://code.git.edu:8042/EGG/NBodySuite. We look forward to contributing new features and improved simulation models to this open-source project. Additionally, we invite potential collaborators to join the Code Repository. A recent finding by Miller and Sheffield establishes that the harmonic measure of a polygon carries the same structure as a Gaussian free field's zero set, after a specific transformation. Building on this discovery, we develop multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution curves in the Riemann surface obtained by removing a polygon's interior, and demonstrate that they converge to a Gaussian free field's zero set as the number of sides in the polygon increases, on a specific branch of the Riemann surface where the conformal mapping is locally analytic. This convergence occurs when the scaling factor meets a critical value related to the Gaussian free field's excess decay exponent. We derive this exponent by solving a specific variational problem that arises from the conformal mapping's asymptotic behavior. Our solution indicates that it can be anywhere between 1/4 and 1/2, and reveals that it is at least 1/6 but not greater than 1/4 when the Gaussian free field is compactly supported, and it is exactly 1/2 when the field's strength is finite. This result holds for any Gaussian free field, regardless of its zero set's connectivity. We also demonstrate that multiple SLE curves driven by the same driving function and residing in the Riemann surface obtained by removing a dodecagon's interior will asymptotically converge to two distinct, intersecting arcs. One such convergence occurs when the starting points are located near the endpoint of one arc and the other arc's starting point, and the other such convergence occurs when the starting points are located near the other endpoint of one arc and the first endpoint of the other arc. These findings can be viewed as multiple SLE curves driven by the same driving function converging to a single Gaussian free field's zero set, providing insight into the structure of this set when it comprises two distinct, intersecting components. Additionally, we demonstrate that multiple SLE curves driven by distinct driving functions will asymptotically converge to two distinct, intersecting arcs when the curves start near the endpoints of these arcs. This result holds for any two independent, zero-mean Gaussian variables with the same variance. This paper discusses the search for tiny new physics scales that are expected to be large compared to the energy reached by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To accomplish this, we need to accurately model two key processes: the production of a single vector boson via a loop from a light particle such as an electron or a neutrino, and the production of two vector bosons with an intermediate heavy particle such as a Higgs boson or a Z' boson. To fully explore the potential of the LHC, we need to consider its capabilities in both forward and central regions. Given that the LHC can achieve high energies, we need to account for any energy dependencies on the new physics scales. To this end, we will establish a set of leading-order cross-section formulas that take into consideration initial-state radiation and color factors, providing a comprehensive understanding of how the LHC's energy influences its sensitivity to these tiny scales. To that end, we will introduce a new variable that quantifies the new physics' impact in a process-independent manner. We will then apply this variable to evaluate the current and projected future experiments' capabilities in detecting these tiny scales at the LHC, including its two planned upgrades. To better comprehend the underlying physics, we will also provide an intuitive interpretation of this variable's physical meaning. Additionally, we will explore the potential of the LHC to distinguish between different new physics scenarios by identifying the most sensitive energy configurations, which can be achieved through a simple yet effective method that forecasts the discovery potential of new physics processes. To facilitate this evaluation, we will introduce a new public software tool that seamlessly integrates with the established LHCCutOptimization code, enabling it to handle any general initial and final states in a straightforward manner. To further enhance this tool's functionality, we will also incorporate an automated feature that optimizes the energy configuration for each new physics process, eliminating the need for a prior understanding of the underlying physics. To complement this software tool, we will provide a comprehensive public database that provides a clear and concise summary of each new physics process, including a descriptive name, a brief description, a reference to the underlying theory, and an interactive visualization of the cross-sections and detection sensitivities at the LHC in its current and upgraded forms. A new method is introduced to analyze the timing characteristics of neutron star and black hole X-ray binary systems. This approach, based on repetition interval distributions, reveals that the majority of dormant X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre follow a distinct pattern. Interestingly, only a small subset of active neutron star binaries with similar properties share this same statistical profile. Conversely, the vast majority of active neutron star binaries exhibit unique interval distributions, with most of the remaining systems displaying a different statistical profile similar to that of active black hole binaries. It is also found that the dormant neutron star binaries within the Galactic Centre exhibit interval distributions more closely related to their active counterparts, rather than active neutron star binaries elsewhere in the galaxy. This discovery has significant implications for identifying dormant neutron star binaries and detecting new low-luminosity X-ray binaries. Furthermore, it is suggested that active and dormant neutron star binaries can be distinguished by observing the repetition intervals of their X-ray bursts over extended periods. Additionally, identifying new low-luminosity X-ray binaries among the Gallactic Centre's populous open cluster may provide valuable insights into the local star formation history. A/NOTES/associated data and software are also outlined in the appendix. A/NOTES/specifically highlights the use of a custom Python script for calculating repetition interval distributions and ranking their significance. This methodical approach to analyzing timing characteristics is deemed more robust than previous methods. Moreover, this technique's wide applicability is not limited to X-ray binaries and can be employed to compare the timing characteristics of diverse astronomical transients. In the case of X-ray binaries, this approach is particularly useful due to the complex nature of their light curves and period distributions. In contrast to other analysis methods, this technique's scalability is well-suited for dealing with large datasets containing numerous repetition interval measurements from various sources. A/NOTES/also touches on potential future applications of this approach, such as studying the timing characteristics of radio binaries and searching for active or dormant neutron star or black hole binaries in globular clusters or the Ultra-Faint Satellite populations of the Milky Way. A/NOTES/also highlights the importance of distinguishing between active and dormant binaries when deriving equations of state for compact objects and the possible detection of such systems by the upcoming e-PeV Gamma-Ray Burst era. A fundamental aspect of gravitational physics, based on the principle of relativity, is the deterministic and continuous nature of gravity. This concept is intricuously tied to the smooth, differentiable characteristics of spacetime. Recent studies have focused on examining gravitational forces in sports, specifically soccer, to educate the public about gravity in an approach known as "binary tests of gravity". Like professional soccer players relying on precise space control to execute their game plan, gravitational forces require precise control over spacetime to achieve their purpose. This connection between soccer and gravity is more than just an analogy, as it can be quantified using a novel mathematical framework that represents relationship between spacetime curvature and soccer ball flight. This framework generates equations that accurately predict ball flight even considering external influences such as air resistance. It also allows us to derive a crucial parameter known as the "soccer gravity length", that provides physical insight into how soccer demonstrates the effects of gravitational forces in modifying spacetime. This parameter's significance is further enhanced when used in a binary test of gravity involving soccer, that combines the predictions of general relativity, Newton's law and the Ryerson experiment to evaluate the validity of gravitational forces in short distances. This test's results, obtained through real soccer games analyzed with advanced statistical methods, show that Newton's law holds true for most games but general relativity does not fit the data while a new law proposing a linear relationship between soccer gravity length and spacetime curvature does fit the data at a 99% confidence level. This discovery's implications are significant as it suggests that Newton's law is adequate for describing gravitational forces in sports, a finding that could be potentially applied to other binary tests of gravity. Additionally, it highlights the need for further research into gravitational forces in sports that could also be influenced by the presence of highly accelerated particles that could be generated through high-energy collisions such as heavy ion collisions or proton-proton collisions. It is possible that these particles could accelerate spacetime at rates that are too fast for our current instruments to detect, a phenomenon that could be observed through sports, specifically soccer, that are highly sensitive to any changes in spacetime. Therefore, extreme sports like big wave surfing, extreme skiing or high altitude parachute jumping that involve highly accelerated particles in extreme conditions could provide a more advanced binary test of gravity that goes beyond our current understanding of gravitational forces in modified spacetime. This could also offer a unique opportunity for scientists and athletes to collaborate on research that could change our understanding of gravitational forces in sports and potentially revolutionize our understanding of gravity in the universe. We explore how high-energy waves produced by massive stellar explosions, specifically Type IIb and IIb+Ib supernovae, interact with the star's remaining envelope. We develop a set of 1D numerical models that account for the wave's effects on the envelope and its impact on the star's overall explosion pattern. Our models reveal that the envelope's irregular shape and any internal inhomogeneities within it can cause the high-energy wave to become highly compressed, resulting in a forward-moving shockwave front. As this front propagates through the envelope, it generates significant heating across a wide range of frequencies. However, if the envelope is sufficiently homogeneous, the wave can instead assume a sinusoidal form and induce a less compressed shockwave front that moves at a constant speed. This is further validated by direct wave simulations. We apply this understanding to scenarios involving multi-dimensional structures within the envelope and find that they can lead to more complex, forward-moving shockwaves that emit large amounts of energy across a broad spectral range. This, in turn, can result in the emergence of highly compressed forward-moving shocks and accompanying radio-brightness patterns from dust formation. Models for SN 2016gkg and SN 1993T, both Type IIb supernovae with visible early-time H-alpha emission, suggest that the high-energy wave induced shocks can persist for up to 400 days after the explosion. These models also provide estimates for shock energies, mass-loss rates, and envelope densities at various times following the supernovae events. If confirmed by observational data, this will provide key insights into the dynamics of these explosions and the evolution of massive stars in the final stages of their lives. Models for Type IIb+Ib supernovae, such as SN 1999R, indicate that the envelope's low density can prevent the formation of forward-moving shocks, resulting in less complex explosion patterns. These models also highlight the role of wave-induced shocks in producing multi-dimensional structures within the envelope and may be applicable to other Type IIb and IIb+Ib supernovae events, such as SN 2001i. This informal note addresses conjectures made by Diamond--Sasaki and Diamond--Kato, relating the geometric modularity of certain non-arithmetic weights to Feigon and Hall's work on arithmetic weights. By applying a theorem from Böckert and Sasaki, we can prove that certain non-arithmetic weights are geometrically modular, and further establish a direct connection between their results and ours. In doing so, we also provide an alternative proof for the geometric modularity of specific weights. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a particular combination of weights will result in geometric modularity, and from this, we derive the implication that a specific non-arithmetic weight is geometrically modular for an infinite number of weight spaces. This, in turn, allows us to make a related hypothesis about the structure of certain weight spaces. In addition, we explore connections between weights with certain Galois action on the minimal polynomial of a geometric Calabi-Yau point and the Serre weights of certain torsion points on this geometric Calabi-Yau curve. By examining these connections and using our main theorem, we are able to identify specific non-arithmetic weights that are geometrically modular for an infinite number of weight spaces. This, in turn, provides supporting evidence for our main hypothesis concerning the structure of certain weight spaces. It is worth noting that our main hypothesis has since been proven as a consequence of the works by Böckert and Sasaki, and the explicit formulas derived by Kato and Sasaki using the geometric Böckle-Landsman method. Nonetheless, our approach here offers an alternative and earlier proof for the geometric modularity of certain non-arithmetic weights, and it highlights the relationship between geometric and arithmetic modularity. This understanding is further illustrated by the discussion provided in the appendix. In the appendix, we clarify the relationship between our approach and the more general strategies used by Böckert and Sasaki in proving the geometric modularity of certain non-arithmetic weights. This analysis serves as a key component in demonstrating how these more general strategies can be applied to establish the geometric modularity of further non-arithmetic weights. In fact, as we show in the appendix, using the methods developed by Böckert and Sasaki, we can prove the geometric modularity of a significantly broader class of non-arithmetic weights, and this proof is explicitly outlined in the appendix. This is illustrated through a quantum chemical Hamiltonian that accounts for both electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational couplings, resulting from a specific molecular vibration, and we show that neglecting this intricate vibrational structure can lead to a substantial misrepresentation of energy level splits due to vibrational effects, potentially exceeding 100%. Additionally, we highlight that this complex vibrational framework is essential for accurately modeling both direct and indirect spin-vibrational coupling and that it holds significant potential for expaining experimentally observed phenomena through the combination of quantum chemical calculations and multi-dimensional spectroscopies. By integrating our model with light-matter interactions, we also obtain an advanced theoretical framework that can treat both ground and excited electronic states, enabling the prediction of phenomena such as coherent vibrational wavepackets and affects involving multiple vibrational modes. This comprehensive model can be applied to diverse molecular systems by incorporating their unique structural and magnetic properties. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be modified to mimic robust vibrational structures using empirical potentials, thus holding the potential to be utilized in a broader range of systems beyond the initially considered molecules. This development of vibrational electronic structure theory also presents new challenges for developing more effective quantum chemical methods, as evidenced by the results obtained with current correlation-consistent coupled cluster techniques, indicating a need for further improvement of these methods in terms of scaling. $\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview. Building from the foundations of representation theory, we have structured the content to cover the core aspects of $\tau$-tilting theory across five sections and will also provide a glossary for quick reference to key terms and their variations used in the field. Beyond its educational aims, this work is intended to provide a clear summary that can be shared on the $\tau$-tilting database website. The database is a publicly accessible platform that contains a wide range of information on $\tau$-tilting modules, including module descriptions, their growth rates, and classification in various equivalence relations such as module and $\tau$-tilting equivalence. By maintaining a focus on the theoretical aspects of $\tau$-tilting modules and their relationship to the underlying algebra, we have kept discussions on growth rates and classification aspects of specific modules brief and instead aimed to establish a solid foundation in the underlying theory of $\tau$-tilting. This approach will allow future expansion of the database's content and is relevant to a broader audience within the representation theory community. It is our hope that this work will not only provide a clear introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory but also inspire further research in this field. To this end, we have included two open questions in the final section.
