Humans naturally employ a diverse range of semantic relationships in their everyday conversations.  While numerous studies have examined the numerous possible semantic relationships expressed through sentences, the current understanding remains somewhat superficial.  A novel dataset called DiscourseNLI is introduced, which furthers the discussion on semantic relationships in conversations by delving into their underlying implications.  Unlike previously established datasets such as NLI datasets, DiscourseNLI focuses on categorizing the implicit semantic connections between sentences within a conversation.  A crucial distinction is that each sentence in a discourse is paired with every other sentence, resulting in extensive diversity in implicit relationships that may exist.  To verify the richness of this variety, a series of rigorous statistical tests was conducted, confirming that the dataset's relationship variety surpasses that of individual sentence pairs, as reported in this paper.  We also introduce models that excel at predicting NLI relationships between individual sentence pairs but fall short when confronted with the more complex discourse settings, which presents an engaging problem for future research.  To facilitate future studies, DiscourseNLI is made publicly accessible through a user-friendly interface that enables the exploration of semantic relationships within conversations.  It is available at https://www.discournli.org/.  We kindly invite researchers to explore this dataset and contribute to the discussion on the semantic structures underlying natural conversations.  A preliminary analysis of pre-trained models has been presented at the ACL 2021 workshop on Discourse and Natural Language Processing, which further highlights the intriguing aspects of this dataset.  As the field progresses towards modeling real-world conversations, understanding the implicit semantic relationships that govern them will be vital.  This dataset will serve as a starting point for advancing this understanding.  To that end, we have incorporated it into a leading NLU competition called the Natural Language Decathlon, which aims to evaluate models on this dataset as well as their performance on other established tasks.  This will help guide future research towards more comprehensive NLU models that excel in discourse settings.  Ultimately, developing models capable of accurately capturing the implicit semantic relationships within conversations will be critical for applying NLU models in real-world contexts.  As the primary challenge facing this field, DiscourseNLI will continue to play a pivotal role in the pursuit of this goal.  In the near future, we plan to explore additional aspects of this dataset, such as the temporal-based relationships that the Paragram++ word representation model employs, which may reveal additional insights into the underlying structure of natural conversations. To address this, they can benefit from a feature extraction tool that uses deep learning to analyze and classify critical scenes. Such a tool was developed for detecting hazardous actions by utilizing deep learning and temporal pattern recognition in a dataset containing annotated video clips derived from a larger collection of automated driving video footage. This tool was optimized for real-time operation by refining its architecture and implementing several optimization techniques. Experimental results show that it achieves exceptional accuracy (>99%) and can handle over 10,000 sample clips at a rate of 5 keyframe detections per second. Notably, this tool can also generate local activity maps for potential hazards, enhancing its overall effectiveness. Compared to alternative solutions, it exhibits comparable performance while being the most balanced and efficient solution in terms of complexity and processing requirements. Automated driving systems equipped with this feature extraction tool can significantly improve their stability and overall performance. A novel approach to modeling afterglows has been developed, based on a global perspective that incorporates both the external and internal dynamics of a GRB's afterglow. This framework uniquely combines dynamical and radiative processes, offering a comprehensive framework that addresses various aspects of afterglows. In contrast to traditional fireball models, this approach omits the assumption of a uniform radius, instead allowing the fireball to change shape over time. It has been demonstrated that in this new framework, fireballs with initially low levels of oxidation can exhibit significant radial expansion during their initial phases, potentially resulting in a transition from highly relativistic to non-relativistic motion. This framework also provides a clear explanation for the existence of late-time afterglows, showing that they can be powered by highly extended shocks when the initial oxidation level is high, or when there is significant external magnetization. Additionally, this approach has the capability to successfully predict key aspects of GRB and supernova observations, such as supernova energies, ejected masses, and radiation energies, as well as the durations and peak energies of GRBs. It has been observed that there is a positive correlation between the amount of energy transferred from a GRB to its afterglow and the peak energy of the GRB, as well as a negative correlation between this energy transfer and the density of the surrounding environment. It has also been found that in some cases, the interaction between the afterglow and its surroundings may become a non-relativistic shock, resulting in an increase in the density of the surrounding medium as seen from the afterglow's perspective. It has been discovered that this scenario describes a conic surface from the afterglow's point of view, which in optical observations appears as an opening angle of approximately 2-3 degrees. It is also demonstrated that in this new framework, the effects of a curved shock front on the afterglow's dynamics can be analytically modelled, resulting in a formula that shows a positive correlation between the afterglow's curvature and its peak luminosity, as well as an increase in the afterglow's dimensionality with an increase in its curvature. It has been found that some afterglows exhibit such high levels of curvature that they must have had highly anisotropic energy distributions, which can result from various causes such as the afterglow being highly magnetized, or it having a very low level of oxidation. A key challenge in approximately solving NP-hard problems lies in dividing a problem instance into two smaller instances of distinct types, as is typical in vertex partitioning problems, where the goal is to split a graph into two subgraphs connected only at their borders, requiring an approximation ratio of at least $|\chi_h(G)|/|\chi_l(G)|$ for some integers $k_l, k_h$ with $k_l < k_h$. For a specific class of graph vertex cover instances, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm that exactly solves the 1-in-$k$ vertex cover problem and employs a novel technique called the 'Bipartite Vertex Splitting Tree' that restricts the original graph's vertex cover space to a bipartite graph before applying a hash function to split it into two subgraphs. We prove that this method yields an FPT algorithm for any $k$ and demonstrate its effectiveness through several experiments. Interestingly, this approach can be applied to exactly solve the minimum vertex cover problem for certain classes of graphs that are hard to approximate, such as the class of all $K_3$-free graphs, and we provide a $2k$-approximation algorithm for the 1-in-$k$ vertex cover problem that significantly outperforms previous approaches and has a significant impact on several practical applications due to the relatively small value of $k$ often required in real-world scenarios. Additionally, this method can be applied to exactly solve several other NP-hard problems, such as the maximum independent set problem, the minimum dominating set problem, and the 3-in-$k$ vertex cover problem, and we provide a $4k$-approximation algorithm for the 1-in-$k$ dominating set problem. Finally, we provide a proof that this approach yields an FPT algorithm and demonstrate the general applicability of the Bipartite Vertex Splitting Tree to other vertex partitioning problems. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet they often struggle with tasks that involve constantly learning from growing datasets and accurately identifying rare categories. Deep learning algorithms that incorporate new classes gradually, starting from previously unseen categories, must also efficiently discard outdated ones to be highly effective. This paper introduces a novel evaluation framework that assesses the performance of various deep learning algorithms in this domain. We conduct a thorough assessment of 13 methods that aim to calibrate and adapt to changing datasets and compare their techniques through the lens of incremental learning, uncovering that certain strategies consistently excel over others and depending on the evaluation method, some methods may perform better than others. Moreover, our study reveals that deep learning algorithms generally underperform comparable hand-crafted approaches and that selecting the most adaptable algorithm is crucial for achieving the best results. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in deep learning approaches for handling categorization tasks that involve constant data updates and accurate identification of rare categories. This study explores the potential for biologically inspired lower body dynamics, specifically bipedal locomotion, to enhance robotic resilience and efficiency. To achieve this, we develop a theoretical model that maximizes energy efficiency through optimal foot placement strategy. However, the model's limitations in providing foot movement guidance leads us to investigate another approach using robotic hips with high degrees of freedom for enhanced mobility. We provide a detailed analysis of the classification for a specific class of distinguished fields known as respected fields within a given differential differential field of characteristic zero. These fields exhibit unique properties where the differential differential map induces a bijection between the residues of the differential differential field and its subfields. A notable subclass, specifically called complete respected fields, is also defined by a specific completeness criterion. These complete respected fields demonstrate an interesting level of robustness by being invariant under the application of the Thue equation solving procedure. A key completion technique is formalized for creating complete respected fields from any respected field, essentially linking them to the solving of Thue equations. This research therefore offers a precise answer to a previously open problem posed by the authors in their previous work and extends the results from a previous paper by broadening the class of differential fields under consideration. Those previous results were specifically focused on the case where the differential differential map has a particular multiplicative form known as the first form. In contrast, the current research generalizes those outcomes by removing this particular constraint. The new outcomes also demonstrate that unlike the class of fields with the first form, the class of respected fields with more general differential differential maps does not possess the required property of being closed under the application of the Thue equation solving procedure. In fact, this failure to close is directly linked to the existence of specific counterexamples that arise only in the case of respected fields with more general differential differential maps. Those counterexamples specifically demonstrate how the property of having more general differential differential maps forms a necessary condition for fields that can fail to close under the application of the Thue equation solving procedure. A key aspect of those counterexamples involves the use of unique curves known as Weierstrass curves and their corresponding differentially defined counterparts known as the Weierstrass differential curves. We utilize the language of tropical curves to demonstrate that the semifield of piecewise linear functions equipped with the Puiseux order has a convenient representation as a set of rational functions defined by a hyperplane arrangement over the semifield of real numbers. This allows us to prove that this semifield is a finitely generated ring when considering the Puiseux order. This result has implications for the study of logical functions on tropical curves, showing that they can be expressed as a set of piecewise linear functions through a specific order when the curve is compact. Furthermore, we generalize this finding to demonstrate that for any tropical curve, the ring of piecewise linear functions, when ordered in a particular way, has a convenient description as a set of rational functions over a hyperplane arrangement, and that this ring is a finitely generated ring. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between this ring and the ring of logical functions on a tropical curve. Building on these findings, we are able to prove that the ring of logical functions on a tropical curve is a finitely generated ring when considering a specific order. This result provides a more general proof of a theorem previously established by J. M. Minsky and S. Yasseri. Finally, we explore how to construct a set of generators for this ring. This construction gives rise to a natural representation of the grid of intersection points on a tropical curve as a semi-module over the ring of piecewise linear functions, and demonstrates that this representation is sufficient to ensure that the ring of logical functions on the curve has a specific property known as idempotency. Additionally, we are able to prove that this construction can be further optimized to generate only the elements of the ring that are involved in the order of the grid, rather than all possible elements of the ring. This optimized construction may have implications for further research into the properties of tropical curves. We've demonstrated that the 1-transpose operation on a long exact sequence in Vassiliev invariants results in an alteration of the sequence's order from n to n+1. Consequently, this implies that the 1-transpose of the sequence on Vassiliev invariants of order three is equivalent to the homology of a specific iterated 1-relator graph, thereby defining a distinct Vassiliev invariant of order three and confirming its non-triviality through a computation of its grading. This new invariant is also linked to the Fox-Hatcher loop, an element previously identified within the homology of a series of iterated 1-relator graphs by J.P. Maynard. Notably, our approach establishes a direct relationship between this loop and the 1-transpose operation on Vassiliev invariants. As a side finding, we identify a new, non-trivial element within the homology of the space obtained by attaching a disk to the complement of a trefoil knot through a map induced by the inclusion of a trefoil knot. This discovery is in line with a conjectured pattern involving the ranks of homology groups of such modified complements. Additionally, we propose and verify the non-triviality of another, distinct Vassiliev invariant of order three utilizing a braid-related construction, which is responsive to Dehn surgery along a torus-boundary component of a rational knot with a specific invariant ratio. This solution demonstrates how the 1-transpose operation can be employed to define complex, non-trivial Vassiliev invariants through the exploration of relationships between homology elements and these invariants. As a technical extension of this discovery, we outline a procedure for evaluating the 1-transpose of a Vassiliev invariant of any order through the examination of homology elements within the iterated 1-relator graphs defined by a sequence of Dehn surgeries on a knot complement. This framework is particularly applicable when the kernel of the operator involved in these definitions possesses a specific characteristic that can be verified for a broad class of knots. Furthermore, we propose that this framework can be employed to tackle various open problems and provide a mathematical solution to a problem posted on the Kirby Archive. Specifically, we demonstrate that the 1-transpose of the Casson invariant, a renowned Vassiliev invariant of order two, can be expressed as the sum of a scalar multiplied by the Casson invariant itself, in addition to another distinct, non-trivial Vassiliev invariant of order two

Kernel-based methods have proven highly effective for tasks like classification, regression, and clustering, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by the significant computational requirements for explicitly computing kernel matrices. This limitation has led to the development of implicit kernel methods, which bypass explicit computation through the use of kernel approximation in iterative algorithms. Our novel approach proposes a data-dependent kernel estimation technique that leverages Fourier features to reduce dimensions, resulting in a computationally efficient and robust implicit kernel method. This method employs a dimensionality reduction step using Fourier features as attributes, which captures the underlying data patterns and relationships. We demonstrate and compare the effectiveness of this approach against other kernel-based methods on diverse real-world datasets, showing its advantages in terms of accuracy, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, our method offers a suitable implicit kernel framework for clustering and dimensionality reduction tasks, which we illustrate through numerical examples. This approach is available as an open-source Python package called PyFDK, which can be used in various computational machine learning contexts. Our study also explores the relationship between Fourier features and other kernel-based methods, providing insights that can guide future research in implicit kernel learning. This includes exploring ways to integrate our approach with optimization-based methods and developing techniques to adapt Fourier features for specific kernel types. Our work lays the foundation for further research into implicit kernel learning, data reduction, and dimensionality preservation, which we hope will lead to a more comprehensive understanding of kernel-based methods and their applications. This understanding will enable the development of more effective and efficient implicit kernel algorithms for complex data analysis and machine learning tasks. Additionally, our study provides a thorough review of kernel-based methods, Fourier analysis, and machine learning, covering key concepts, techniques, and applications. This knowledge will provide a solid foundation for researchers to build upon, addressing pressing challenges in machine learning and data analysis. Using a first-principles approach, we have investigated the electronic properties of SrMnO$_3$ in a hybridization-based model with a strong correlation. Focusing on the 3d states of manganese, we divided the frequency spectrum into two regions - one with high frequencies where states are atomic-like, and one with lower frequencies where states are more band-like. Our results show that a strong correlation model is necessary to capture the atomic physics across the entire frequency spectrum. Additionally, we found that the atomic states in SrMnO$_3$ exhibit exotic moments, with a large, non-zero imaginary part of the self-energy and a significant contribution from inter-orbital interactions. These results have significant implications for our understanding of transition metal oxides and the need for a multi-band, strong correlation model that captures both atomic and collective phenomena across the entire frequency spectrum. Furthermore, this study highlights the challenges involved in constructing a strong correlation model and the importance of experimental data on the spectral function to guide model parameters. We expect this study to contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion on the limits of strong correlation models and the potential of first-principles approaches to resolve such issues. We also hope that this study will prompt further discussion on the choice of initial conditions in the numerical non-equilibrium simulations. Finally, we show that a multi-band, strong correlation model is an essential tool for studying the dynamics of electrons in transition metal oxides and that such models will continue to play a key role in the investigation of these materials. This research focuses on creating robust Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian perturbations to balance out the entanglement generation when dealing with large motion modes - a problem that typically limits such implementations to only a few modes. By choosing appropriate duration and phase angles, it's possible to selectively cancel out the effects of certain motion modes while maintaining the desired outcome of the gate operation. As a result, this approach allows us to successfully implement GS gates with high fidelity when using a large number of motion modes - in this case, 25 fundamental modes and 5 overtones in the $^{171}$Yb$^{+}$ isotope. To validate this method, a series of GS gates were created with various numbers of motion modes and Gaussian perturbations, resulting in an average fidelity of 0.993 for single-qubit operations and a record-high 0.992 for a two-qubit operation using 25 fundamental modes. This gate protocol can be combined with other unitary operations to create a wide range of digital quantum applications, making it a crucial step for the development of robust multi-qubit quantum processing using trapped ions. Furthermore, this work demonstrates the potential for efficiently executing a range of digital quantum operations on this paradigm, further expanding the possibilities for quantum computation beyond single-qubit operations. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios is a difficult face alignment problem due to frequently missing facial details, especially in older images. This challenge is compounded by the widespread use of low-quality faces in social media, which often lead to inaccurate face models that struggle to perform well. To break down these obstacles, this paper introduces a self-alignment strategy that separates easy and hard face alignments into two concurrent tasks. A simple network is designed to align low-resolution face templates in real-time, while a more complex network focuses on solving the more difficult three-dimensional face reconstruction problem. To bridge the gap between these two tasks, we employ a novel dual-face alignment framework that incorporates face templates in both orientations. This approach is validated through extensive experiments on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets, showing notable enhancements in face alignment and reconstruction metrics when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. This approach also demonstrates immense robustness in handling a wide variety of real-world face images. To further showcase its practical applications, this paper also presents a 3D face animation example created using the reconstructed face models. We investigate how translation symmetry breaking in effective quantum field theories relates to fractons, examining several models that effectively describe this symmetry breaking.  By explicitly analyzing the low-energy properties of these theories, we can pinpoint the origins of fracton behavior in their spectra and spectra-generating mechanisms.  Our analysis covers a range of models, including those with spontaneously generated Goldstone modes, excited states with fractional localization, and cross-localized degrees of freedom.  We explore the interconnection between translation symmetry breaking, the associated Goldstone modes, and the origins of fracton behavior in these models.  Our study provides a clear understanding of the relationship between translation symmetry breaking, the resulting Goldstone modes, and the existence of fractons in these theories.  We also examine the implications of our findings for models exhibiting both translation and galilean symmetries, revealing the possibility of dual descriptions involving effective superfluid descriptions.  We conclude by outlining an experimental strategy to detect fractons in nuclear physics experiments involving scattering off gold at high energies, where translation symmetry is likely broken due to the material's complex crystal structure.  Our analysis suggests that at sufficiently high energies, the Goldstone modes associated with this translation symmetry breaking could manifest in scattering data as excited states with fractional localization, potentially revealing the existence of fractons in these systems.  Our study provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between translation symmetry breaking, the resulting Goldstone modes, and the existence of fractons in these theories, also exposing a broader principle under which any theory featuring a zero-momentum state with a non-trivial algebra of symmetries will necessarily give rise to cross-localized degrees of freedom or excited states with fractional localization.  This principle can be applied to any quantum field theory, even those involving more comprehensive symmetry groups, to identify the existence of cross-localized degrees of freedom or excited states with fractional localization in these theories.  Our analysis establishes a connection between translation symmetry breaking, the resulting Goldstone modes, and the origins of fracton behavior in these theories, and we anticipate this relationship to hold broad applicability in both theoretical and experimental areas of physics. In recent years, significant progress has been made in understanding the behavior of linear models under over-parametrization. This research focused on examining a specific aspect of model performance - robustness to misfitting - and formulated a new theoretical framework to analyze it. The framework, applicable to time series linear models with over-parametrization, provides conditions under which a small misfit in parameters leads to a significant increase in the accuracy of the model. This framework demonstrates that even minimal deviations in parameter estimates can result in a substantial reduction in forecast errors, providing a practical guarantee for achieving optimal performance in forecasting through slightly oversized models. Planetary atmospheres that rotate quickly can develop long-lasting circulation patterns in their upper atmospheres. These patterns are often seen in gas giants and can extend all the way to their upper atmospheres. To understand this, we've developed a simple model that simulates atmospheric circulation under various conditions. By changing the temperature difference between the planet's day and night sides, as well as its rate of rotation, we've observed how different types of atmospheric circulation develop. Our findings show that increasing the temperature difference causes faster atmospheric rotation in the upper atmosphere, leading to the formation of strong winds that circulate around the planet in a short amount of time. On the other hand, faster atmospheric rotation in the upper atmosphere results in the formation of circulation patterns that are more evenly distributed between the day and night sides. On quickly rotating planets with small temperature differences, their atmospheres will typically rotate at the same speed as their surface. However, this isn't always the case, especially when the temperature differences are large, in which case the atmosphere will rotate faster, a phenomenon known as "turbulence." Slightly slowing down the atmospheric rotation in these cases will result in the formation of strong winds that circulate around the planet in a short amount of time. Notably, atmospheric rotation that isn't influenced by its surface can exhibit super-rotation, while being influenced by it can exhibit geostrophic turbulence. These findings have implications for studying the atmospheres of exoplanets. To better understand these atmospheres, we need to consider a wide range of rapid atmospheric rotations, especially in those that don't match the rotation of their surface, as indicated by recent studies. Our model also suggests that detecting the direction of atmospheric rotation is more difficult when the temperature differences are large, due to the formation of circulation patterns that distribute heat evenly across the day and night sides. This makes it visually similar to scenarios with no temperature differences at all. Our model will be utilized in a follow-up study to compare its predictions with more detailed models of atmospheric circulation. This will involve using observational data on the upper atmospheres of gas giants to evaluate how different types of atmospheric circulation develop under various conditions. Our model will also be used to make predictions on the direction of atmospheric rotation in multiple planets. The vast disparity between large-scale model training and frequent inference tasks can be attributed to the significant computational differences. To bridge this gap, we propose a innovative approach, called Dynamic Learning, which learns from a reduced ImageNet dataset comparable in size to the CIFAR-100 dataset. This approach is characterized by two key aspects: first, a unique data augmentation method with spatial constraints is employed; second, a simplified and adaptable loss function is used that reduces the size of the dataset required for learning. Our results demonstrate that Dynamic Learning is capable of producing models that achieve 22.3% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet validation set, a level previously reached only by fine-tuned models, and is significantly more efficient in terms of both memory and clean accuracy. Notably, this approach excels in robustness, achieving a notable 2.4% improvement in top-1 clean and 6.5% improvement in top-1 robust accuracy compared to the current state-of-the-art on the CIFAR-100 dataset. Moreover, our findings indicate that Dynamic Learning yields models that are 5-6 times more versatile in terms of transfer performance compared to models trained on the CIFAR-100 dataset. This approach has the added benefit of enabling both efficient fine-tuning and a more effective few-shot learning on small datasets. In contrast to other methods that rely on the full ImageNet dataset, Dynamic Learning demonstrates the feasibility of developing models that are both highly accurate and versatile using just a fraction of the dataset. As such, this approach provides a more accessible path to large models that excel in various benchmark tasks. Recent advancements in Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) aim to combine the flexibility of neural networks with the mathematical exactness of Hamiltonian Dynamics. We investigate if HNNs can successfully replicate the role of gradient calculations in existing optimization methods. By leveraging a novel Hamiltonian optimization framework, we find that HNN-trained Hamiltonian Hamiltonian Hamiltonians can serve as a viable alternative to batch calculations. However, this replacement comes with an increased computational expense due to hamiltonian Hamiltonian Hamiltonian evaluation. In order to mitigate this, we suggest a Hamiltonian Hamiltonian Hamiltonian-based approximation that significantly improves performance by reducing both memory requirements and calculation time. Our results demonstrate that this approximation yields state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark games in complex policy-based games, despite playing with a significantly reduced action repertoire. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits superior performance when compared to a straightforward batch update alternative. The code for our experiments is available open-source at https://github.com/andersonzuniga/HNN-Gradients. The original paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08751. This study normalizes the Gamma function via an integral expression involving a weight function that can be manipulated to obtain the reciprocal Gamma function. By introducing a parameterized integral expression for the Gamma function, we derive a beta function representation and a hypergeometric function expression for its reciprocal. Utilizing a specific weight function, we obtain a closed-form approximation of the reciprocal Gamma function, accurate to a relative error of less than $10^{-3}$ for inputs within the range $0 < \Gamma(s) < 10^3$. This approximation serves as a benchmark to evaluate the performance of several regularized versions. We investigate the effects of different regularization techniques, including Tikhonov, approximate Bayesian, and noninformative methods, on the integral expressions. These regularized versions demonstrate comparable performance to their unregularized counterparts at a relatively low computational cost. As an independent verification, we employ the Dirichlet L-function to obtain an unregularized integral expression for the reciprocal Gamma function, confirming our previous results. Additionally, we explore alternative regularized formulations that provide accurate approximations of the reciprocal Gamma function at a significantly lower computational cost. These formulations hold promise for extending the development to other special functions, such as the zeta function. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of these formulations to obtain an integral expression for the Riemann zeta function itself. As expected, when applying these formulations to the zeta function, we obtain approximately normalizable solutions that describe the function's behavior in the range $1 < s < 2$. However, due to the limited nature of our study, we are unable to determine an explicitly definable weight function capable of accurately capturing the zeta function's behavior in this range. Nonetheless, we remain confident that our work lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive investigation into the relationships between special functions and their integral representations. As our study demonstrates, the choice of weight function plays a crucial role in obtaining an integral expression for a specific special function. We anticipate that further research in this area will yield novel insights into the adaptive nature of mathematical functions and their underlying structures. To facilitate such investigations, we have taken the initial steps in adapting our integral formulations to account for external influences, which we term "perturbations." We have successfully applied this approach to derive an integral expression for the reciprocal Gamma function in the presence of an external harmonic potential, which we have subsequently regularized to obtain an accurate approximation. To facilitate user discovery, video podcast descriptions are often created to summarize content for viewers. This task is particularly challenging for audio-only podcasts, such as music playlists. To address this, we propose the task of melody captioning, which involves generating a written description of a musical segment. In this study, we assemble a large-scale dataset comprising 10,000 entries, along with a novel captioning model designed to improve performance on this task. Our experimental results reveal that both a score-based selection method and a captioning model excel at accurately identifying musical segments, surpassing a random selection approach. Our model's effectiveness is further demonstrated by its ability to create engaging descriptions for users. These findings provide a foundation for further research into melody captioning. To facilitate future work, we open-source our dataset and a baseline model. Like traditional captioning, melody captioning raises concerns related to intellectual property, including the potential infringement of musical copyrights. To address this issue, we propose the use of synthetic music data, which could be created through a generative model like our proposed score-based generator. Nonetheless, evaluating the copyright implications of such approaches is a topic for further exploration. In this study, we utilize the NUS-WIDB dataset, a large-scale musical corpus consisting of segments lasting up to 10 seconds. Notably, each entry is accompanied by a written description generated through a crowd-sourcing approach. Both datasets are substantial-enough to support the development of advanced models, as verified by a series of experiments. Moreover, it successfully produces engaging captions for users, as shown by results of user studies. Furthermore, our model achieves top-performance in both melodic and non-melodic captioning tasks, according to evaluation metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE and CIDER. In addition, we investigate the application of our model in creating music playlist descriptions, which can summarize up to 30 seconds of musical content. Interestingly, our model exhibits a strong preference for using descriptive words that are commonly associated with the genre of music from which the score is derived. Temporal activity detection, a sub-task of action detection, is a visually complex task involving the identification of precise time frames within videos where a specific action occurs. A common challenge in this task is the lack of annotated boundary information, as existing datasets only provide overall duration data for specific actions. This paper introduces a novel approach, called Dual Context Attention Network (DCAN), which combines two context attention mechanisms to effectively capture the start and end boundaries of a target activity. By incorporating a study on attention mechanism interpretability, we further investigate the context-aware attention weights of DCAN, leading to enhanced understanding of its contextual preferences. A comprehensive evaluation of DCAN is conducted across three benchmark datasets, with notable improvements achieved over baseline models and a notable expansion of the current context-aware attention research. The implemented code and models are publicly available for reproducibility and future reference. Notably, this study paves the way for exploring context-aware attention mechanisms in action detection. In addition, two influential open-source action recognition datasets are also made publicly available for the community by the current authors. These datasets, named ActivityNet-2.0 Boundaries and Anthology Dataset (ANTHologyBD), comprise annotated boundary data for the evaluation of temporal action detection. A theoretical analysis of single-beam absorption spectroscopy is conducted to assess the impact of photon recoil on its implementation using an ultracold strontium vapor. Typically, this technique is used to measure the rest mass of a particle, and researchers are moving towards using it with larger atoms like strontium. As these atoms have larger momentum changes due to light absorption, the photon recoil impact becomes a significant consideration. Our study shows that if the vapor is highly optically thick, the photon recoil can actually improve the signal-to-noise ratio, but this improvement may be overwhelmed by systematic errors. To achieve accurate results under the best conditions, it will be crucial to accurately calculate the momentum distribution of the atoms and incorporate this information into a model that predicts the observed spectrum. We propose a new method for determining the absorption coefficient at specific internal energies, one that can handle correlated atoms and account for light scattering. This approach can also provide the absorption coefficient at different detunings, which could be of use in its own right. Ultimately, our study indicates that achieving the necessary conditions to measure the rest mass of a particle using single-beam absorption spectroscopy with an ultracold strontium vapor will be very challenging with current technology. As such, it may be worthwhile considering other methods for making this measurement. We discuss one such alternative that relies on different aspects of single-beam absorption spectroscopy. On the experimental side, work is ongoing to develop the necessary techniques for producing an ultracold vapor filled with only two hyperfine levels of strontium. While this research may not immediately yield a measurement of the rest mass of a particle, it is still important because it has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of interference measurements, which are used to calculate the fine structure constant in atomic physics. This constant, in turn, is a key component in the derivation of the mass of the electron in units of the meter, a unit that is currently undergoing a major change. This change has significant implications for scientists who use atomic interference experiments to study the mass of subatomic particles over long periods. This is the second part of a series of studies on single-beam absorption spectroscopy; the first article provides a comprehensive overview of this technique, while the third article explores another method that can measure the rest mass of a particle using ultracold atomic gases. The shear thickening transition in dense mixtures of particles suspended in a fluid has been the subject of various recent studies. Researchers have made progress in understanding its microphysical mechanisms but still need to fully capture its macroscopic behavior. A key aspect of the shear thickening phenomenon is the sudden increase in frictional energy dissipation rates when the sample is subjected to high levels of shear strain. This study focuses on analyzing this increase through a new measure called the shear augmentation index. By using this index, researchers were able to confirm that the shear thickening transition can be classified into two distinct regimes based on their slope values. These regimes correspond to a weaker or a stronger response to increasing shear strain. Additionally, they found that the shear thickening transition exhibits a global scaling behavior that is solely defined by the volume fraction of the suspended particles. This discovery is applicable to different types of particles with varying geometries. It is also noteworthy that the index's value is directly proportional to the rate at which energy is generated by the frictional interactions of the particles. This approach, which we call "fabric spaces," enables us to represent and differentiate between various lattice configurations by mapping them into a non-linear, four-dimensional surface. To investigate the onset of the phase transition, we focus on a specific cross-section of this surface and employ mathematical techniques to determine the point at which it becomes topologically complex. Our findings are corroborated by numerical simulations using the Ising lattice gas model, which also allows us to investigate the universality of our results. Additionally, our framework can be extended to model phase transitions in other systems that rely on interacting dimers. A recent related study explored the relationship between fabric spaces and Fortuin-Kasten graphs. A key component of our work involves extending the dual Ising model to study systems that involve interactions between multiple dimensions, and demonstrating that it can be used to analyze the geometry of the Ising model's free energy landscape in these systems. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring sparse models that use novel optimization techniques to reduce unnecessary connections. Meanwhile, machine learning has seen significant progress in using alternative models that leverage structured noise to enhance performance. In this study, we introduce a unique approach to graph neural network sparsification. Instead of relying on optimization methods, we propose learning a model that identifies essential nodes and edges directly. To achieve this, we develop a framework that incorporates two main components: a node importance indicator that uses a meta-learning algorithm to identify crucial nodes based on their degree and neighborhood characteristics; and a edge importance indicator that uses a score-based method to assess the importance of each edge in relation to the node importance indicator's findings. We further investigate how our approach can be employed in both single-layer and multi-layer GNN models. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on three different datasets using both node classification and graph classification tasks. Our results show that our method not only yields highly interpretable models but also achieves comparable or even better performance in comparison to other sparsification methods. We believe our approach's flexibility to be applicable to both single-layer and multi-layer GNNs makes it a suitable solution for addressing the interpretability issue in GNNs. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where the querying vectors are deliberately crafted to bypass the sketch's resistance to approximation. In addressing this shortcoming, our research offers an enhanced dimensionality reduction technique called EstimateSketch, which utilizes randomized linear measurements to estimate the squared magnitude of a target vector's components. With $k$ significant components in the target vector, EstimateSketch ensures its estimate is an accurate representation of the original vector's components, overcoming the limitations of CountSketch in cases of cunning input vectors. This study investigates the production of a double Higgs resonance at an electron-positron collider, specifically examining its sensitivity to unusual Higgs interactions that could arise in new physics scenarios. To approach this, we develop a comprehensive Effective Field Theory framework that encompasses a wide range of new physics signatures, from contact interactions to heavy new physics modifications across energy scales. Building on this framework, we evaluate the efficacy of an electron-positron collider in detecting a double Higgs resonance across various new physics configurations, focusing on production mechanisms that yield a distinctive double Higgs signature with missing energy resulting from an invisible Higgs decay. Our analysis reveals that a 1 TeV electron-positron collider with 1 ab$^{-1}$ of data at an 250 GeV center-of-mass energy can reliably identify a double Higgs resonance induced by a dimension-5 operator with a 3$\sigma$ significance threshold, provided the operator is coupled to lepton pairs with an appropriate magnitude of 0.25. For new physics affecting the Higgs self-interaction, a more stringent coupling of 1.5 is required for a 3$\sigma$ discovery, while in the case of a dimension-7 operator, a more attainable magnitude of 0.5 is necessary to achieve the same level of significance. We also found that new physics affecting the Higgs-strahlung process via an on-shell Higgs mediating a dimension-5 or 7 operator can be as effectively probed by a double Higgs production process than the dedicated process of on-shell Higgs pair production. Moreover, we observed that a dimension-5 operator that new physics may induce in the Higgs non-derivative couplings, potentially making it more readily detectable through Higgs decay to bottom or top pairs than the double Higgs production process. In the case of a dimension-7 operator, the discovery reach varies significantly based on the specific combination of initial and final state particles involved. To facilitate further research, we have established a public repository that contains a comprehensive collection of EFT Wilson coefficients, new physics contributions to the universal Higgs couplings, and relevant production and decay amplitude files that can be integrated into the existing EFT-FENIX framework. This repository is available at https://github.com/DoubleHiggs/e7-studies. Additionally, we have outlined a detailed benchmark for the expected performance of a double Higgs search at an electron-positron collider, which can serve as a useful reference for the development of dedicated search strategies. Validating the consistency and completeness of Large-Scale RDF datasets pose a significant challenge due to their size. Current state-of-the-art techniques are hindered by limited scalability when confronted with such datasets. To break through this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages a highly scalable hybrid structure combining elements of both trie-based and prefix-tree approaches. This innovative architecture enables fast and efficient querying of RDF datasets, thereby supporting the rapid detection of errors in such datasets. We have implemented this approach as part of an open-source tool called RDFVal, which can handle extremely large datasets with millions of triples. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets have shown that RDFVal outperforms existing validation tools in both scalability and performance. For example, RDFVal can validate a dataset with 8 million triples in approximately 21 minutes, in contrast to 5 days for a leading alternative tool. Moreover, RDFVal has the unique ability to detect certain types of errors at least an order of magnitude faster than existing techniques. To facilitate seamless integration with existing validation tools, RDFVal can also handle synthetic datasets generated from such tools. Notably, a variant of RDFVal has been selected as the official validation tool for the 2020 Triple Retrieval Benchmark (TRB) challenge, recognizing its state-of-the-art performance in balancing validation speed and accuracy. We have also conducted a comprehensive scalability evaluation using actual dataset validation results, further highlighting RDFVal's superiority over other state-of-the-art techniques. To support fair comparisons, we have open-sourced the source code of all contemporary state-of-the-art validators, reusing and integrating them into an updated version of RDFVal called RDFVal 2.x, which is available under an permissive license. Experimental evaluations using up-to-date datasets have again validated RDFVal's state-of-the-art performance in both scalability and performance. Moreover, we have introduced an memory-efficient variant of RDFVal, called RDFVal-EE, which has achieved the record for largest validated dataset to date, with over 18 million triples validated in 48 hours using a single machine. We expect this breakthrough to accelerate the development of more robust and versatile RDF data management tools, given its potential to handle large-scale RDF datasets efficiently and effectively. We have also shown that state-of-the-art RDF data management tools can be accelerated and scaled up using RDFVal-EE, demonstrating its value in the broader data management community. We have established a public repository for hosting state-of-the-art state-of-the-art validation tools, as well as a benchmarking suite for evaluating their scalability and performance

This study presents radio continuum observations of Seyfert galaxies from the PAWS sample, enabling analysis of extranuclear star formation and radio emission. Despite initial findings of linear relationships between ultraviolet and radio emissions in these galaxies, our observations reveal significant deviations in 13 objects, with enhanced radio emissions not accounted for by star formation. We propose a model involving shocks producing additional non-thermal radio emission, which may result from gas interactions with dense accretion discs or swirling agitators of dust and gas. Our data also display correlations between ionized gas and radio continuum, as well as optical and near-infrared, indicating connections between the optical/IR emissions and radio continuum. A separate component is necessary to explain these relationships due to their break at high luminosity rates, which may indicate a maximum non-thermal radio power. Our study further reveals relationships between PAH and radio continuum at 5.5 GHz, as well as between gas and radio continuum at this frequency; however, these correlations only hold when excluding the most luminous objects. We establish a threshold for radio continuum that differentiates between radio emissions caused by star formation and other factors, and discuss the possibility of identifying shocks through Hα velocity maps. Additionally, our study presents evidence for gas ionization through shocks outside the axis of AGN ionization, and reveals connections between this ionization and radio continuum, as well as optical/IR emissions. We discuss the potential for photoelectrons generated by AGN to fuel star formation, and the need for further observations of velocity maps in order to better comprehend the interactions between AGN, star formation, and gas in these galaxies. Moreover, our study raises implications for the use of radio continuum as a star formation indicator, and highlights the importance of considering shocks as an additional radio emission factor when studying the interactions between AGN, star formation, and gas in Seyfert galaxies. Finally, our study presents opportunities for further research into the interactions between AGN, star formation, and gas through the observation of velocity maps, as well as the study of extranuclear star formation and radio emission in these galaxies. Additionally, we suggest considering shocks as an additional radio emission factor when studying the relationships between radio continuum and other emissions in Seyfert galaxies, and highlight the importance of differentiating between radio emissions caused by star formation and other factors using a suitable threshold. This involves outlining a method for achieving this differentiation, as well as presenting further implications of this differentiation. Lastly, we propose a key area for further research that arises from this study.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances is a crucial yet demanding task in 3D object detection. A positive correlation exists between an object's distance from the camera and its size in the image, its speed of movement, and whether it represents an approaching or receding object. These factors collectively make the 3D identification of distant objects even more complex. Current approaches to 3D detection are primarily based on two-dimensional feature extractors, such as PointPillar, which extract three-dimensional information using a single LiDAR sensor. However, using a single sensor with a limited coverage angle may overlook certain objects, particularly those situated far from the sensor. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes the Far3Det method, which utilizes two LiDAR sensors mounted on vehicles and spatial fusion of their shared boundaries to develop a 3D detection system capable of identifying distant objects. To compensate for the limited coverage of each sensor, a rectangular region of interest is defined based on the size and speed of nearby objects obtained from the 2D detection system. Notably, Far3Det introduces two key distortion factors that are incorporated into the coordinate transformation of the 3D detection system. To evaluate Far3Det's performance, a distant 3D dataset was created, and results show that it outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in terms of mean average precision (0.354 vs 0.264) and surpasses human expertise. Moreover, Far3Det demonstrates its superiority over close-range 3D detectors in detecting distant objects. The code for this project has been made open-source on GitHub at https://github.com/leofengt/Far3Det. Future work will explore integrating Far3Det with close-range 3D detectors and enhancing its performance using robust estimation methods. The proposed dataset and evaluation protocols for distant 3D detection have also been introduced, providing a valuable reference for researchers working in this area. For autonomous navigation and decision-making, estimating scene flow is a crucial task that requires accurate 3D point tracking over time. However, training dense 3D displacement fields from scratch can be difficult due to limited and expensive 4D lidar data. This project proposes a self-taught scene flow estimation framework that leverages easily obtainable 2D image datasets for initial training and later refines the model using 4D lidar data. A unique feature of this approach is the introduction of a novel adversarial metric that assesses displacement field diversity, encouraging the production of various flows during self-training. By doing so, the model becomes more adaptable to new scenes and robust against noise. Comprehensive evaluations using both lidar and stereo data have shown that this framework surpasses flow-based baselines and achieves comparable results to flow-free baselines in outdoor scenes. Notably, it outperforms flow-free baselines in some scenarios. Additionally, experiments with real-world 4D lidar data have demonstrated the framework's potential for real-world applications. To facilitate future research, this project also introduces a publicly available, easily expandable dataset called the Self-Taught Scene Flow Dataset. Overall, this project provides a solution to scene flow estimation that can be robust, efficient, and scalable for real-world applications. It has been evaluated thoroughly and has contributed significantly to the development of open-source code. Furthermore, it has inspired a new research direction for 3D lidar-based scene understanding. The open-source code for this project is called STSFlow and can be found on https://github.com/kaist-vision/stsflow. The dataset and models associated with this project have been made available on https://github.com/kaist-vision/stsflow-dataset. STSFlow is a state-of-the-art flow-based model that has been released open-source at https://github.com/kaist-vision/stsflow. It has outperformed other flow-based models in outdoor scenes and has been applied to real-world 4D lidar data. Additionally, a self-taught training protocol for 3D displacement fields has been introduced and has shown improved performance when applied to new scenes. This protocol enables 3D displacement fields to be trained from scratch using 2D image datasets and refines the model using 4D lidar data in a self-supervised manner. A novel adversarial metric has been introduced that assesses the diversity of 3D displacement fields and has been incorporated into the self-taught training protocol

During operation, Timeloops analyzes a container's system calls over a defined period, using a hybrid approach that combines techniques from formal languages and machine learning to create rules for future system calls. We've tested Timeloops on a sample e-commerce microservice and found that it effectively generates accurate rules, reducing errors by 90% compared to a random rule set. Additionally, Timeloops can handle a significant number of system calls within a defined timeframe. We believe this method has the potential to enhance security in production environments by automating system call rule learning for containerized applications. We've open-sourced Timeloops, and its source code is now available for review and use. Given that the dark matter particle interacts with the Higgs boson, it may either be a pseudo-Goldstone boson or have a mass comparable to the electroweak scale. This model demonstrated exceptional performance on both the training and evaluation sets, showcasing its consistency with a 42% boost in regaining ball control on the evaluation set. It's worth mentioning that previous work on essential situations using reinforcement learning and artificial potential fields was building upon, and our paper improves that by achieving more successful regains and a greater increase in regaining possession within the allotted time. Additionally, our model addressed the issue of soccer agents getting trapped in each other, resulting in an unfair time limitation, and we highlighted the challenge of large state and action spaces in soccer games. It is also proposed that utilizing state-of-the-art models pre-trained on vast datasets can be an area of future research. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray transient IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 outburst. The system comprises a compact accreting neutron star and a late-type giant companion. IGR J19294+1816 displayed a typical high-mass X-ray binary spectrum with a power-law component, along with iron emission from its accretion disc. The presence of a quasi-periodic oscillation at mHz frequencies and a cyclotron line was evident at ~13.1 GHz, with the line's width being relatively high at ~1.1 GHz^-1. The detection of the cyclotron line and the variable X-ray spectrum during the 2019 outburst provides a crucial measure for determining the binary system's inclination angle and the radius of the neutron star. Additionally, the detection of the cyclotron line allows us to infer the neutron star's magnetic field strength, which displayed significant variation during the 2019 outburst. A comparison of the inclination angle and magnetic field strength estimates from different observations is also presented here. Moreover, the increase in the neutron star's accretion rate during the 2019 soft state, which lasted from Day ~10 to ~30 after the initial outburst, might be attributed to the presence of a disc shadow cast on the neutron star's surface due to its elevated temperature. A possible explanation for the varying width of the cyclotron line, specifically during the 2019 outburst, is also provided. However, most assessment tools fail to consider the underlying assumptions made by these models, particularly the fact that they operate under a one-to-many mapping, where a single encoder input corresponds to multiple possible decoder responses. Consequently, this study aims to evaluate whether the encoder representations captured by these models are sufficient to distinguish between assigned responses from unassigned ones. To achieve this, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called the Assignment Discrimination Accuracy (ADA), as well as a straightforward yet effective method to obtain unassigned responses. Furthermore, we found that both the ability to preserve meaning and the autoregressive nature of models contribute significantly to their performance in this aspect. In order to produce more reliable evaluations, it is essential to validate the internal workings of neural network-based conversation models in a rigorous and systematic manner. Deep learning methods have significantly improved in recent years, becoming a popular choice for detecting locations in 3D point clouds. However, many current approaches still struggle with recognizing location primitives due to the inherent complexity of 3D data and the limited diversity of training sets. To address this issue, a new system called AttDLNet has been developed, which uses a unique attention-driven deep learning network to accurately identify locations within 3D scenes. By utilizing both spatial and angular features extracted from LiDAR data, AttDLNet's multi-task learning approach allows for simultaneous detection of location primitives and orientation estimation. To mitigate the limited diversity of training sets and reduce overfitting, a method called multi-task based sample selection was implemented, which leverages unlabeled data to identify key locations in 3D scenes. Comprehensive evaluation of AttDLNet was conducted using a large-scale dataset called SUN3D, which demonstrated its superior performance in location recognition when compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, results showed AttDLNet's robustness in handling multiple orientation classes and its ability to adapt to various environments. To further validate the method's effectiveness, a user study was conducted with multiple participants, who were asked to annotate locations within 3D scenes using a developed system called AttDLNet-UI. The analysis of the results revealed a significant reduction in annotation time and minimal discrepancies when compared to ground truth, indicating AttDLNet's potential for practical location recognition applications. To facilitate further research, the developed system, including both code and datasets, is openly available on GitHub. Overall, AttDLNet represents a groundbreaking approach for location recognition in 3D scenes, exceeding the performance of existing methods and demonstrating its potential for real-world applications through extensive evaluation and user studies. Furthermore, the method's simplicity and effectiveness make it a suitable baseline for future location recognition challenges. This paper shows that the Hermitian version of the Gnutzmann and Smilansky matrix is equivalent in nature to a combination of submatrices derived from the Schur complement, resulting in a factorization that explicitly expresses the scattering matrix in terms of the Hermitian matrix and diagonal entries associated with nodes isolated at the energy $E$. A method for constructing the Hermitian matrix is also introduced through a supergraph technique, where adding edges between two isolated nodes at the energy $E$ is equivalent to a specific modification of the Hermitian matrix. This approach enables the determination of a combined Hermitian matrix for a given graph, and further enables identification of a combined scattering matrix in a combined supergraph. This combined scattering matrix is found to possess a particular property known as single nonchirality. Finally, an algorithm is also provided for constructing either the Hermitian matrix or the scattering matrix based on the combined Hermitian matrix associated with a given graph. This study analyzes leading contextualized language models with multiple configurations for their ability to identify semantic changes in text, using a recently developed dataset named SemAlter. The most common individual identification method involves using their name and date of birth, which are usually found on government-issued identification documents. In Indonesia, the population grows at a rate of 1.2% annually, outpacing the national ID card issuance rate, which poses issues with name-based identification methods due to potential conflicts. To address these issues, a more efficient approach is needed to accurately match individuals based on their unique characteristics, such as facial features, fingerprints, or voice. However, this method is costly and only feasible for a limited number of high-risk individuals. To tackle this problem, our research focuses on name-standardization and date-of-birth extraction from Indonesian ID documents using optical character recognition (OCR) technology combined with natural language processing (NLP). Furthermore, we discovered that using a 4-layer neural network outperformed all other approaches tested. Additionally, we found that even with a relatively small data set, a 4-layer neural network could efficiently process name-format normalization tasks compared to other machine learning models. In conclusion, we successfully developed an application that can normalize the name format and extract the date of birth from an Indonesian ID document using OCR technology combined with NLP. We also demonstrated the application's high accuracy rate using a machine learning-based approach and a 4-layer neural network model. We believe that our research could serve as a foundation for further development of ID document analysis applications. In addition, we suggest that the name-format normalization approach we introduced could be a useful tool for various tasks, such as duplicate name detection, data sorting, and data aggregation. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored using Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning (SSVRL) to extract universal features from visual data. SSVRL methods typically employ contrastive learning to obtain consistent representations of the same visual data from different angles or transformations. In response, we present a novel contrastive learning approach that leverages two innovative elements: Modulated Cyclic Activations and a novel multi-task learning framework. Modulated Cyclic Activations is a unique activation function that alternates between two distinct activation methods to capture both local and global visual information. This activation function is integrated into a multi-task learning framework that combines the learning of global representations and the classification of local features. Our proposed approach produces visual representations that are both generalizable and accurate, outperforming multiple benchmark methods in various visual classification tasks. Notably, our results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the MNIST, CIFAR-100, and Vestiaire Collective datasets. The Solar Vector Magnetic Field (SVMF) information plays a critical role in understanding solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Post-flare CMEs have the potential to impact planetary magnetic fields and spacecraft, highlighting the need for accurate SVMF information. This paper delves into the source of uncertainty in deriving parameters from SVMF data and presents a statistical approach to identify and reduce bias in derived results. We propose using the Bayes factor to select optimal filtering settings, eliminate outliers, and thereby reduce the impact of bias in data. This approach is illustrated using magnetic flux values from the CESE Solar Data. Results show a significant reduction in the median of the Bayes factor, eliminating the bias in the data by a factor of more than ten. This study provides a foundation for investigating other physical properties of solar magnetic fields and contributes to the pursuit of accurate SVMF information. We've analyzed young stellar associations (YSAs) in three nearby galaxies - the Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud, and Small Magellanic Cloud - to determine the two-dimensional dimensions of these structures. Previous studies have primarily focused on one-dimensional velocity dispersions. By comparing velocity and spatial dispersions, we found that the sizes of YSAs vary significantly, ranging from 1-27 parsecs in physical extent, while their velocity dispersions range from 0.2-1.5 kilometers per second. Notably, the ratio of spatial to velocity dispersion, a measure of a YSA's two-dimensional extent divided by its one-dimensional velocity spread, forms a tight normal distribution with an average of 8.5 parsecs/kilometer per second. This ratio is invaluable for identifying YSAs in the face of signal noise and will be employed in our pending publication "Uncovering Young Stellar Associations in the Milky Way and Nearby Galaxies with Gaia and Hubble" (SSA). Additionally, we've used the two-dimensional dimensions of YSAs in combination with their galactic locations to classify associations as local, colliding, or unassociated structures. We've also used the dimensions to estimate the masses of low-mass stars within YSAs, which will be the subject of a forthcoming publication "The Mass Function of Young Stellar Associations in the Milky Way and Nearby Galaxies" (SSB). These analyses will enhance our comprehension of YSAs and how they form, as well as the formation and evolution of stellar groups within nearby galaxies. These results will be incorporated into upcoming publications of the study's extended data set. Due to the limited Gaia satellite data for the Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud, our analysis of YSAs in these galaxies is less comprehensive than in the Milky Way. Nonetheless, our study provides a foundation for further research on YSAs in these nearby galaxies. We anticipate that upcoming more detailed analyses of YSAs, along with additional data from the satellite, will yield a more complete understanding of these stellar associations in the Magellanic Clouds. Recent breakthroughs in numerical modeling, driven by complex-valued neural networks, have successfully minimized the Hubbard sign issue for large-scale simulations. These models eliminate the need for artificial sign flipping methods by naturally producing well-balanced wave functions. We examine a specific complex-valued neural network called the complex-valued graph neural network and apply it to solve the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Our results, compared to a renowned neural network implementation, show comparable accuracy without the need for sign flipping. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of this approach by discussing potential solutions to fundamental issues facing neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our work highlights the potential of complex-valued neural networks to resolve long-standing challenges in quantum simulation. We also contribute a publicly accessible code for training complex-valued neural networks, taking inspiration from open-source quantum simulation tools. This code is written in PyTorch and is easily modifiable to accommodate custom Hamiltonian projections. We demonstrate the efficiency of this code by providing high-resolution data for the half-filled two-dimensional Hubbard model. This data shows exceptional agreement with existing data and marks a significant advancement in complex-valued neural network-based simulation. We make this code available on the NeuralNetworkHubbard GitHub repository. It builds upon previous work by incorporating an updated neural network architecture that addresses the sign issue and showcases the benefits of complex-valued learning. This architecture has the added benefit of eliminating the need for artificial sign flipping methods, a problem that neural network-based QMC faces. Our results also highlight the accuracy of complex-valued neural networks, demonstrating a maxima energy error of 0.048 for the 38-site lattice and further highlights the potential of these models to model ground states in QMC simulations. We leave for future work the investigation of anti-ferromagnetic states using this model due to the inherent imbalance of the wave function. Despite only eliminating the sign issue, our results show that neural network-based QMC faces an even greater challenge in achieving the correct phase of the ground state. This is further compounded by the fact that neural network-based QMC is only capable of modeling un-improved versions of the Hamiltonian due to the inherent over-counting that occurs with improved methods. This presents an even greater sign issue that needs to be addressed, making anti-ferromagnetic state simulations an even more difficult task. Nonetheless, we believe that complex-valued neural networks offer a promising path forward for addressing this challenge and potentially other complex issues in quantum simulation. We also highlight another potential solution to this problem, namely the use of quaternion-valued neural networks

A key finding is that the performance improvement from differential encoding is most significant in low SNR scenarios and varies depending on CPM order, symbol spacing, and phase modulation type. Notably, differential detection can offer a greater than 6 dB advantage in required signal energy for certain CPM implementations, indicating its potential for reducing transmission delays in applications with limited bandwidth. Finally, as the bandwidth of wireless communication systems continues to expand, the need to maintain low transmission delays will become more critical, making differential detection a more attractive solution. Rainfall on optical sensors causes the distortion known as rain optical distortion, which hinders weather monitoring and affects other fields. To address this issue, we need to eliminate rain from the images. However, traditional image-to-image translation methods can't effectively tackle this problem due to rain elimination opposing the direction of the image translation. This limits their capability to learn a successful transformation. To overcome this challenge, we propose a joint rain formation and elimination model that utilizes two separate translation directions. This bidirectional approach enables the model to learn a rain-elimination transformation by constructing an inverse transformation for rain formation. To achieve this, we introduce a disentangled image transformation strategy that separates the optical distortion process into two independent components - light scattering and attenuation. This strategy permits the model to learn these processes independently, which facilitates the development of an inverse transformation for rain elimination. Our joint rain formation and elimination model is based on this strategy and employs a dual latent code to represent the input image and derive the rain-eliminated image. Notably, the model's second latent code is an inverse transformation of the first code, which allows it to eliminate rain through reverse calculation. To optimize the model, we introduce a multi-view latent code learning approach that facilitates the disentanglement of the two codes. This approach involves two main processes: code disentanglement and quality assessment. Code disentanglement employs a contrastive loss function that encourages the model to extract independent representations for light scattering and elimination, while quality assessment leverages an image quality assessment (IQA) model to evaluate the rain-eliminated images. Our joint rain formation and elimination model achieves the best performance to date on the Rain12 and Rain13 datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Moreover, our model's code disentanglement ability contributes to the improvement of rain elimination performance. Notably, our model can effectively remove light scattering and attenuation from images in real-world weather conditions, as demonstrated by our codemasking code. This code masks the light scattering and elimination codes used to regenerate the input image, resulting in a clean background. Our model's ability to eliminate rain in video sequences is demonstrated by our video demonstration code, which shows our model's application in the "Weather Conditions" module of the FuYi intelligent surveillance assistant.
