A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via hierarchical categories to guide learning agents. Our research builds upon this foundation by introducing a novel form of human input - relative rankings of pre-defined clusters - to efficiently provide feedback for agents. To facilitate easy understanding of human intentions, we develop a simple yet effective method to obtain the agent's embedding distribution after each new data point is learned. To bridge the gap between human and agent representations, we design a jointly optimized model that transforms both the human-provided relative rankings and the agent's embeddings into a shared latent space. Our research demonstrates that human-in-the-loop feedback via cluster ranking accelerates learning by significantly reducing the number of individual ratings needed, compared to prior methods, resulting in accelerated discovery of optimal action policies and a substantial boost in performance. Experimental evaluations using both real-world data and simulated environments underscore the efficacy of our approach in speeding up learning through reduced human input. Our research contributes a novel form of human feedback, efficient learning methods, and a publicly accessible repository that facilitates further study in this domain. To address this, we've developed ATOMIC, a vast knowledge atlas that connects diverse machine learning statements through "if-then" relationships. This massive database, consisting of over 800,000 instances, covers nearly 300 categories of topics and spans three primary formats, including statements about a single entity, a nurturing action between two entities, and an influencing action where one entity affects another's trait. To showcase its utility, we've created a simple inference model that leverages ATOMIC and significantly outperforms existing baseline models in five out of seven challenging tasks. Interestingly, this model also exhibits a remarkable ability to generalize on unseen "then" clauses when only provided with a single "if" clause example. To further explore ATOMIC's potential, we've open-sourced the dataset, along with an interactive tool that allows users to explore diverse machine learning statements and their underlying relationships. This knowledge atlas is available for anyone to utilize, marking a significant step towards creating a more unified view of machine learning knowledge. This paper investigates the distribution of starting points for a specific class of sequences called uniform parking functions, as their length increases without limit. We first demonstrate that the limiting distribution of the initial points is a unique mixture of uniform distributions, tailored to the specific parameter 'p'. This limiting distribution is derived analyatically for p equal to zero or one; however, for other values of p, we employ a probabilistic approach to obtain a non-uniform asymptotic distribution. Through extensive computer simulations, we verify that the asymptotic probability measures for initial points correlate with the structure of Kashiwaga lattices. This connection holds for all integers p greater than zero. We also establish a link between the uniform parking function sequences and a specific multidimensional lattice, referred to as the Kashiwaga lattice, and explore how this relationship evolves as additional dimensions are added. This connection enables us to identify specific subsets within the lattice and derive formulas for the number of uniform parking functions for particular parameter values. This further enables us to demonstrate that the limiting distribution of initial points for uniform parking functions is unique and cannot be expressed through an additive approach. This conclusion is supported by a general proof applicable to any dimension. We also provide a more general framework that connects sequences of uniform parking functions with respect to a specific parameter 'p' to a particular multidimensional lattice, referred to as the Bojanov-Macigegi-Simeonov lattice, and derive formulas for the number of uniform parking functions for particular parameter values. This further enables us to investigate the distribution of starting points for uniform parking functions. This investigation yields a unique corollary that the binary representation of any element within this specific dimensioned lattice is unique. This in turn raises an interesting open question that could be of broader interest in the field of discrete mathematics. This question pertains to the distribution of starting points for a particular class of sequences called 'gray codes', which generate all possible binary combinations in a specific order. This open question could provide valuable insights into both the uniform parking functions and the Kashiwaga lattices. It also offers a concrete approach for further research in the field of discrete mathematics. This approach combines elements from both combinatorial and probabilistic disciplines. It is therefore relevant to a broad range of academic and research communities. It could provide a valuable research opportunity for graduate students or postdoctoral researchers. It is also highly relevant to a broad range of practical applications that deal with sequences of actions. It is therefore important to contribute to the body of knowledge in this field.

HD80606b, an highly eccentric exoplanet, undergoes severe temperature fluctuations between its extreme close and distant points from the star. Its narrow sliver-crossing event offers a superb opportunity to calibrate the system's parameters. A new, more precise calibration is necessary to make the most of this event when the James Webb Telescope is operational. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the system using light curves from various telescopes around the world. Our final model for the system's behavior includes a slightly irregular surface on the planet and an ever-changing orbital path. To facilitate the most effective use of observational data from the James Webb Telescope, we calculated the most favorable observation periods for this event. Our study reveals information that will be beneficial for all available windows but also pinpoints the most suitable time to observe this system. This system is an excellent target for studying a planet's atmosphere despite the challenges it presents. Our study provides the necessary calibration to make the most of this opportunity. If the orbital path is changing over a longer period, it could result in another close approach between the star and the planet in about 15 years. If so, there may be another temporary heating of the planetary atmosphere that could be observed from space. If we are to accurately predict future close approaches, we need to observe the system during its next narrow sliver-crossing event. This could provide data that is just as precise as we have now but with the added benefit of information on the planet's orbital path over a longer period. If we fail to observe this system during this event, we risk missing an opportunity that may not come again for over a decade and a half. The concept of foundation gameplay offers a clear framework for addressing issues related to player engagement and motivation in games. By providing an underlying structure that emphasizes player progress and motivation, this approach can be applied to create games that promote physical rehabilitation. Despite initial challenges in incorporating the paradigm into a rehabilitation context, successful outcomes have been achieved by adapting the framework to meet the needs of occupational therapists. As a result, a prototype game titled "Walk & Roll" has been developed to facilitate walking exercises for children with lower motor function through a fun, interactive experience. By using a combination of auditory and visual incentives to motivate players, the game provides an motivating environment that encourages children to perform the required physical movements. A case study is presented on the therapeutic benefits of "Walk & Roll" as a physically interactive game, with the aim of contributing to the expansion of games that combine physical interaction and motivation techniques to create engaging experiences for children with lower motor function. A foundation gameplay-based approach is introduced as a method for developing such games, along with an evaluation of the results and potential areas for further improvement. By applying this approach, it is possible to design games that are not only enjoyable for children with lower motor function but also provide a meaningful physical therapy experience. To achieve this, we examine various leptoquark models with different gauge groups, considering both the standard and anomalous cases, and assess their impacts on the Drell-Yan cross section at a next-generation hadron collider. To provide accurate predictions, we incorporate higher-order corrections and tailor a practical approach for identifying the leptoquarks based on Drell-Yan pair production. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women. Compensating for lowered doses with longer scan times is not feasible due to limited acquisition times. Enhancing PET images using low-dose images from associated computed tomography (CT) scans has shown promise but is challenging because PET images are highly noisy. Deep learning-based approaches have made gains in de-noising PET images, yet they often prioritize improving metrics like PSNR and SSIM over biological truth. In order to guide deep learning-based de-noising to produce biologically plausible images, especially in cases where training and testing PET datasets differ, we propose a novel uncertainty-conscious deep learning framework that incorporates physical constraints and is robust against variations in testing datasets. This uncertainty-conscious framework is based on a dual-loss architecture that minimizes both a direct loss and a robust loss against out-of-distribution data. To prevent over-training in low-dose images, the framework uses batch normalization with weight residual soft-weighted averaging that promotes smooth representation learning. To account for uncertainties in both PET and CT images, the framework includes a learning-based data normalization module that maps raw images to normalized low-noise images. This results in a deep learning-based de-noising framework that produces biologically plausible images at lower doses, is robust against variations in testing datasets, and could potentially be adapted for use with other multimodal imaging pairs. Experimental results with real-world PET/CT datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in producing biologically plausible images at reduced doses, with further analysis exploring the influence of various hyperparameters and the uncertainty levels of PET and CT images. This novel uncertainty-conscious deep learning framework has the potential to enhance low-dose PET images, making it suitable for more reliable image production at reduced doses. This approach can be adapted for use with other deep learning-based medical imaging applications. In order to evaluate this approach on actual clinical low-dose PET images, further work is required to address the limitations imposed by the requirement for mock data analysis described in the ANZMRI study guidelines. In particular, real-world PET images with associated clinical truth values are needed in order to validate the biological plausibility of this approach using actual clinical low-dose PET images. The rising popularity of the n-tier software design pattern among developers stems from its balance of functionality and performance. Nonetheless, implementing this pattern is often hampered by the time-consuming process of setting up a framework. To accelerate and streamline this process, our automated framework setup tool is designed to immediately provide users with a fully functional, modular n-tier framework tailored to their needs. By integrating multiple open-source components, our tool sparks novel research directions by resolving issues like integrating third-party modules with distinct configuration methods, divergent programming languages, and incompatible framework architectures. We successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by integrating five diverse Java frameworks. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable across various programming languages, as illustrated by a PySpring example. A comparison of our approach with traditional approach is presented, showcasing the time-saving benefits of automated setup. Additionally, we highlight the scalability and security implications of using open-source components in automated framework setups. A survey among 300 developers further sheds light on the interest developers have in automated framework setup tools. A discussion on potential pitfalls, along with a research roadmap for automated framework setup, is also presented. A working prototype of our tool is made available for download, along with a demonstration of a PySpring setup. For the Dyson Sphere, a massive structure enclosing a star to harness its energy, we examine the possibility of it existing in the form of a hollow shell. Assuming the shell is composed of refracting non-luminous material and maintains a temperature similar to that of the star, we perform a thermal analysis under the assumptions of local thermodynamic equilibrium and incident radiation's negligible impact on the system's temperature. We then derive radiative transfer equations applicable to this scenario and employ numerical modeling to simulate a black star system. Our findings show that an ideal Dyson Shell would appear as a dark object with a temperature comparable to that of the star, in contrast to the conventional view that it would emit vast amounts of energy. This interpretation has implications for detecting such a structure, as its dark appearance would make it more difficult to identify. We also explore the possibility of this shell hosting life and the associated optical signals, which would require additional energy and, hence, a different temperature distribution. The complexity of these systems demands a multidisciplinary approach, combining astrophysics, biophysics, and mathematical modeling. Ultimately, identifying a Dyson Shell relies on a deeper understanding of exotic star systems that support life and the optical signals such life forms would produce. We conclude that detecting a Dyson Shell is a critical problem in modern astrophysics and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). As such, radio and optical searches for Dyson Shells are essential areas of research in the search for life beyond Earth. Additionally, we propose that the search for extraterrestrial life should focus on a wider range of spectral types than previously considered. This entails expanding the search to all spectral types, including G-K main-sequence stars, as well as other candidates such as the Sun-like stars, blue and blue-white sub-dwarfs, and A-F sub-dwarfs. Moreover, we highlight the importance of selecting promising targets for radio and optical searches, as well as the need for further theoretical studies on the structures and temperature distributions of Dyson Shells. We propose a cutting-edge 3D scintillator sensor design that gathers comprehensive information about neutron interaction points, enabling the reconstruction of the scattering process and subsequent extraction of relevant physical properties. This new approach is being developed into a comprehensive database of neutron scattering cross-sections on carbon, incorporating data from ab initio simulations and a material model of 6H-SiC. In our previous research, we discovered that sticking probabilities increase with temperature on the surface of dust grains in protoplanetary discs, leading to accelerated growth of grains into larger bodies. This effect is most pronounced in the inner regions of the disc, where temperatures are highest. There, water molecules exhibit significant impact on the adhering surface at these temperatures, losing their volatile H atoms and becoming OH radicals that can attach to other grains. 

As the water molecules move further into the disc, they experience higher temperatures that cause the H atoms to re-evaporate, restoring the water molecules' original composition. This leads to an increase in the sticking probability of these water molecules with other water molecules, forming longer hydrogen bonds that can withstand higher temperatures.

However, in our current study, we discover that at temperatures above 1000 K, the water molecules undergo a more significant transformation, eventually losing their OH bonds as well. As a result, they can once again easily re-evaporate, losing their ability to adhere to other grains by means of hydrogen bonding. This has an accelerated effect in the inner regions of the disc, specifically in the hot spots near the disc's centre and in the areas closest to the star where temperatures exceed 1000 K.

In our previous research, we found that dust grains can grow into bodies large enough to generate electromagnetic interference even without the influence of planetary movements. Imitation learning has emerged as a prominent approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward task setup. Unlike optimization-based methods that can be complex to set up, imitation learning eliminates the need for explicitly modeling task constraints. However, current imitation learning methods for complex tasks like point-reaching and circle-drawing neglect nonlinear rigid constraints and often result in fierce competition between following the learned trajectory and meeting the end-effector position requirements. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel imitation learning framework that can handle complex tasks involving linear and nonlinear constraints. Our framework can also be used for evading barriers by incorporating penalty costs, learning from multi-threaded demonstrations that include desired trajectories, unconstrained trajectories, and forbidden regions. We test the performance of our framework on various tasks, including linear and nonlinear reaching tasks, as well as avoiding specific regions, and comparing it with state-of-the-art imitation learning methods. Our results demonstrate that our framework outperforms these methods and efficiently learns from compact, high-quality demonstrations. The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/robot-talk/EKMP. The paper also provides a clear derivation of the Jacobian matrix and discusses several possible extensions. We believe our work will serve as a ground for future research on imitation learning for complex robot tasks. Despite the advancements of robust optimization-based approaches for robot control, imitation learning remains a vital method due to its straightforward task setup. We have taken significant steps in developing an effective imitation learning framework that can handle complex tasks involving linear and nonlinear rigid constraints. As future work, we plan on integrating our framework with robust learning methods to handle noisy data and on extending it to multiple robots learning from each other. We have already initiated discussions with potential future collaborators on these topics. In the near future, we aim on testing our framework in real-world applications involving collaborative robots and examining its performance on even more complex tasks like drawing specific shapes. We have already identified a potential application in collaborative robot assembly tasks. We are also considering submitting an extended version of this work to a top-tier robotics conference. We have already started gathering data and writing an extended version of this paper. We are confident that our work will serve as a reference for future research on imitation learning for complex robot tasks. We have taken the first step in combining robust optimization-based approaches with imitation learning, and we are excited to see the future research that will arise from this. We have already initiated conversations with potential future collaborators, and we are optimistic that our work will result in successful applications of our framework in real-world robotics projects

A novel spin-singlet topological superfluid (TSF) is proposed in a model that incorporates Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a two-dimensional Rashba interaction in the presence of a suitable external magnetic field. This model, which is based on a Hubbard-like Hamiltonian with attractive interactions, has been investigated using a Monte Carlo simulation. The results show that the Rashba interaction and corresponding magnetic field induce a strong Rashba pairing tendency, leading to the creation of a spin-singlet TSF with nontrivial topology. Notably, the Rashba interaction can be used to tune the topological invariant, $ChI$, between 0 and 1. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Rashba interaction enhances the superfluid density, while also increasing the gap energy in proportion to its magnetic contribution. These features are further exemplified in real materials using the Rashba Hubbard model, where the Rashba interaction is represented by exchange interactions in a Rashba double-exchange model. The results of these calculations indicate that suitable doping levels in these materials can give rise to a spin-singlet TSF with nontrivial topology, characterized by zero energy pseudo-Gap, high superfluid density, and a significant Chern number. The mere existence of a spin-singlet TSF in these materials suggests that they possess a unique and versatile ground state that could potentially be manipulated to achieve both magnetic and electrical responses without the need for an external magnetic field. This, in turn, creates opportunities for the exploration of exotic superfluid phenomena in these materials through electrical transport rather than magnetic susceptibility. The results of these studies are further expected to lead to the identification of suitable materials that can host a spin-singlet TSF, a state that is both topologically nontrivial and superfluid. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R is sufficient if it reduces the number of points required to uniquely identify all vertices in G. The smallest number of points needed to achieve this minimum requirement is the graph's shortened metric dimension, denoted as sdim(G). In this study, we calculate the exact shortened metric dimension for specific graph types, including series graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and their respective sub-classes, and compare it to a previously proposed upper limit. Additionally, we introduce the concept of modified shortened metric dimension, which takes into account the maximum possible reduction, and provide a corresponding formula; however, no algorithm is available to calculate this dimension directly. To address this, we present a general formula and a corresponding proof for the original shortened metric dimension when a graph has at least as many vertices as the number of its unique equitable partitions. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting several open questions and potential areas for further research. For the case of complete bipartite graphs, we derive the shortened metric dimension formula, expressing it as the maximum number of distinct equitable partitions multiplied by two, minus one if this product yields a square number. Moreover, this result can achieve the upper limit defined by a previous theorem. This arrangement ensures that all pairs of vertices have a distinct distance. With this understanding, we can calculate the shortened metric dimension for any graph by analyzing its Wyatt counterpart. The serial dictatorship method ranks voters in a specific order and assigns the item to the first voter in this order who is willing to accept it. This method is known for its simplicity but lacks a clear theoretical basis. We investigate what improvements can be made to this method and identify two essential requirements: social welfare efficiency and fairness. From a social welfare perspective, the best variant is one that maximizes the overall ranking of assigned voters. However, this may lead to unfair outcomes. A more equitable approach would ensure that every voter has an equal chance of being assigned the item. We explore a wide range of variants and provide a framework for evaluating any serial dictatorship method. This framework is applicable to any ranking system and can be used to identify the most efficient and fair variant for a specific social welfare objective. We also discuss general fairness criteria that any serial dictatorship method should meet. These criteria are independent of the underlying ranking system and are therefore applicable to any serial dictatorship method. Additionally, we discuss alternative methods that generate multiple assignment outcomes, all of which satisfy the same fairness criteria. These methods are particularly useful when the assignment decision cannot be finalized and may need further review or negotiation. We refer to these methods as "efficient social welfare fronts". They have several attractive features, including the ability to balance different social welfare objectives and the capability to incorporate additional preferences, such as those related to the assignment process. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of these methods, along with theoretical guarantees and results from a crowd-sourced experiment involving over 500 participants. These findings provide valuable insights into the design of these methods and highlight the importance of conducting thorough experimentation involving a large and diverse group of participants. We also discuss potential extensions to our work, along with existing and potential alternative methods, and examine the general properties of serial dictatorship methods through the lens of graph theory. This includes a discussion on strategies for optimizing different social welfare objectives and the design of methods that can handle cyclic rankings. We explore the practical applications of our work, along with methods for scaling up evaluation and ranking multiple items. We also discuss the use of numerical optimization techniques for assigning multiple items and the design of methods that can handle a large number of voters. Additionally, we examine the theoretical guarantees of our methods, along with existing work on the efficiency of serial dictatorship methods. This includes a discussion on fairness, along with social welfare efficiency and other important criteria. We discuss the design of methods for assigning multiple items, along with existing and potential alternative methods. We explore the general properties of serial dictatorship methods, along with methods for assigning multiple items.

Every year in our solar system, hundreds of thousands of near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) pass close to Earth. Some NEAs are known to have companion asteroids, which can provide valuable insights into their formation and evolution. To increase detection rates of these binary asteroids, we've developed an efficient statistical approach to identify potential companions in images of NEAs taken by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope. By applying this method to extensive archives, we found 14 newly discovered companion asteroids and confirmed 27 existing binary asteroid relationships, including the satellite of the large asteroid (16) Psyche. Our research also produced a large dataset of potential companion candidates awaiting further confirmation, which can be verified through targeted observations or when the asteroids pass through a total solar eclipse. By exploring these binary asteroid systems, we gained insights into their orbital patterns, which in some cases appear more circular than expected, based on observations of the NEA and its potential companion in multiple epochs. Additionally, by linking our detections to NEAs with known taxonomic classifications, we found that binary asteroids involving a larger primary component are more likely to have an orbit that is circular, whereas smaller primary components are more likely to have an elliptical orbit. This preference for certain orbital configurations in binary asteroids could provide evidence for how these systems form and evolve over time. By studying these binary asteroids and their orbital patterns, we can gain a better understanding of how they were created and how they interact with each other. This knowledge is essential for predicting the motion of these asteroids, which are potentially hazardous to Earth in certain asteroid collision scenarios. Additionally, binary asteroids can affect each other through gravitational forces, causing one asteroid to collide with Earth if the other asteroid passes too close to our planet. Therefore, accurate predictions of these asteroid systems are crucial for protecting Earth from these small bodies in the solar system. In the future, the Pan-STARRS2 telescope will offer higher resolution images of these binary asteroids and their approach paths, providing even more detailed data on their orbital patterns, which can be used to validate our current findings and make even more precise predictions of these asteroids' motion. We've developed an innovative information-theoretic approach, tailored to handle image boundaries as valuable information sources. Our method leverages boundary-aware data generation and utilizes mutual information as an objective function, facilitating seamless segmentation. We've implemented a convolutional neural network-based boundary generator and integrated it with a conditional variational autoencoder. Our proposed framework, called ICME-NS, effectively handles boundary effects and promotes efficient, self-supervised segmentation. ICME-NS has been applied to myocardium segmentation from cardiac MRI images, with impressive results compared to state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised approaches. Interestingly, it's observed that certain models excel at detecting both gradual and abrupt changes in word meanings, while others perform well on specific types of changes alone.  This research not only breaks significant ground in the study of word sense evolution but also contributes a significant dataset and a set of effective detection models to the field. We provide a categorification of the extended affine Hecke algebra (EAHA) in the form of a degenerate higher Hecke algebra, specifically within the symplectic mapping class group of a torus of high genus. This connection is established by demonstrating that the EAHA can be derived from the Fock-Rosso-Kashnikov type decomposition of the singular cohomology of the torus's high-genus blowup. Furthermore, this relationship enables the generation of higher braid operators from the simplest generators, leading to an interpretation of the structure constants of the EAHA through geometric means. Additionally, this framework allows us to explore degenerate higher braid relations and their associated algebraic closures. Through this setup, we also demonstrate the presence of a nilpotent automorphism in the EAHA, resulting in its isomorphism to the tame Hecke algebra. Moreover, we establish that the algebraic closure of the degenerate higher Hecke algebra encompasses the tame Hecke algebra itself. Lastly, we investigate the relationship between the symplectic mapping class group of a torus's high-genus blowup and the affine Hecke algebra, particularly considering the algebra's representation through its action on the cohomology of the blowup's boundary. This representation serves as the source of the name "extended affine Hecke algebra," despite not being a true extension of the affine Hecke algebra in the classical sense. Instead, it is an autonomous algebra with its own nilpotent element, separate from the affine Hecke algebra's own nilpotent element. This distinction holds for both the EAHA and its algebraic closure. Moreover, we establish that the EAHA's algebraic closure can be viewed as the algebra of the symplectic mapping class group of the torus's high-genus blowup mod its center, providing a direct connection between their structural properties. This relationship is further confirmed by the geometric derivation of both the EAHA and its algebraic closure, stemming from the inherent symplectic properties of the torus itself. In contrast, the affine Hecke algebra and its algebraic closure originate from the combination of the torus's symplectic properties and its embedding in the genus-zero manifold. This combined framework results in the algebra's center being isomorphic to the lattice of the affine Hecke algebra itself, a fact that can be deduced either geometrically or algebraically. In this study, we examine the irregular Nambu-Goldstone (NG) modes found in quantum systems that break a SU(N) global symmetry. These models can be either relativistic or nonrelativistic in nature. We demonstrate that the odd components of the NG modes, resulting from the spontaneous symmetry breaking of a global SU(N) symmetry, possess non-zero masses, in contrast to the even components which remain massless. This phenomenon is universal, applying to all quantum systems described by either the chiral perturbation or the Wess-Zumino-Witten theories. Furthermore, we show that the mass matrices of the odd components can be expressed in a simple form, displaying their general structure which is a consequence of the low-energy properties of these systems. We discuss the implications of this analysis for the masses of the odd components, stating that at very low energies, these masses can be approximated by a specific quadratic form that directly relates to the Lagrangian density of the underlying theory. Additionally, we explore the dimensionality of the ground state manifold and its associated spin transverse to the NG modes, establishing a more general framework that is independent of the specific system under consideration. This framework enables us to pinpoint the origin of the mass splitting between the even and odd components of the NG modes. We also present a new, more intuitive explanation for this mass splitting, which is essentially driven by the decay constants of the NG modes. This decay constant, in turn, is an intrinsic property of the underlying theory and is a consequence of the global symmetry breaking. It holds the key to understanding the irregular NG phenomenon observed in certain quantum systems. It is interesting to note that the models we analyze here, describing physics related to irregular NG phenomena, can be applied to a broader class of theories that include certain supersymmetric theories. The co-rotation regime of an ideal polymer-based injection system consists of alternating polymer domes and nearly solid'slugs'. To determine the stability of this configuration, we examine the possible two-dimensional patterns of a single slug in the limiting case where the slug's molecular weight is infinitely high. By applying a modified version of the Ginzburg-Landau equation that accounts for viscoelastic effects, we find that the slugs' borders will exhibit oscillatory behavior. This leads to the emergence of periodic patterns in a two-dimensional cell analogous to those seen in Rayleigh-B\'enard convection. Leverage is taken from the simplicity of this scenario to propose a new instability criterion for the co-rotation regime, which suggests that the onset of elastic effects will significantly impact the polymer's heat transfer performance. This is further investigated through numerical simulations of a single dome and a mixed dome-slug cell using a non-Newtonian heat transfer model. The results of these simulations are presented in a map illustrating the various possible patterns that may arise within the ideal polymer system. This work provides a theoretical foundation for studying the dynamics of more complex polymer-based multiphase systems. By applying this knowledge to such systems, it may be possible to optimize their performance through appropriate choice of operating conditions or material properties. Additionally, this research offers a pathway for investigating other viscous fluid-based systems through the use of a modified Ginzburg-Landau approach. This strategy enables the direct application of established techniques from nonlinear dynamics and bifurcation theory to the study of complex fluid dynamics. If we assume that the vector bosons are primarily composed of light unobservable components, the irregularities in the data can be seen as evidence of a mass gap in the range of 250-700 GeV in the quark-scalar sector. If we consider a scenario where the vector bosons are largely made up of dark matter, the data's irregularities can be used to set limits on the quark pair's decay width, ultimately leading to constraints on the vector bosons' masses and widths. If at least one star in the binary has a significant spin or the orbit is highly elliptical, a specific irregularity appears in the gravitational wave signal. We examine an accelerated version of the ASEP system from a dynamical perspective, focusing on velocity variations which result in ASEP particles moving at different speeds. This accelerated model maintains exact equivalence to a system where ASEP particles interact with additional "half-particles" in a way that resembles the ASEP's own equilibrium behavior. Additionally, we observe that in cases where all ASEP particles have the same speed, the accelerated model is equivalent to a system of "half-particles" that are all bound together. This equivalence gives rise to specific insights into the behavior of ASEP velocity variations, particularly in relation to TASEP and ASEP systems with obstacles. Building upon this understanding, we are also able to identify some of the accelerated model's space-time forgetting rates. Just as in the standard ASEP, we find that in cases where all ASEP particles have the same speed, the system's macroscopic speed can be either stuck at a lower rate or asymptotically approach the fastest possible rate. Notably, in scenarios where all ASEP particles have the same speed, we are also able to precisely determine the system's final density distribution. This knowledge extends our current understanding of the ASEP's own velocity variations, particularly in cases where the acceleration procedure results in ASEP particles moving at different speeds. In such scenarios, we are able to identify some, but not all, of the system's final density distribution components. Ultimately, our research provides a formal definition of a system's "equilibrium velocity distribution", which gives rise to many of the ASEP's own velocity variations. This definition leverages the accelerated model's properties in a way that pins down some, but not all, of the system's final density distribution components. This new definition also arises from considering the accelerated model's own variations, which are governed by a system of "twisted interactions" that are analogous to the standard ASEP's own interactions. This understanding is expected to provide a foundation for addressing many of the open questions that currently surround the ASEP's own velocity variations. In the context of TASEP, we are also able to identify some, but not all, of the system's final velocity distribution components for cases where the rate of the leftmost TASEP step is less than one. This understanding is anticipated to provide a starting point for exploring other systems that feature time-point variations in a way that is analogous to the standard ASEP. Various mathematical models have been developed to analyze dynamic systems across multiple fields, and compartment models have been particularly effective in studying disease epidemics. We've examined recent SARS-CoV-2 pandemic modeling using a range of compartment models, highlighting their differences and highlighting the need for models to address several critical factors including varying levels of infection asymmetry, the impact of immunity on disease severity, and the effects of immunity on infection likelihood. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of using daily change rates and alternative methods of modeling temporal changes. Finally, we discuss the importance of combining mathematical models with empirical data, reporting on recent CoDa analysis of time series data and the implications this has for modeling the ongoing pandemic. We also explore potential methods for modeling systemic changes, such as using state-space models or generalized linear mixed models, and consider the potential for transmission models to be informed by time series data analysis. We conclude that compartment models remain a valuable tool for understanding and managing the spread of disease, and that further research is needed to address the complexities of infectious disease transmission dynamics. This involves a deeper exploration of how to model non-linear change rates, accounting for the effects of immunity on infection likelihood and disease severity, infection asymmetry, and how to integrate statistical analysis of time series data into transmission models. This would provide a robust framework for addressing these issues, one that could be applied not only to the ongoing pandemic but also to future infectious disease outbreaks. These surfaces have unique properties that make them immune to non-singular crossings in momentum space and allow for highly tunable magnetic responses in paramagnetic materials. Doctors typically employ two methods to diagnose brain tumors: segmentation (identifying the tumor) and classification (determining the tumor type). To address this challenge, this paper introduces the Multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net), an attention-based model that simultaneously performs brain tumor segmentation and classification. By incorporating a directed attention mechanism, MAG-Net is able to direct attention to areas most relevant for both tasks, improving both delineation and categorization of brain tumors. A directed attention mechanism can be incorporated into both encoder and decoder components of the model, allowing for the sharing of attention information between tasks. Experimental results on the BrainMRI dataset demonstrate MAG-Net's ability to accurately classify and outline brain tumors. Compared to baseline multi-task models, MAG-Net exhibits improved performance on both segmentation and classification tasks. A further analysis of the model's intermediate outputs offers valuable insights into tumor classification processes. To facilitate further research, this paper provides comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analyses of model predictions against ground truth annotations. High-definition video delivery relies on interlacing to minimize data transfer needs, but this technique requires precise deinterlacing to restore the full HD video. Unfortunately, common deinterlacing methods, such as simple average and lateral line average, can distort the video and leave artifacts. To effectively address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel deep learning approach that utilizes convolutional neural networks to deinterlace video in real-time. By using a single input frame, this method avoids the need for additional video data, making it suitable for applications involving low-quality video captures or streaming from old equipment. Moreover, this approach displays excellent performance compared to existing deinterlacing techniques, as demonstrated by comprehensive evaluation results. In particular, this method exhibits superior performance on account of its minimal memory requirements, real-time processing speed, and exceptional deinterlacing quality. To facilitate further research, this paper also provides an open-source deinterlacing benchmark that can run on both Linux and Windows platforms. With its outstanding performance and flexible architecture, this deep learning deinterlacing model is adaptable to a wide range of applications, from live video deinterlacing to post-production editing. Furthermore, this approach can be easily extended to handle 3D video deinterlacing and video enhancement tasks. To further enhance its performance, this model has been found to benefit from additional training using motion analysis and video preprocessing techniques. By optimizing memory usage and model size, this paper also presents a memory-optimized variant of this deep learning deinterlacing model. This optimized model achieves comparable performance to other state-of-the-art deep learning deinterlacing approaches while requiring significantly less memory. Notably, this optimized model uses approximately 1.5GB of memory, making it one of the lightest deep learning models across multiple benchmarks. With its exceptional performance, this optimized model is highly suitable for real-time live video deinterlacing applications on mid-range and high-end hardware. In contrast to previous deep learning deinterlacing approaches that rely on super-resolution and multi-field methods, this paper presents a pioneering model that directly addresses real-time live video deinterlacing using a single input frame. This optimized model has been thoroughly evaluated and shows superior performance compared to all existing deep learning deinterlacing approaches. Recent studies suggest that users of encryption systems are not adequately protected due to the increasing computational power of hash functions used for password verification. While this concern has sparked interest in post-quantum cryptography, a different security issue often goes unaddressed - the misinterpretation of security indicators, which can lead users to incorrectly assume their data is encrypted. This phenomenon is particularly common among non-technical users who rely heavily on visual cues and are prone to common psychological pitfalls such as confirmation bias. To gauge the prevalence of this issue, we conducted a survey among a diverse group of everyday individuals using various encryption applications. Our findings revealed that a significant number of users are not aware of potential attacks and have unrealistic expectations about the security of their data, underscoring the need for clear and accurate information to be provided to users through effective user experience design. To address this issue, we propose a new framework for evaluating the user-centered security of encryption applications and apply it to identify weaknesses in several popular products. Our study serves as a call to action for the encryption community to prioritize user experience and safety education to mitigate these vulnerabilities. By doing so, we can minimize the risks to users even if their data is compromised due to weaknesses in encryption or hash functions. Additionally, we believe this study contributes a user-centered security framework that other community projects can build upon. With user-centered design at the forefront, we can ensure the ongoing security and trustworthiness of encryption applications for all users. Furthermore, this study also highlights potential research opportunities for our community to explore more abstract concepts such as how users perceive security levels, or what influence lifestyle factors have on users' security-related decisions. We hope this study paves the way for future work in this area, and we are more than happy to collaborate with other community projects that may choose to build upon this study. We've developed L2Explorer, an open-source evaluation platform for continuous reinforcement learning challenges, addressing a critical need in the field. Many significant tasks, such as robotics and game scenarios, require persistent learning from ongoing interactions with dynamic environments that reward agents indefinitely. However, existing methods often ignore critical aspects like variable reward scales, sparse rewards, and dynamics changes. To tackle this, we've created a comprehensive evaluation framework that incorporates multiple metrics and visualization tools to assess key aspects of agent performance. Our platform is highly adaptable, suitable for both individual and collective evaluation of agents in multiple environments, and is designed for infinite data storage, streamlining the refinement of agent behavior through continuous learning and evaluation. L2Explorer is an open-source project available on GitHub at https://github.com/BU-AILab/L2Explorer. Humans exhibit a unique ability to reflect on their past mistakes, incorporating a self-critical assessment that often precipitates a decline in future transgressions. However, this framework is typically solved using a numerical method that relies on a flawed assumption, which needs reevaluation using a more precise, Monte Carlo-style computation. Nonetheless, this framework still offers an intriguing, albeit incomplete, explanation for many flavor phenomena in the Standard Model and its extensions. The rapid growth of remote work forced many employees to rely heavily on insecure public Wi-Fi networks. A survey was conducted to evaluate the security measures of employees using their personal devices for work. The survey showed that although employees were aware of basic security best practices, they failed to implement them properly. As the shift to remote work is likely to continue, it is essential that employers refresh their employees on secure work protocols. This paper provides a scorecard for assessing an organization's remote work security policy. This scorecard evaluates the protocol's coverage, complexity, and effectiveness, helping to identify potential vulnerabilities and areas for improvement. To this end, we also introduce a novel method for formally verifying the correctness of a protocol by model-checking. This technique can be used to check a protocol's correctness locally, without divulging sensitive information. We apply this method to evaluate the security of a protocol designed for image processing tasks. This protocol ensures secure coordination of distributed computers, or "astrobots," by verifying the correctness of each computer's work locally. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by analyzing a real-world protocol for image processing. This method and the scorecard can be used to evaluate the security of other distributed work protocols as well. We also introduce an open-source tool for verifying the correctness of protocols and discuss its performance. This paper provides a security assessment of the SDSS-V protocol, which is a distributed system for detecting variable stars. We outline several vulnerabilities in this protocol and propose solutions to address them. We also discuss the results of our study with the developer team of this protocol. These graphs are part of a twisted variant and exhibit chordal connectivity. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. We investigated how a third generation of active neutrinos and a specific $f(R)$ gravity model affect the turn-around radii of dark matter structures, typically assumed to be unchanged for dark matter components. By examining six different $f(R)$ gravity configurations and a range of neutrino masses from 45 keV to 2.5 GeV, we discovered that both neutrinos and $f(R)$ gravity have a significant impact on the universal turn-around radii of dark matter structures. The effects vary depending on the density threshold, ranging from only 9% to as much as 50% in influence. These effects also become more pronounced in regions with lower density. We found that in some cases, the $f(R)$ gravity's influence on the turn-around radii could actually outweigh that of massive neutrinos. This paper aims to find the strongest shortest path cover for graphs that are commonly used, including trees, planar graphs, and hypercubes. Additionally, it explores the minimum number of strong shortest path covers in these graphs and presents a 3-k stronger variant of the 2-center problem, before focusing on the minimum strong shortest route cover in specific graphs. Specifically, it finds the minimum strong shortest path cover for particular trees, planar graphs with a certain structure, and some hypercubes, but doesn't have a general formula for all trees or planar graphs. It uses a polynomial-time algorithm to find the minimum strong shortest path cover for some trees and planar graphs, while leaving the question of whether such covers can be found non-constructively for all trees and planar graphs open. It also introduces the k-strong shortest route cover for graphs and raises further research questions on the topic. This study examines the amphibian model, a random graph process where islands represent nodes in a tree-like structure, and the density of connections between them is variable. Specifically, we focus on the critical point at which the largest island spans the entire graph. Notably, this critical point is inherently defined by the specific structure of the tree. As the tree's degree increases, the density required to isolate a single node naturally decreases, eventually reaching a minimum where the node is no longer isolated. We demonstrate that this natural decrease in required density is exactly equivalent to the critical point of a random graph in a specific degree distribution. We use this understanding to place the amphibian model's critical point within the broader context of random graph theory. Finally, we explore some open questions related to the amphibian model. Additionally, we correct an existing heuristic for the critical point and provide a more accurate method for calculating it. This correction applies specifically to the case where the tree has a degree that varies according to a power law with an exponential cutoff. We use this opportunity to introduce a new heuristic for this specific case and demonstrate its effectiveness through both theoretical proof and empirical testing. This new heuristic provides a more precise estimate of the critical point, especially for large values of the exponential cutoff. However, it is worth noting that this improved accuracy comes at a higher computational cost compared to a simpler alternative. We also use this analysis to derive a new conjecture regarding the behavior of the largest component in a random graph when the degree distribution follows a power-law with an exponential cutoff, particularly in relation to a specific critical point. We demonstrate that this conjecture holds true for both trees and graphs, using both theoretical proof and empirical testing. This analysis provides a more precise method for calculating the largest component in a random graph when the degree distribution follows a power-law with an exponential cutoff, especially for large values of the exponential cutoff. This understanding has implications for our previous research on the amphibian model, specifically in relation to a specific component of the model. Imitation learning achieves high performance on limited data, yet its potential is hindered by poorly labeled examples. To begin with, human supervisors often struggle to create precise demonstrations due to their own limitations. Moreover, existing imitation learning methods fail to effectively utilize contextual information present in auxiliary attributes associated with demonstrations. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Context-Aware Trajectory Refinement And Label Correction (TRAIL), a two-stage framework that combines imitation learning with supervised learning to process attribute-based feedback from human teachers. Specifically, TRAIL uses contextual information to guide a latent optimization process that generates high-quality states for the policy to learn from. Moreover, a label correction module leverages attribute-based data to refine the policy's behavior across different contextual settings. Experimental results on three diverse games - Navipilot, CarRacing, and Locomotion - consistently show that TRAIL achieves close-to-ideal performance using only a small set of high-quality demonstrations and additional context-conditional data with potential errors. Notably, our work offers actionable insights on strengthening traditional imitation learning through the effective utilization of contextual information and human feedback. Instead, our proposed framework allows robots to learn from each other's experiences, eliminating the need for individual demonstrations. In co-observation learning, one "expert" robot successfully completes a task, and its counterparts "observe" its performance. In contrast to traditional social learning, which relies on the expert's intentional actions, our approach leverages machine learning techniques to capture both the expert's intentions and accidental observations. We demonstrate a specific application of our framework with multiple navigation agents, where some agents serve as experts, and the others learn from their behavior. Our results show that our approach successfully enables agent exchange benefits without requiring specialized demonstrations. Additionally, we explore how the number of expert observers influences task success and find that our method effectively facilitates learning with just one expert observer. Our work targets collaborative tasks that are naturally symmetrical, such as achieving a common goal or navigating to a shared target. In contrast, tasks that are inherently asymmetrical, like pushing a ball into a goal, may not be naturally facilitated by our approach. Therefore, we introduce a novel method that introduces a virtual agent to represent the external environment, enabling both natural temporal logic-based action reasoning and safe policy transfer between observed expert behavior. This method successfully enables agent exchange benefits for asymmetrical collaborative tasks. In addition to pushing a ball into a goal, our results show that our approach also successfully facilitates agent exchange benefits for other asymmetrical tasks, including placing an object in a target location and arranging objects in a specific order. Notably, our approach achieves comparable or better performance compared to demonstration-based methods in all evaluated tasks. Moreover, our method is highly adaptable to various task modifications, outperforming demonstration-based methods by a significant margin. In particular, our approach excels in tasks with a high degree of spatial complexity, such as arranging objects in a specific order. Nevertheless, the application of this operator leads to distinct modes of the Laplace-Beltrami equation. We also identify how the biharmonic hypersurfaces with the recurring operators P appear, specifically when they occur within the Euclidean space. Notably, we find that these hypersurfaces will minimize, solve, or stabilize under the Euclidean operator P, similar to how they do with the other established operators. We also establish that these hypersurfaces will solve the Laplace-Beltrami equation with a specific potential when the Euclidean operator P is applied. We conclude by examining how these hypersurfaces will appear when the Euclidean operator P is applied repeatedly, which results in solutions to the Laplace-Beltrami equation with increasing degrees of differentiation. We provide specific examples of biharmonic hypersurfaces with the recurring operators P when it is applied in an even or odd number of times. We conclude by highlighting the numerous outstanding problems within this field that await solution. In contrast to common applications of CNNs, where images are treated as self-contained pieces of information, medical image analysis often requires combining adjacent image slices to achieve accurate diagnosis. This problem is particularly challenging due to the inherent variations that can exist between slices. To address this, we propose a novel 4D image recognition approach based on edge-gated layers, which leverages external information from neighboring slices by adjusting the layer's functionality. Our model builds upon this concept, incorporating an edge-gated layer that is designed to blend internal and external visual data. This architecture is specifically optimized for 3D semantic segmentation tasks and is mathematically defined as a layer that computes the weighted average of two operations: the primary operation on internal data and a secondary operation on external data. This layer is then applied to 3D data in an unsampled fashion. We applied our proposed architecture in two medical image analysis scenarios: pupil detection in 3D OCT images and cardiovascular MR image segmentation. Our results show that our edge-gated layer consistently outperforms the equivalent standard layer. We also conducted a thorough sensitivity analysis of our model, publishing the results of our experiments across multiple scenarios. These experiments highlighted the significant impact of the layer's parameter, which models the data's internal and external relationships, on the model's performance. To facilitate reproduction of our findings, we made all experiments fully reproducible by openly sharing our code. Despite its effectiveness, our model has a considerable increase in parameters compared to the standard layer, which could impede its application to image recognition tasks involving large datasets. To address this limitation, we explored a compressed version of the edge-gated layer, verifying that it is feasible to achieve high accuracy with a relatively small number of parameters. This achievement paves the way for potential applications of our model in large-scale medical image analysis problems. To facilitate easy integration of the edge-gated layer into existing frameworks, we released an open-source implementation of the proposed architecture. This implementation is built on top of the popular PyTorch library and is easily adaptable for use in other deep learning frameworks. We also contributed a new challenge dataset for pupil detection in 3D OCT images, along with detailed evaluation guidelines and a comprehensive report highlighting our results. This dataset, combined with our open-source implementation and the findings of our experiments, will enable further exploration of edge-gated networks in the context of medical image analysis. Occasionally, the solar breeze is strong enough to prevent the solar wind from gaining speed beyond a certain point, and in these cases, the wind speed in the outer heliosphere is found to be slower than anticipated. This finding has implications for how the solar breeze is modeled, and it highlights the importance of incorporating observations from the inner heliosphere in developing these models. Developing speech-based emotion recognition systems is complicated due to the limited availability of annotated data, differing emotion recognition standards, and the need for systems to adapt across various domains. A major challenge lies in creating systems that can effectively recognize emotions in real-time conversations across multiple domains. To tackle these issues, this paper presents a novel deep reinforcement learning-based approach that combines a neural network named Convolutional Neural Hypergraph (CNH) for emotion recognition and a multi-domain adapting algorithm called Dynamic Inter Domain Adaptation (DIADA). CNH uses a hypergraph convolutional neural network (HCNN) model to identify emotions from speech signals. However, these models typically struggle with overfitting and have limited generalizability across different domains. Our proposed DIADA method leverages a non-stationary target distribution to adapt the training data and switch between different domains. By continuously updating the hypergraph structure based on adaptability, HCNN can effectively recognize emotions in real-time conversations across multiple domains. Our experimental evaluations on the widely used SEMAINE and SAVEE emotion recognition datasets have shown promising results for both single and multi-domain adaptation scenarios. Our proposed approach outperforms multiple deep learning-based models, demonstrating the superiority of our DIADA method in adapting HCNN for speech emotion recognition. The emergence of advanced computational models has significantly improved our understanding of fundamental phenomena, enabling precise predictions and pinpoint measurements. Despite this progress, many complex systems still pose challenges for a comprehensive theoretical description. In such cases, empirical models, often based on practical observations, have provided valuable insights in the past. A notable example from the 1950s involves the empirical description of magnetic recording on disk drives, specifically the noise observed under high-speed readout systems. In this report, we revisit this historical episode from the world of computational modeling, where the efforts of physicists in the 1950s-1960s are highlighted in developing a noise model that effectively explained recording limitations and later became a cornerstone for modern signal processing. This historical account serves as an accessible introduction to the fundamental problems associated with modeling real-world systems and the importance of empirical descriptions in the absence of a theoretical framework. It is intended as a primer for students and a historical review for experts in the field. The simple models presented can be readily understood through basic computational simulations, making this an ideal topic for teaching the basics of computational thinking. The models considered here are also relevant to today's research in the study of complex systems across multiple disciplines. The issues faced by physicists in the past, such as the slowing of relaxation in real-time experiments, the onset of turbulence in fluid dynamics, and the erratic fluctuations in financial markets, remain just as pressing today. The development of supercomputing power has given way to numerical simulations, rendering analytical solutions often sufficient. However, there are instances where a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics cannot be derived from simulations or empirical models alone. In such cases, a new theoretical framework is necessary to provide a comprehensive description of the problem, thereby revitalizing research in the field. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using recent LHC jet data, specifically focusing on measurements from JADE and ATLAS studies spanning various energy scales. As nuclear PDFs play a crucial role in these interpretations, our analysis also evaluates the impact of different nuclear PDF sets on results. Furthermore, since thermal initial-state effects are influenceable through nuclear PDF choices, our analysis aims to minimize thermal impact by selecting parameters that balance jet scale and nuclear PDF influences. We selected a medium-modified jet spectrum model based on the Bertsch-Gyulassy-McLain form, considering three distinct scales corresponding to the LHC energy range. We examine the accuracy of first-principles tight-binding models used to simulate electron-photon interactions in photonic devices, specifically testing their measure-invariant properties. To achieve this, we apply multiple independent unitary transformations to the models, eliminating any accidental symmetries. Our analysis focuses on a tight-binding model describing interactions between electrons and electromagnetic fields in a honeycomb lattice with a honeycomb optical cavity. We utilized both a minimal two-band model and a larger model representing valence and conduction bands in graphene. Our results show that the electron-photon matrix elements can vary significantly depending on the choice of tight-binding model and representation, even if the two models have the same equilibrium lattice parameters. Consequently, this highlights the importance of conducting an in-depth analysis before applying a tight-binding model, particularly those involving light-matter interactions, where simple intuitive descriptions may no longer be sufficient. Our study offers a thorough examination of the reliability of first-principles tight-binding models used to design photonic transitions in solids and suggests that more precise models are needed to accurately predict electron-photon interactions. Additionally, we discuss an open issue regarding the choice of suitable tight-binding models that could describe interband light-matter interactions in solids. Our research was published in a recent issue of Physical Review B. Our findings also demonstrate that time-reversal symmetry plays a crucial role in determining the accuracy of these models, similar to how it does in other cases. To achieve accurate descriptions of electron-photon interactions, it is essential to select a tight-binding model that properly retains time-reversal symmetry. We have made our numerical codes for evaluating time-reversal symmetry in tight-binding models publicly available upon request. These models can be utilized to analyze a plethora of light-matter interactions in solids, encompassing phenomena like the generation of DC fields, creation of a persistent electric current, and optical transitions mediated by a magnetic field. Nonetheless, it is crucial to validate the accuracy of these models through a thorough analysis, as their descriptions of interactions can vary significantly based on the chosen representation. Nonetheless, these models remain a vital tool for the investigation of time-and momentum-resolved light-matter interactions in solids. A massive explosion from the star AD Leo in 1985 April 12th was studied using computer simulations.  White-light observations from the IUE satellite were analyzed with a technique called maximum entropy method to model the extreme brightness increase of more than 1000 times the pre-eruption level.  The simulations suggested the eruption was powered by a shock wave propelled by mass ejections and moving at a significant portion of the speed of light.  Additionally, the existence of a highly energetic and massive low-velocity shock front was discovered along with evidence suggesting it interacted with the star's accretion disk, potentially triggering the massive eruption.  The models also provided insights into the behavior of the stellar magnetic field during the eruption.  A comparison with optical observations in broad and high-dispersion spectra suggested the presence of multiple interacting shock fronts and the existence of localized magnetic field increases, which could offer an explanation for the temporary formations of magnetic loops often seen in this star's activity fluctuations.  The models also predicted further interactions between the star's accretion disk and the magnetic field, including the possibility of additional eruptions or flares from this and other active close-by stars.  The models were subsequently used to develop a predictive mathematical framework for white-light observations of stellar eruptions in broad spectra.  This new approach was successfully applied to model another massive explosion from AD Leo in 1994 October 1st.  The models indicated a much weaker shock front in this second event and it was found to be a more internal magnetic explosion likely triggered by the interaction of mass ejections with the star's magnetic field.  It was also discovered that this type of event can produce significant optical continuum increases undetected by broad spectra.  The models were further used to study another massive explosion from this star in 2003 June 11th and it was found that it shared many characteristics with the 1985 April 12th event, suggesting that it was also a shock front propelled by mass ejections. This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's transmitting properties uses mathematical models to predict transmission patterns in both periodic and isolated units.  A new concept, "bidirectional clarity," is defined to measure the clarity of transmission and contrasted with the PT-symmetric phase's behavior.  Our findings show that bidirectional clarity is unaffected by phase transitions in periodic units, while in isolated units it can achieve perfect values, representing undistorted wave transmission.  We term this as "coherent flawless absorption-lasing," a phenomenon where PT-symmetric phase transitions are prevented, and we validate our results with numerical simulations using the Helmholtz equation.  This research provides a mathematical foundation for analyzing PT-symmetric waveguide networks and their transmitting properties.  Finally, potential applications and future directions for PT-symmetric optics are discussed.  We introduce the concept of "coherent flawless absorption-lasing" (CFAL) based on a bidirectional clarity model, which contrasts with the behavior of PT-symmetric phase transitions.  Our CFAL model includes equations that describe time and space coherence in PT-symmetric waveguide networks, and we analyze a new property called bidirectional clarity.  While coherence is affected by phase transitions in PT-symmetric systems, our findings show that bidirectional clarity remains unchanged with such transitions.  In contrast, coherence is influenced by phase transitions in PT-symmetric systems, and our findings indicate that bidirectional clarity remains constant across these transitions.  Our research provides a foundation for studying the behavior of light in PT-symmetric optics through a new framework, and we discuss potential applications and future directions for this field. We study the performance and structure of a complex system that consists of multiple inter-connected nodes, where each node represents a simple logical element that produces an output based on the sum of its inputs. This system maintains its own internal state through multi-node interactions, a characteristic that differentiates it from traditional neural networks. Observing how this system evolves over time provides valuable insights, specifically in regards to the critical point at which a memory storage capacity is achieved, as well as the distribution of error rates across different temporal steps. These insights reveal that certain spatial and temporal patterns are fundamental to the functioning of this system, and that they arise necessarily as a result of the system's design. Furthermore, modifying certain aspects of the system's architecture can lead to a significant increase in its capacity for storing information over time, a phenomenon that arises independently of the specific error rates of the system's components. This conceptual network serves as a metaphor for understanding the functioning of biological systems that the mind interprets as intentional movements. This understanding has implications for optimizing the system's performance, especially when it is subjected to external influences that cause temporary fluctuations in the system's state. This paper focuses on an unexplored phase of the system's dynamics, specifically the phase in which the system is capable of storing information over time, and identifies the underlying structural features that generate the temporal patterns that the mind perceives as causal relationships between movements. This analysis provides a framework for addressing a more complex question about the system, namely how it processes multiple simultaneous inputs that are received at different points in time. This question is relevant because it is equivalent to the mind's question of how it perceives the system's output as a continuous causal sequence of movements from a discrete memory storage. This paper concludes by highlighting the limitations of the research and the potential for further exploration of the system's dynamics.
