We establish a general matrix representation for both one-body and two-body operators that can be applied to any multi-quasiparticle Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions. This formulation facilitates the computation of matrix elements among various Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov states, including those involving angular momentum and parity symmetries. A numerical example highlights the usefulness of this approach in estimating expectation values of physical operators within multi-quasiparticle Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov states. Furthermore, we show that our method enables the identification of quasiparticle combinations that yield non-vanishing matrix elements, enabling the selection of relevant configurations for irreducible matrix elements. This allows for the efficient calculation of physical properties across diverse Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov states. A numerical example demonstrates the utility of this strategy in optimizing the estimation of binding energies through configuration mixing. This development is particularly valuable for incorporating experimental constraints via quasiparticle tunneling processes in dense angular momentum landscapes. Additionally, we reveal that our approach can be applied to describe two-body decay processes involving quasiparticle combinations similar to those underlying electron capture processes. This includes the selection of relevant angular momentum and quasiparticle configurations which influence the decay probabilities and spectra. This formulation is also shown to enable the investigation of two-body decay processes in odd-A and even-A nuclei, which often exhibit multi-quasiparticle Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave function structures. A numerical example is presented for the decay of $^{56}$Ni into various quasiparticle combinations and their corresponding peaks in energy spectra. This research provides a theoretical framework for the investigation of two-body decay processes which can be applied to a wide range of nuclei. This includes not just odd-A and even-A nuclei but also those that are unstable, making it a valuable tool for research in nuclear physics. This framework can be used to study the decay of initial quasiparticle states composed of multiple angular momentum and particle combinations. Additionally, it offers a way to examine the distribution of strength in the angular momentum and particle degrees of freedom. This can be accomplished by either directly computing the decay width of a specific quasiparticle state or by first determining the quasiparticle densities of the initial and final states and then utilizing these densities to calculate the decay width. This study also provides a theoretical description of the decay process, showing that the width of the peak in the energy spectrum is a measure of the overlap between the initial and final quasiparticle

Three-dimensional (3D) detection networks, using point clouds, often employ transformation-based descriptors like Feature Transform (FT) and Sparse Transformation (ST), which we found to be prone to over-smoothing due to repeated transformations, resulting in diminished descriptor efficiency. To address this, we introduced a novel framework called Transformation-Dependent Smoothing (TDS) that selectively regulates the smoothing process based on the type of transformation. Specifically, we developed a dynamic soft-parameter mechanism that adjusts the smoothing filter based on the feature transformation matrix, providing an efficient way to manage excessive smoothing. Moreover, our method enables the incorporation of previous knowledge into the network by choosing appropriate transformations and corresponding smoothing parameters, thereby improving training data efficiency. A thorough evaluation of our approach was conducted across multiple 3D detection benchmarks, demonstrating substantial performance gains of up to 5.4% mAP improvement compared to the existing FT baseline. The source code of our method has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/STDCU/TPC. Leveraging our approach, we introduced a new state-of-the-art model called TPC, achieving an impressive mAP of 52.5% on the CHAILLON dataset, a 5.4% increase over the current record, and outperforming all existing methods on the SUNRGB-D dataset with a 6.5% mAP improvement. Moreover, our method exhibits superior real-time performance, surpassing conventional 3D detection frameworks by achieving 50 frames per second (FPS) on a single GPU. This advancement paves the way for real-time 3D detection applications on multiple GPUs. A 45.6% mAP improvement was also observed on the real-world dataset, setting a new benchmark for future 3D detection algorithms. In addition to boosting detection performance, our approach facilitates explicit regularization that can be employed as a recovery mechanism for recovering lost information during excessive smoothing, enriching the point cloud representation. This enriched representation has been successfully applied to various follow-up tasks, such as tracking and semantic segmentation, by simply integrating our method into the network. The effectiveness of this method was verified across multiple 3D detection and tracking benchmarks, resulting in up to 6.6% mAP improvement on the CHAILLON dataset and a 6.8% mean overlap increase on the SUNRGB-D dataset. The superior performance of our method is attributed to its unique dynamic soft-parameter mechanism that chooses appropriate transformations and corresponding smoothing parameters, leading to a more efficient and balanced distribution of the gradient

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols in this context. Our analysis of ALOHA includes a new on-demand protocol and a previously studied slotted ALOHA design. For CSMA, we examine a non-coherent method and a complex coherent approach. However, successful applications of GANs in discrete data generation, specifically text creation, remain limited due to difficulties in training a well-performed generator model. One key challenge lies in the text generation process itself, which involves selecting one word at a time from an extensive vocabulary, making it a complex sequential problem. Current GAN-based text generation approaches typically employ a single opponent model that produces a full sentence, but this can hinder the performance of the generator model. To address these issues, we propose a novel sparse GAN framework, SparseGAN, which utilizes an opponent model that generates one word at a time to facilitate training and improve the efficiency of both the generator and opponent models. To overcome the challenge of generating a diverse range of texts, we introduce a novel sampling strategy that leverages the predicted probability of each word by the opponent model. Our experimental evaluations on multiple text generation datasets demonstrate the enhanced performance of the proposed SparseGAN framework. Notably, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the Semantic Evaluation Task, a widely-recognized evaluation benchmark for GAN-based text generation. Our results for this text inpainting task demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods. To facilitate easy reproduction of our results, we have open-sourced the code for SparseGAN-Inpainting at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN-Inpainting. Our study offers novel insights into the development of high-performance GAN-based text generation models and provides free-access code and models for the community. Our analysis predicts that HI intensity mapping experiments using interferometric techniques will cross certain thresholds in signal-to-noise, where they'll begin to incorrectly identify foreground components due to residual signals from the sky. This prediction holds particularly for experiments targeting the era of reionization ($z>7$). As a result, we propose that such experiments will struggle to recover the HI power spectrum accurately below a certain redshift threshold, which will be dictated by the specific characteristics of the experiment and its sky coverage. To better understand how to eliminate foreground signals effectively, we need to thoroughly examine the spatial structures present in these signals across various scales. This, in turn, will enable us to develop more precise models for removing foregrounds and estimating the HI power spectrum more accurately. We investigate how our current understanding of foregrounds can be enhanced through studies of real and random components in the data, as well as through the use of blind component analysis, and propose a new statistical approach to evaluating the accuracy of such removals. This approach involves assessing how well the removed signals match our current understanding of foreground structures, as well as how well they align with each other. We apply this approach to a specific HI intensity mapping experiment, but it's a method that could be utilized across a wide range of real and theoretical data sets. We specifically analyze how our approach behaves when removing signals at low redshift, and our results indicate that there's a specific redshift threshold below which the remaining foreground signals will become distorted due to the removal process. This, in turn, will make them more difficult to remove effectively, further exacerbating the challenges of accurately estimating the HI power spectrum at these low redshifts. This distorted structure is largely caused by a single foreground component that exhibits a relatively simple structure and exists over a relatively narrow range of scales. We also show that when we use our approach to remove foregrounds, the resulting estimates of the HI power spectrum will be subject to a bias that increases as we move to higher redshifts, primarily due to the removal of a single large-scale structure in the data. This, in turn, will make it even more challenging to accurately estimate the HI power spectrum at these low redshifts. This is a critical consideration, given that many HI intensity mapping experiments are primarily designed to study the dynamics of the universe at these low redshifts. This is the first in-depth analysis of how foreground removals impact the estimation of the HI power spectrum, and it provides a solid foundation for further research into this critical aspect of HI intensity mapping. To investigate the frequency and location of these localized patterns, we develop a novel method that focuses on the system's equilibrium state. By applying this approach, we create a localized measure, which quantifies the disparity between a system's internal components and assesses it in the context of the system's overall structure. We utilize this method to analyze multiple examples, including discrete versions of the Ising model and a dynamic traffic model, to determine how their localized occurrences are affected by varying parameters. Evaluating a team's performance in sports, particularly in football, involves complex considerations of multiple factors such as offense, defense, and chance. Previous research employed discursive valuation to assess teams' likelihood of winning a game, but faced issues with negative values and difficulty of comparison. To address these limitations, this study used the Cho-Kwon model to determine the probability of each team winning and conducted an exhaustive analysis of the points earned by national teams in the UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022 tournaments using their geographical locations. The results showed that offense played a more significant role than defense in determining the likelihood of winning, and notable regional performances included the dominance of European and South American teams, as well as the strong showing of African and Asian teams. Notably, teams' performance was highly variable, with some countries excelling in just a single Euro tournament. The data also highlighted the importance of offense over defense in winning games, and revealed that African and Asian teams' games were more likely to go to overtime. Finally, it was observed that teams' performance did not always correlate with their ranking in offline matches. To better understand these findings, a Generalized Defense Model was proposed, based on the Michaelis-Menten model, to analyze the relationship between teams' offense and defense in determining the likelihood of winning a game. The model was validated using data from the UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022 tournaments, and estimated the strengths of top-ranked teams such as Brazil, Argentina, and France, and the weaknesses of underperforming teams like Germany, Spain, and Italy. The model also identified the most consistent teams, such as Belgium and France, as well as the biggest upsets, such as Japan's win over Spain. Additionally, it was found that offense played a more significant role than defense in determining the likelihood of winning a game, and that African and Asian teams' games were more likely to go to overtime. The model can be applied to other sports competitions and is a valuable tool for predicting outcomes and identifying the strongest and weakest teams. The study of teams' performance using mathematical models also opens up research into dynamic processes such as adaptation and learning. The proposed model can be modified to investigate these concepts, such as the impact of a team's previous wins on its current performance, or the effect of a team switching coaches on its offense and defense. The study of dynamic processes in sports using mathematical models can provide insights into the underlying mechanisms and patterns, and can be applied to other fields such as economics, finance, and biology.

With this property in place, a Hermitan matrix's upper triangular entries become independently distributed given its diagonal entries, leading to a broader application of the traditional freeness concept. We also explore "freeness of kind B" in multiple Hermitan matrix ensembles, including the GOE-GOE and GUE-GUE ensembles, and derive conditions for their respective sub-ensembles to demonstrate this property. This condition is satisfied in the GOE-GOE and GUE-GUE ensembles due to their independent entry generation process. A powerful tool is developed to analyze a Hermitan matrix's anti-Hermitan sub-ensemble, allowing its quasi-minor to be expressed as a linear combination of multiple Hermitan quasi-minors, thus leading to the strong form of "freeness of kind B" for such sub-ensembles. Recently, research on knowledge distillation has shown that multiple instructors can label a single sample efficiently. However, the current approaches to combine instructors' predictions are either simplistic or cumbersome to optimize. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Coalition (PILE) model, which collaboratively trains a student by iteratively integrating the predictions of multiple instructors in a two-player format. The model first uses a coalition of two instructors to generate a label for a sample and undergoes multiple iterations of optimization. In each iteration, a student and an instructor engage in a learning process where the student makes predictions based on the instructor's output, and the instructor refines their predictions according to the student's forecast. We demonstrate that multi-instructor labeling (MIL) through iterative approaches like PILE outperforms single-instructor labeling across multiple benchmark datasets. Moreover, our findings indicate that PILE's performance continues to improve with an increasing number of instructors and that it successfully expands the dataset through novel data augmentation techniques. Our research also highlights that certain instructors may provide conflicting or inaccurate labels, which can negatively impact the performance of the student. To address this issue, we introduced a filter method that selects a coalition of high-quality instructors for labeling a sample, resulting in a further enhancement of the student's accuracy. Our approach and source code are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/PILE. This investigation seeks to provide empirical evidence regarding the impact of distant learning on students' ability to maintain pace with the curriculum during the pandemic. We generated a novel unitary measure of staying on schedule that integrates multiple indicators of academic performance. Our research analysis of national data for 38,776 ninth-grade students in the US, collected during the pandemic, reveals that remote learning generally accelerated curriculum completion for all students. However, this acceleration varied significantly by student background: students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds, those with pre-pandemic access to digital tools, and those whose parents hold higher levels of education, significantly accelerated curriculum completion; in contrast, those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and certain ethnic groups experienced no change or actually fell behind. Notably, our findings indicate that when accounting for prior academic performance, abilities, and motivation, the positive effect of remote learning on accelerating curriculum completion was more pronounced for underperforming students. Additionally, our research discovered a significant and positive interaction between remote learning and prior achievement, indicating that underperforming students gained nearly a 10% greater acceleration in completing the curriculum compared to average performers. Our study also validated the robustness of its findings across various empirical approaches and identified potential mechanisms that could be explored in future research. These initial findings provide valuable insights that can inform policy decisions and educational strategies to mitigate potential learning losses associated with remote education and promote more equitable outcomes. Moreover, they highlight the importance of closely monitoring the long-term consequences of remote learning on students' ability to maintain pace with the curriculum. To this end, we recommend that educators, policymakers, and researchers give due consideration to the diverse effect of remote education on students' ability to stay on schedule and complete the curriculum. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To further understand the value of phylogenetic networks, researchers need access to tools that create these networks from genome-scale data, and accordingly, the field of phylogenetic network creation has gained significant momentum. Given the diversity of available methods for network creation, a comparison of these tools based on the underlying structure of created networks is a missing aspect of research. Our study initiates this comparison by assessing six popular network creation methods - DND, UNDP, LGLN, GLGN, UNDP*, and GLGN* - using a dataset of binary genome sequences. We analyzed the networks produced by these methods using a variety of structural measures, including the number of nodes and edges, different topological indices, and the minimum and maximum reticulation numbers. Our findings reveal that the structure of created networks significantly varies based on the method used, even when the input genome data remains the same. Some network creation methods produce smaller, more complex networks, while others generate larger, less compact networks with higher reticulation numbers. These results have implications for the selection of network creation tools, highlighting the importance of considering the structural properties of generated networks. Furthermore, this study contributes to the theoretical development of network creation algorithms by providing a framework for evaluating these methods in terms of network structure. Ultimately, this comparison is expected to guide further research in network creation, spanning both algorithmic advancements and applications involving real genome data. Additionally, this study is an attempt to attract mathematicians to the field of phylogenetic network creation, primarily through its algorithmic aspects. By incorporating techniques from graph theory and discrete mathematics, this field offers numerous challenges and opportunities for innovative solutions. Our study is an extension of previous research, conducted independently by Chen et al. and by Wang et al. Our findings expand upon those previous studies by employing more rigorous statistical methods and a broader range of structural measures. Similarly, our dataset comprises a wider variety of genome sequences, along with a larger population of generated networks. These enhancements enable us to draw more dependable conclusions and provide a more comprehensive comparison of network creation methods. Our study is a significant contribution to the field of phylogenetic network creation, specifically in the evaluation of network structure. This research is an important step in assessing the diversity of phylogenetic networks

The PHENIX Collaboration has released initial findings on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011 data. These results provide early evidence for jet-medium interactions and offer insights into jet production and medium response. A significant excess in same-side near-side yields in Au$+$Au collisions distinguishes them from $d$$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions, indicating extra particles emitted at the same azimuthal angle as the jet. This excess is more pronounced at higher transverse momenta and lower $p_T$ counterparts, and its magnitude is proportional to the binary collision count in A$+$A collisions. This feature vanishes in $d$$+$Au collisions at the same $p_T$ range, and Au$+$Au results exhibit an increase in same-side near-side yields with rising $p_T$, ultimately exceeding $d$$+$Au results by five-fold at 39 GeV/C $p_T$. These findings are compared to the JETRY model, which relates jet production to medium response and incorporates jet quenching, also being interpreted to indicate jet energy being extracted from the medium at a rate of 5 GeV/c per unit length. Furthermore, this excess in same-side near-side yields is largely independent of centralities and isolated photon $p_T$. Additionally, the results show no significant dependence on the photon's $p_T$, and a notable deviation in Au$+$Au results is observed for back-to-back and opposite-side cases. These findings offer valuable insights into jet production and the medium's response, and it is suggested that a more comprehensive understanding can be attained through the combination of direct photon-hadron correlations and semi-inclusive hadron production. Moreover, the results in this analysis provide a foundation for further investigation into jet-medium interactions and the properties of quark-gluon plasma at various collision energies.

Many animals, such as single-legged jumpers like frogs, use their feet to absorb shocks from landing, maintain stability during takeoff, and propel themselves forward. The unique properties of a jumper's foot, which include a soft and flexible base attached to a longer rigid leg, play a crucial role in their movement. The foot's impact on the ground affects not only local skin tissue but also the entire jumping dynamics. Considering this, we develop a comprehensive mathematical model that incorporates foot dynamics, adhering to the principles of mechanics, to simulate how the foot interacts with the ground during takeoff, landing, and sustained jumping. By numerically analyzing this model, we identify key factors that either hinder or facilitate successful takeoff. Notably, we discover a specific critical condition for takeoff, which involves a critical takeoff angle that can be adjusted by modifying the foot's anisotropic properties. Additionally, we investigate how the foot's structure affects its ability to jump out of compacted soil. Successful takeoff is achieved at a higher angle than necessary for hard ground due to the foot's elastic response when released from rest. Our study provides valuable insights that can be used to design more efficient, natural foot structures for single-legged jumpers. The models and simulations presented can also be applied to other dynamic systems involving flexible feet in motion. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the evolution of a Hamiltonian through continuous modifications to its interaction strengths, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes. This study investigates the precise cover problem, a constrained kernelization problem, by rapidly switching two Ising Hamiltonians that comprise a precise cover instance. Our research demonstrates that, regardless of the specific quench interval used, the final annealing interval will always be apparent and easily identifiable. Furthermore, this interval serves as a dividing line that differentiates two distinct dynamics in the quench process. Specifically, regions on either side of the annealing interval exhibit distinct minimum state energies following quenching. This distinction arises from the unique properties of the Ising Hamiltonians that define a precise cover instance. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for implementing a precise cover problem solution utilizing a quantum annealing algorithm and pinpoint potential pitfalls when reproducing experimental results that involve quenching dynamics. This study offers a guiding framework for integrating the interplay between quantum annealing and quenching dynamics into further research on exact and approximate quantum dynamics following quenching in Ising-type systems. Our results also highlight the precise cover problem's unique properties as an Ising Hamiltonian system that can model real-world magnetic materials. This connection serves as a bridge between theoretical and experimental approaches in studying this type of system. Our research demonstrates the value of combining theoretical and experimental studies in tandem. Our findings show that, in cases where a combined approach is feasible, the interplay between theoretical and experimental research can yield a deeper understanding of the subject at hand. This understanding can, in turn, provide a framework for addressing other challenging issues that arise in constrained kernelization problems. The superconducting properties are then understood by analyzing this one-electron Hamiltonian. We show that doped holes primarily occupy the lower-band than the upper-band due to a hole-like effective mass in the upper-band and a electron-like effective mass in the lower-band. The resulting wavefunction will exhibit heavy isospin mixing. We identify the Peierls-like dimerization as the driving force for dimerization-induced splitting around 1.5 eV, and it results in the upper-band shifting down in energy. The superconducting state then arises from electron-electron interactions within this altered bandstructure. The heavy isospin mixing and dimerization-induced band-splitting are both crucial for the $C_{2g}$-symmetry broken and the associated doped-site asymmetry. The model has direct implications for the material's magnetic properties, particularly in regards to spin-rotation symmetry and the observed magnetic transitions. Finally, we offer a possible solution to the remaining puzzle of nickel valence, suggesting it to be in a mixed state between 2+ and 3+. A new model has been developed, based on a density-wavelen interaction, which can explain the observed conduction and resistance oscillations in cuprates and provides a quantitative estimate of the oscillation amplitude. This model takes the form of a resistivity equation that incorporates a sinusoidal function related to the carrier concentration and incorporates the shaltiel parameter which is a measure of the cuprate's anisotropy. The characteristics of dense hadronic matter within compact stars and the sound speed of this matter are the focus of this study. We examine the sound speed in dense hadronic matter, investigating its relationship with density and chemical potential. Specifically, we show that in dense hadronic matter, the Gravitational Wave dispersion relation takes the form $k^2=\frac{4\pi G\rho}{c^2}(\rho+2p/c^2-4B/c^2)$, where $B$ represents the bag parameter. It's been demonstrated that in compact stars, sound speed is highest for strange quark stars and lowest for hadronic stars, with a $\sim 0.4c$ difference. This sound speed disparity raises intriguing possibilities for gravitational wave observation, potentially enabling the identification of strange quark stars through the detection of specific gravitational wave frequencies. Furthermore, the sound speed in dense hadronic matter is found to be sensitive to the presence of neutron star binaries and could be used as a means of distinguishing between different quark and hadronic star overtones. This research also highlights the utility of sound speed parameters in hadronic matter models to reconcile the discrepancies found in previous studies. Lastly, it's worth noting that in dense hadronic matter, sound speed becomes linearly dependent on chemical potential at sufficiently low densities, a phenomenon that may be experimentally verified through the analysis of neutron star spectra. This study's findings provide valuable insights into the properties of compact stars and their gravitational wave signatures, underscoring the importance of sound speed parameters in hadronic matter models. A further implication of this research is that the detection of certain gravitational wave frequencies could serve as a probe of the sound speed parameter in hadronic matter. A numerical example is provided to highlight the detection capabilities of current gravitational wave detectors for this sound speed parameter. This research sets the stage for a more in-depth investigation into how the sound speed parameter in hadronic matter influences gravitational wave spectra. A specific example is given for the RAX stream neutron star binary candidate, which is being observed by the LIGO Virgo collaboration. If this binary is indeed a neutron star-neutron star system, research into its gravitational wave signal offers valuable insights on the sound speed parameter in dense hadronic matter, including a possible value for this parameter of approximately $0.64c$. A further study into this research direction is now being pursued. A study on the sound speed in dense hadronic matter has been expanded to examine its relationship with strangeness and compact stars. A numerical example is provided

The Compass system, a recent model for studying compressed quantum systems, is analyzed in this paper in relation to two key factors: the level of compression and the position of the compass in the Fock space. A detailed examination is performed for two scenarios, both with a fixed compression level but varying compass positions, and with a fixed compass position but varying levels of compression. Our findings indicate that the former leads to alternating major and minor transitions between compass states, while a more complex, nonperiodic pattern emerges in the latter case. Additionally, this paper investigates the relationship between the compass system and its environment, identifying conditions under which the compass system exhibits the most varied behavior. Furthermore, a condition is determined for the compass system to undergo the largest transition between its states. This research provides a foundation for exploring the interactions between the compass system and its environment in future studies. Additionally, we derive an analytical expression for the compass system's Hamiltonian in a full Hilbert space, extending the model's principles to systems beyond compressed regimes. This extended framework paves the way for investigating compressed systems in a more comprehensive and nuanced manner. Overall, the compass system presents a valuable paradigm for investigating the intricate dynamics that arise within compressed quantum systems. Its study is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to our understanding of complex phenomena resulting from the interplay between compression, nonlinearity, and system-specific bases. With its numerous unanswered questions and numerous unexplored scenarios, the compass system also offers a promising platform for interdisciplinary research involving both theoretical physics and mathematical aspects. As such, we confidently predict that the compass system will continue to serve as a vital benchmark problem for advancing our knowledge of compressed quantum systems. In conclusion, the compass system has provided significant insights into the intricate nature of compressed quantum systems and it is our hope that this research will inspire a new generation of researchers to engage with this subject. With the vast array of future studies awaiting resolution, we are confident that the compass system will endure as a pivotal reference point for all future work related to compressed quantum systems. As such, we consider it our pleasure to contribute this comprehensive compilation of our research on the compass system to the ongoing scientific community discussion. With the current knowledge reuse perspective, we believe that the existing model is a well-developed representation of compressed quantum systems. Nevertheless, we also recognize that there are numerous prospective model variations awaiting discovery. With this understanding, we are willing to cede the stage to the next generation of researchers who will undoubtedly propel the compass system model forward in a manner that exceeds our current understanding. Convolutional neural network (CNN) models often employ multiple levels of feature extraction,
using successively larger filters to capture diverse pattern sizes. However, traditional CNN
architectures, like DenseNet and ResNet, usually incorporate multiple identical input channels
in their block inputs, which can result in information overload and diminish the impact of earlier
feature extraction layers. To rectify this issue, this paper introduces a novel layer called Dynamic
Entrance, which selectively incorporates previous layer outputs based on global context.
Exploiting a global average pooling (GAP) component to determine the importance of each layer
output, this layer combines them via a weighted sum. Our model, a DenseNet variant featuring
Dynamic Entrance blocks, achieves top-notch performance on multiple benchmark datasets, outperforming
the original DenseNet by a significant margin. Notably, it uses the fewest parameters among all
DenseNet variants while achieving a notable improvement in accuracy. Our model also exhibits a
substantial reduction in model size and increased Robustness, in addition to facilitating flexible
implementation in both encoder and decoder architectures. The code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/DE-pytorch.

reveals that the DE layer is particularly effective when employed in the encoder of a model. The paper

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor in this model is a post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which was previously determined to be around 1.00125, but still retains a small margin of error. Our research analyzes the current uncertainty surrounding this parameter and its effects on astronomical measurements from Gaia-like missions. Although it's currently precise to at least $10^{-5}$, we investigate what impact a more refined measurement of $\gamma$ could have on astronomical data. Our study involves simulating Gaia-like observations of over 1 billion non-stellar objects across the sky and includes correcting its parallax measurements for any gravitational distortions. However, since such corrections are highly unlikely given the current precision, they can be safely omitted. Our results show that even a highly precise measurement of $\gamma$ would likely have a minimal impact of around $10^{-8}$ units on parallax measurements. This is because other sources of error, such as internal noise, exceed this value by at least an order of magnitude. Therefore, a more refined measurement of $\gamma$ based on astronomical data is likely to face a limitation in precision. This method generates a linear hybrid coordinate system tailored to minimize the dimensionality of the representation, eliminating the need for a fixed subspace or basis. This innovation enables rapid model reductions that capture the present behavior of the high-fidelity model, integrating advances in global sensitivity analysis and dynamic mode decomposition. A specific type of wave known as a soliton maintains its original form over time. It achieves this through a continuous balance with the surrounding medium, which is created by a specific reaction-counteraction mechanism between the soliton and its environment. However, this balance is disrupted when a new wave with the same frequency as the soliton is introduced, as a result of the interaction with the medium. Interestingly, we've discovered that the new wave can take on a soliton's characteristics, establishing a new equilibrium with the medium. This new soliton form is remarkably robust, as it is not significantly affected by the presence of the original soliton or any remaining residual forces. Notably, this phenomenon occurs even when the original soliton is located far away, allowing for the creation of a self-sustaining soliton-through-soliton reaction-counteraction chain. This process is further analyzed in a three-dimensional setup, where the required initial conditions are identified and the resulting wave dynamics are studied over extended periods of time. The resulting film demonstrates high peak powers and a high average power, achieving a record 2 GW of average power. The potential applications of this discovery include the creation of powerful, coherent light sources and the development of novel methods for treating diseases. The reaction-counteraction mechanism that gives rise to these self-sustaining solitons could also be employed to improve the performance of photonic devices. Additionally, this mechanism may be employed in other contexts where a wave interacts with the same type of reaction medium, potentially leading to the creation of a self-sustaining wave-through-wave chain. The specific conditions and variables of this phenomenon suggest that it may be observable in other areas, such as the study of sound waves in air or fluid dynamics. The name "self-boosting solitons" captures the idea that these solitons generate their own balance with the surrounding medium through a back-and-forth reaction-counteraction with the same type of wave. This concept is opposite to the traditional understanding of solitons, which are often seen as being isolated from the surrounding medium. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and an untrusted server. The goal is to prevent the client from obtaining sensitive information other than the model's final output. To achieve this, a protocol is developed to securely execute an ML inference task, comprising the sharing of encrypted input data and model shares among the client and server. A critical component of this protocol is a shared library that encrypts the model's output in response to decrypted intermediate results from each party. To further enhance privacy, a modification is made to redirect the library's encrypted output to the server instead of the client. A performance assessment is conducted for the modified protocol, applying a publicly available dataset and various open-source ML models. To facilitate replication and further research, the study's source code is freely available for download. Moreover, a high-performance variant of the protocol, named SIMC 2.0, is also introduced. This new protocol reduces overhead by simplifying encryption operations within the shared library and transferring encrypted data blocks directly between the client and server. A comparative analysis is provided between the original and improved protocols. Additionally, SIMC 2.0 is integrated with an open-source framework for scalable ML training and inference, ensuring that both accuracy and performance requirements are met. The study's results demonstrate substantial improvements in overhead and runtime for both single-threaded and multi-threaded executions, with further optimization potential identified for large-scale ML models. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 is found to experience memory access patterns resulting in suboptimal cache performance, which presents an area for future research in cache-friendly model partitioning. The research concludes by highlighting potential applications and future directions for integrating SIMC 2.0 with encrypted data storage and leveraging it for encrypted ML training. The development of more efficient, scalable protocols is critical to enabling private ML inference across multiple clients and a trained global model. The protocol's code is made available on an open-source repository. In addition, a technical video detailing the study's work is available for viewing. The study has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW) 2023. The research was conducted by a single author at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). The study has received no external funding and the author is not affiliated with any organization. The author is not open to further research collaborations at this time. The study does not involve human subjects, but does involve the use of publicly available datasets. The study does not include any experiments involving animals

The galaxy M101 is a member of a nearby galaxy group that also includes four other spiral galaxies. Observations using the FAST radio telescope allowed for a wide-area survey around M101, covering an approximate area of 1 deg^2 with high sensitivity. The resulting data showed significant detection of HI (neutral hydrogen) emission beyond the galaxy's optical boundaries, revealing multiple faint HI structures in the surrounding intergalactic medium and an extended HI tail extending from M101 itself. These findings are significant, with potential implications for galaxy interactions and the distribution of HI gas in the group. We present HI maps of the M101 galaxy group and an extended environment around M101, providing new insights into this region's HI gas architecture. Furthermore, our data are suitable for follow-up research, such as optical/near-infrared observations of HI-associated stars and ultraviolet observations of HI emission in the intergalactic medium. By integrating these methods with advanced signal processing techniques, we significantly improved their performance. Our research encompasses three main areas, with direct parallels to immune system functions: (1) detecting unusual patterns (equivalent to detecting anomalies), (2) identifying specific patterns (equated with antigen recognition), and (2+) combining pattern detection with data filtering (comparable to the elimination of pathogens). The art of compound medication design involves a delicate balance of multiple elements including disease treatment, drug properties, and opposing reactions which existing machines struggle to manage well. One crucial aspect is medication pairing, where matching two drugs can treat a disease but their interaction data are scarce. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed that leverages relational learning to utilize a vast amount of property information about drugs. Specifically, it builds on a comprehensive model integrating graph networks that can work with complex relationships and point-to-point models that can handle multiple connections. This proposed model is tested on a large dataset of antineoplastic drugs with partial interaction data and notable improvements is achieved compared to a baseline model. Notably, it is observed that models focusing on single relationships performed worse than the comprehensive model suggesting that existing models are not sufficiently complex to accurately evaluate medication pairs. Furthermore, this approach is superior to other relational models with similar complexity indicating that the proposed model's performance is a result of its comprehensive design rather than its use of advanced models. Finally, the results demonstrate the potential of this approach to enhance the evaluation of medication pairs with property information. The Itô-Wentzell theorem enables the representation of solutions to stochastic differential equations (SDEs) in terms of change of variables. However, this connection is typically conditioned on the coefficients being differential maps between even tangent spaces. This research relaxes that requirement, allowing differential maps between uneven tangent spaces, thereby broadening the applicability of the Itô-Wentzell theorem. We demonstrate that given an SDE with smooth, locally bounded coefficients, its solution can be expressed through a change of variables involving differential maps between uneven tangent spaces. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which weak uniqueness of solutions can be determined from properties of these differential maps. This advancement has implications for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to SDEs with non-Lipschitz components. We also introduce an alternative condition for the Itô-Wentzell theorem that is more readily verifiable in practice. This condition is linked to the existence and uniqueness of solutions to SDEs with bounded and smooth coefficients. We showcase our results through the derivation of novel existence and uniqueness proofs for SDEs with bounded coefficients and the verification of our conditions for specific examples. This includes the existence and uniqueness of solutions for an SDE with a geometric Brownian motion and an SDE with a stochastic geometric variation of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. Additionally, we explore an extension of the Itô-Wentzell theorem to include an external control variable, demonstrating the existence and uniqueness of solutions for an SDE with a stochastic geometric variation of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle with control. This research provides a foundation for future investigations of the Itô-Wentzell theorem in higher-dimensional spaces. We conclude this study by outlining several open problems and potential future research directions. These results are further illustrated through the use of the Feller test, which we introduce in this context. We also derive an alternative method for verifying the condition of the Itô-Wentzell theorem through the use of the Lie derivative. This has the advantage of simplifying the computation of the condition in cases where the Hamiltonian vector fields of the drift and diffusion components have common components. We demonstrate this through the verification of our condition for an SDE with a stochastic geometric variation of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. This includes the computation of the Hamilton vector fields, the determination of their intersection, and the derivation of the skew-symmetry matrix of the Hamilton vector fields. We discuss how our results can be applied to establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for an SDE with a stochastic geometric variation of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

This paper introduces a novel approach, called Random Stroll, that enables a master node to infer user information without directly accessing their data. Typically, a master node relies on a user's dataset to train a machine learning model, but Random Stroll deviates from this standard method. To achieve this inference, the master node employs a random model that reflects the characteristics of a specific user. This random model is developed by utilizing ensemble methods, specifically ensemble neural networks, that combine the predictions of models trained on unrelated datasets. As a result, the master node can provide a model that accurately represents a particular user without needing access to that user's data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Random Stroll through a series of experiments on the MNIST and Adult datasets, showing that it can produce models that are virtually identical to those trained locally. A prominent method for using unlabelled medical image data in combination with labelled training images is semi-supervised deep learning.  One widely adopted approach in semi-supervised learning involves using a model that is trained on both labelled and unlabelled data and includes a regularisation component to ensure consistency between predictions made on image data and mask information.  We have investigated modifying this approach by directly incorporating the unlabelled data into the optimisation process without employing a separate model for unlabelled data predictions.  Our results show that this modified method produces similar or superior outcomes compared to the established approach in multiple benchmark challenges.  A particular advantage of this modified method is reduced memory usage, lower memory per layer, and fewer optimisation parameters.  We have additionally explored applying this method to a dataset that was not previously studied in the context of semi-supervised medical image segmentation and demonstrated its efficacy.  Our code is publicly available for review and use.  We propose the name "An Awkwardly Basic Consistency Regularization" (AABCR) for this modified method and detail our methodological differences with prior approaches.  A key distinction involves using a single optimisation process for both labelled and unlabelled data rather than employing a dual-process strategy.  We attribute the improved performance of AABCR to its ability to exploit shared representations of image structure across both labelled and unlabelled data.  We explore AABCR in the context of three benchmark datasets using a consistent protocol and demonstrate that one of the datasets, specifically the Cityscapes dataset, requires additional data when using AABCR due to its relatively simple class definitions.  We study the effect of AABCR on segmentation output uncertainty and find that it results in more consistent predictions on both labelled and unlabelled data.  We investigate the effect of AABCR on network interpretability using both qualitative and quantitative measures and find that it produces more regular and predictable segmentations on unlabelled data, specifically in terms of boundary sharpness. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been upgrading its Level 1 trigger system to keep up with an increasingly complex particle landscape. A key component of this upgrade involves a new digitization and readout system for the calorimeter. Our project centers on the development of an advanced readout and digitization module known as the Level 1 Calorimeter Trigger Module (CTM). This CTM board will utilize an Xilinx Kintex UltraScale+ chip, enabling a more sophisticated calculation of energy and positions within the calorimeter. By leveraging a 6.4 GB/s high-speed data link, the CTM can efficiently transfer its data to the ATLAS First Level Trigger (FLT) module. Our team has been working to enhance the velocity of data transfer, which initially stood at just over half of the available bandwidth. Through the implementation of a multi-stage buffer system and optimized output controller, we have successfully increased the data transfer rate to nearly full bandwidth, reaching around 5.7 GB/s. This improvement has also resulted in reduced latency, achieving the desired total latency of 425 ns while maintaining low flush buffer rates. This project has provided valuable hands-on experience for our team members in the development and implementation of leading-edge digital trigger technology. We expect this work to contribute significantly to the successful deployment of the ATLAS Level 1 trigger system in 2024. Additionally, our project's findings and methods may be applicable to other LHC experiments and forward pilot beam conditions. We intend to continue contributing to the ATLAS Level 1 trigger effort and explore potential collaboration with other HEP experiments. Knowledge tracing has gained significant traction in recent years as a task focused on modeling user knowledge based on performance data, leveraging knowledge graphs and student performance information. Various knowledge tracing models have been developed using deep learning techniques, often compared in benchmark studies, but the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and tools hinders complete assessment of their effectiveness. To address this issue, we present pyKT, a novel open-source framework that enables comparison of knowledge tracing models on a level playing field. pyKT combines multiple user interface options for dataset importation, model training, and evaluation, as well as a versatile data manipulation module that facilitates both dataset replication and diverse visualization of results. This framework is available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. pyKT is an essential resource for the knowledge tracing community, providing a clear roadmap for developing deep learning-based knowledge tracing systems and a comprehensive framework for evaluating their performance. Furthermore, pyKT is an ideal platform for open-source collaboration and contribution. Given any complex variety $X$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ has a limited spectrum when applied to functions defined across $X$. Additionally, if $X$ comprises multiple components $X_0$, $X_1$ $\ldots$ $X_n$, and the lowest non-zero eigenvalue for the Laplacian across $X_0$ is not reached, or if $X$ includes at least two distinct components, we prove that $P$ is injective. Furthermore, if $X$ is an algebraic set with only one component, the issue of whether $P$ is injective depends on its differential order and whether it includes terms that are tangent to that component's algebraic submanifolds. This result generalizes previous findings from Guan and Xiong, as well as a subsequent note by the same authors. This inclusion of higher-order terms and a broader definition of $X$ represents a key advancement. A further consequence of this research involves the development of a new approach to establishing the injectivity of elliptic operators via the definition of their principal symbols. This method enables us to extend established results about the Laplacian to a broader class of elliptic operators. A significant outcome of this research involves a new proof of the Birkhoff-Guenther-Nirenberg theorem, which describes the smooth surfaces in projective three-dimensional space that have a trivial symplectic area. This proof provides a clear illustration of how an operator's injectivity can be established via the definition of its principal symbol. A key aspect of this proof involves the use of algebraic techniques, such as Bezout's theorem, to demonstrate the injectivity of the Laplacian across certain algebraic varieties. This research also introduces a new definition of an elliptic operator being non-singular, which is equivalent to it being injective and having a restricted range. This definition enables us to generalize established results about the Laplacian to a broader class of elliptic operators. A further consequence of this research involves the development of an new approach to solving the Dirac equation in the presence of external electromagnetic fields. This approach involves the use of algebraic techniques, such as the definition of algebraic sets and the Bezout theorem, to establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this equation. This, in turn, enables us to provide a new proof of the sum rule for the Dirac operator, which states that if $P$ has a zero at zero, then so does $2P$.

In this poster, we will be presenting further details on our previous work and highlighting recent improvements, such as integrating multiple SMT solvers and defining a framework for describing SMT proofs that are not yet fully automated. These improvements will be demonstrated through verifications of selected sorting algorithms. Alethe evidence files can facilitate better interaction between proof-based verification and SMT solving, but there is still room for improvement, as our experience has shown. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly slow down training. The Federated Averaging algorithm shaves time by allowing devices to send updates at any time, but it imposes strict constraints on gradient norms, hindering the algorithm's efficiency and broad usability. We present a novel, unconstrained algorithm that enables devices to send updates at any time and aggregates them in a way that minimizes bias and variance. Our method uses a buffer to accumulate and process updates from devices, producing a converged model in each batch. We derive a formulation for optimizing the batch size and show that our method surpasses Federated Averaging in terms of efficiency and wide usability. Our results demonstrate near-optimal performance on non-convergence cases and achieve 2.5 times speedup over Federated Averaging on a dataset with 1,000 devices. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengdengdeng/Buffered-FedAvg. Notably, our method facilitates implicit regularization that achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10 and SVHN without label noise and gradient clipping. For example, our method achieves 6.92% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 after 1,000 iterations without any data augmentation. Our analysis of failure cases highlights the importance of explicit regularization in various settings. Our method allows devices to send updates with any gradient norm, making it particularly suitable for applications with diverse user environments and potential attacks. Our results show that our method achieves better performance than FedAvg on noisy datasets and accelerates training by at least 2 times on datasets with 10,000 devices. Online social networks experience fluctuations as users disconnect from and reconnect to the platform, resulting in shifting community structures. The effectiveness of node embeddings is often evaluated based on their ability to preserve community proximity and structural roles. However, most evaluations occur in static settings. We introduce the Twitch player dataset, derived from online game data, in conjunction with corresponding node embeddings for comparison. These embeddings capture the structural roles of players and their distances to each other. We leverage diffusion-based methods to enhance the spatial distribution of the embeddings and establish benchmarked experiments to assess the Twitch player dataset. The results indicate that both prescribed procedures and alternative methods can achieve comparable performance in evaluating the embeddings' quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applications of the Twitch player dataset in predicting player departures and in-class predictions. The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/eduardobm/twitch-players. This dimension, though undetectable, affects our own by creating an infinite, ever-changing "marshland" of entities, including Primordial Black Holes that we can't see. The Dark Matter we observe is a product of this marshland, with its mass also being made up of the falls from the hidden dimension. Our universe's age is, in fact, a fraction of a much older age that is not measurable, determined by the time it took for the Primordial Black Holes to form and start influencing our universe's expansion. This theory explains many phenomena of the universe, including why dark energy, with a negative pressure, is necessary to expand it further, and why dark matter and energy have nearly equal amounts. Furthermore, I suggest that the hidden dimension's influence on our own is seasonal, with its impact causing the acceleration of our universe's expansion during its early stages and potentially explaining seasonal changes in gravitational force and the expansion of the universe during its early stages. A calculation of the mass of Primordial Black Holes in our universe is also provided, with its value being approximately 10^16 times the mass of a typical asteroid. The existence of these small objects would also explain the observed high energy cosmic rays. A name for this theory and its implications on various physical constants are also offered for consideration. Additionally, I explore potential experimental validation of the theory and the necessity to revise the Hubble Constant's value as well as the speed of light in vacuum. A new unit of length that reflects the complex relationships between fundamental physical constants is also introduced. A brief historical context and a personal perspective on the theory's development are provided from the author's point of view. A list of papers and a personal statement of no conflict of interest are included at the end. Our study focuses on non-uniform configurations where the two fluids do not mix, and we investigate how their respective temperature ranges affect the physics of the system. Our research reveals that in certain situations, a fluid with a higher temperature will expand over the cooler fluid, influenced by gravitational potential energy, yet this behavior is not limitless. Additionally, we identify constraints on a fluid's temperature range that must be met to maintain stability and non-mixing within the gravitational field. Furthermore, our work demonstrates that a fluid with a significantly higher temperature cannot occupy the center of the celestial body, and thus cannot be at the heart of a neutron star. This finding counterintuitively suggests that in such systems, the fluid with the higher temperature will actually shrink in proportion to its temperature difference with the cooler fluid, ultimately leading to a collapse into the center of the celestial body. Our research has significant implications for modeling both neutron stars and white-dwarf stars. It imposes constraints on their internal temperature distributions, potentially affecting their stability and behavior in various astronomical processes. Our analysis suggests that such systems should be modeled as two-fluid systems, considering both the fluids' temperatures and their relative distributions. However, there are challenges in using artificial neural networks for COVID-19 detection, primarily due to the similarity between COVID-19 and other lung infections as seen by an artist, the variability in image quality, and the need for larger COVID-19 training data. To address these issues, a new neural network method called Infection-aware Contrastive Mixup Classification was developed. This approach involves first segregating COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 classes and training two neural networks on these separate classes. These two neural networks are then combined using a contrastive learning loss function that uses COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 X-ray images to improve their performance. To mitigate class imbalance during training, the method was modified to include noise COVID-19 samples. Experimental results showed that this method achieved high accuracy on both the original dataset and a dataset enhanced with artificial COVID-19 images. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, it yielded the best results on a widely-used dataset and matched the best baseline method on another dataset. The method was found to be effective in differentiating COVID-19 from other lung infections and outperformed the baseline methods on a dataset involving three classes. Most current research on grammatical error rectification (GER) focuses on a single domain, which is not representative of the diverse range of languages used in real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we're working on a new few-shot domain adaptation approach for GER, which aims to minimize the need for native data in target domains. By applying meta-learning techniques to aggregate information from multiple non-native domains, our model can effectively switch between new domains with only a few examples. In experiments using the L1 corpus and a recently introduced GER dataset, our results show a novel few-shot learning method and a simple data preprocessing technique both improve performance. Interestingly, we discovered that both native and non-native speakers can benefit from a few shots of target domain data, challenging the long-held assumption that non-native speakers only need native language guidance. With only 5 shots per domain, our model achieved a 62.8% improvement in F1 score in target domains compared to traditional fine-tuning. Notably, we observed significant room for enhancement in the few-shot setting for native speakers. By applying a mix of both native and non-native data, our model achieved a 12.3% higher F1 score in the few-shot setting than the current state-of-the-art method in the fully supervised setting. Our research also highlighted the challenge of adapting highly accurate models from other NLP tasks to the GER task. With only 10 shots per domain, the score dropped to a 23.6% F1 score. In contrast, models trained from scratch achieved a 5.4% higher F1 score in the few-shot setting. To facilitate further research, we're open-sourcing all preprocessed data, along with a novel few-shot learning method that can adapt models to rectify errors in new domains with only a few examples. This initiative aims to accelerate advancements in both GER and low-resource NLP tasks by providing accessible data and a scalable evaluation frameworks. In the future, we plan to explore both multi-domain and unsupervised adaptation settings, along with the integration of additional NLP components to enhance error rectification performance. This way, we can accelerate further research in both GER and low-resource NLP tasks, paving the way for more reliable and highly accurate models in the future. Researchers typically gather information about a total by collecting individual data points, which are often subject to measurement errors. For positive integers, the collection method usually involves averaging rounded to the nearest integer. Given that y represents the true total and the method of collection, we establish mathematically and statistically what this implies about the distribution of collected data points x, given that they are based on the average of n observations of x/n. It is shown that when n is large enough, the distribution of x can be modeled by the formula P(x=k)=2*P(y*k.5)-P(y+k), leading to a binomial distribution when y is an integer and a Poisson distribution when y is an integer and n is large enough. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy.

A leading cause of failures in modern Machine Learning projects is the poor quality of training data, stemming from difficulties in sourcing and cleaning vast amounts of information. Pinpointing and rectifying data-related issues proves challenging due to the intricate relationships within ML processes and data sets. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called Data Troubleshooting with Shapley Significance, combining exact Shapley value computations with significant feature testing for both supervised and semi-supervised learning tasks. Our method assesses each data point's contribution to an ML model's performance and identifies crucial features affecting the classification outcome. By pinpointing crucial data points with inadequate information or misleading information, our framework enables targeted data revision, incorporating cleaning or weighting schemes. Comprehensive experiments on publicly available data sets reveal our approach's effectiveness in detecting vital data points, improving model performance by up to 275%. Furthermore, we apply our method to evaluate real-world data sets, containing over a million data points, with a focus on the computational efficiency of our approach using recent high-performance computing technology. Our code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/amirveyseh/DataTroubleshooting, along with our data analysis results for the UCIML dataset on COVID-19 https://github.com/amirveyseh/Covid19DataAnalysis. Additionally, we introduce DataTroubleShooter, an open-source Python package providing a user-friendly interface and versatile tools for data evaluation, such as important data point detection, feature significance testing, and model performance assessment. By incorporating our approach into an end-to-end ML pipeline, we achieve comparable or better performance compared to baseline models trained on revised data sets. Our results demonstrate the method's efficiency and model improvements resulting from data revision. In addition to its applications in ML, our approach can also be used for prioritizing feature construction techniques. Overall, our work provides a groundbreaking solution for identifying crucial data points and features in large datasets with complex relationships, enabling targeted data revision and improvement of model performance. This approach opens up new research directions in advanced feature construction methods and data revision strategies. Additionally, we explore potential collaborations with other techniques in the ML pipeline, such as feature selection and model selection. Our approach sets the stage for further research into complex ML tasks, such as reinforcement learning and clustering, and we anticipate its effectiveness in those domains as well. With the growing use of large datasets in modern ML projects, our approach becomes increasingly vital in helping data scientists pinpoint data-related issues and rectify them, leading to improved model performance. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning methods often struggle with high variability in data, particularly when working with trajectories that have been artificially extended for educational purposes. The key challenge lies in the fact that only successful trajectories are provided, containing both desired and undesired actions. To tackle this issue, we present a novel offline learning framework called Positive Trajectories Learning (PTL) that leverages data with artificially extended desired states. PTL employs an attention-based model that pinpoints crucial segments of each trajectory and assigns them different attention weights. By incorporating a robust trajectorily loss function that resists data noise, we integrate these attention weights into our offline objective function. We further introduce an auxiliary model with a different objective function that focuses on reinforcing desired actions within extended trajectories. Through thorough evaluation on multiple scenarios, including a self-driving application, our method consistently outperforms existing offline learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/ghiyoshi/PTL. The theoretical analysis of our model's robustness is presented in the supplementary materials. Additionally, we include results from ablation studies and additional experiments in the appendix. Thanks to strong data efficiency and low memory requirements, our model is well-suited for learning in complex, multi-agent domains with limited data. We anticipate our approach to yield superior results in various offline learning tasks across multiple domains. We have analyzed the behavior of the classical nova V392 Persei, which exploded in 2018.  Observations from the Hubble Space Telescope reveal that the pre-outburst and post-outburst spectra of the star are remarkably similar, with just a small shift in wavelength, a rare phenomenon for a nova.  The star appears to be an overabundant, low-mass close binary system with a white dwarf companion and a large convection zone on the Sun-like primary.  Estimates suggest the outburst was incredibly powerful, with energy released at a rate 25 times more powerful than average and potentially detectable by gamma-ray satellites.  The star's orbital period remains elusive, but all other characteristics including its outburst pattern and lack of hydrogen-rich material in its atmosphere are consistent with a very small nova explosion.  The star is now in a state of minimum luminosity, but its large convection zone suggests it is on the verge of another powerful outburst.  We have also analyzed the star's light curve and found it to be an example of a rapidly declining nova with little to no intermediate plateau stage, which is more commonly found in very small novae explosions.  The absence of any significant increase in the system's orbital period or mass loss from the primary suggests the outburst was extremely powerful and likely resulted in the ejection of a significant amount of material into a highly elliptical or even gravitational escape trajectory around the binary system.  We have further analyzed the possible presence of a small skirt or hump in the light curve's declining stage and its potential link to the star's rapid decline and large amplitude, which could be an identifying feature of very small nova explosions in close binary systems.  Finally, we have also considered the possibility of detecting this star's future outburst from space with the help of all-sky X-ray monitors like those on board the Astrosat, Stron Astro, and future wide-field X-ray observatories.  If detected early enough, there may also be a small opportunity to study its radio emission with radio telescopes like the Very Large Array.  We have also included some general considerations on how to identify very small nova explosions from the ground, which could result in the detection of a significant amount of material that is likely being ejected into highly elliptical or even gravitational escape trajectories around the binary system. We create initial mass functions (IMFs) tailored to each cluster and model the evolution of compact object binaries within them. Our study takes into account a wide range of binary interactions including gravitational waves, as well as detection capabilities of advanced detectors similar to LIGO. We predict binary merger rates for each cluster and explain how various factors such as detector sensitivity and signal characterisation affect these predictions. Our analysis suggests that advanced detectors similar to LIGO will likely detect several binary mergers from the Milky Way's nuclear clusters every year. However, the actual rate of detections will also depend on how effectively these events are identified and characterised. Our study also shows that there will be a diversity in sources of binary mergers that can be detected through gravitational waves, and understanding this diversity is crucial in interpreting the data from these detections. This diversity arises from how the density of stars in these clusters affects the formation of binary mergers, with the most dense having a significantly higher rate of neutron star mergers. This implies that when we see a neutron star merger, it is more likely that it is coming from an intermediate to dense cluster rather than a low density one. This diversity will increase as even more sensitive detectors like the proposed LIGO+ are used. Using this understanding, we can gather valuable information about these clusters, their host galaxy and how binary mergers form and evolve. This information will further enhance the significance of detecting these events. This research is being carried out in collaboration with the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration. We are also expanding our research to model the formation and evolution of binary mergers in other types of galaxy environments.
