In the context of clustering, we developed a new algorithm called Dynamic $k$-Means Grouping (DKG) that leverages ongoing arrivals of data points. DKG begins with an initial set of data points and progressively improves its clustering by operating on expanding data subsets. Notably, our analysis ensures that, regardless of the dimensionality of the data, DKG can converge to a cluster solution close to the optimal solution, even when the number of data points grows exponentially in relation to the dimensionality. This achievement is significant because it addresses a critical limitation of traditional clustering algorithms, which often require accessing the entire data set at once. Additionally, we introduced a data structure known as a Ball Tree that facilitates efficient insertion of new data points into the algorithm. As such, DKG represents a pioneering example of a practical algorithm capable of handling real-time data processing in high-dimensional spaces. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of DKG, indicating that it produces high-quality clusters that are only slightly inferior to those produced by traditional $k$-Means algorithms. Furthermore, DKG exhibits superior performance in comparison to other dynamic clustering algorithms. A further analysis of the algorithm's parameters is also provided, and we have made the algorithm publicly available under an open-source license. It is worth noting that, in theoretical terms, a variant of the algorithm requires only a ball depth of $O(\sqrt{k})$, indicating that there is still room for optimization, given that $k$ is relatively small in most clustering applications. A more advanced variant of the algorithm employs a different data structure known as a $k$-Tree, that enables it to process data points that exhibit complex mixtures of categorical and high-dimensional numerical features. This variant has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of large-scale clustering operations. It is also possible to combine this variant with a different placement strategy for the initial centers, which could be of interest to individuals working on different dynamic clustering problems. We introduce a new framework for modeling a significant class of stochastic dynamic games, which includes as subsets several important categories such as partially observable multi-agent games, infinite-horizon SISO games, and concurrent SISO games. Our framework is based on a hierarchical structure of game sub-sets that are isolated from one another by impenetrable barriers. A key aspect of our framework is the identification of an upper bound for solving general games, which is derived from the combination of individual game sub-sets. We establish conditions under which this combined solution achieves optimal performance comparable to solving the original game directly. Furthermore, we explore efficient methods for computing solutions within our hierarchical framework, which can be highly beneficial due to the potential exponential increase in complexity when modeling entire games through their isolated sub-sets. We support our theoretical findings with a practical example involving a multi-agent scenario in a partially observable environment. We demonstrate and analyze code for our approach using the Pymc3 library in Python. We also discuss potential extensions to our framework and the implications of our results on future research. We refer to games within our framework as "hierarchically isolated stochastic games" (HISGs). A key strategy in this area has been the use of unsupervised cycle-consistent transformation-based models to map standard-dose CT images to low-dose images and then reverse the transformation to obtain enhanced low-dose images. However, these models often struggle with overfitting, especially when there is a significant dose difference between the input and output images. To address this issue, we propose a novel AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN framework that introduces a channel-wise adaptation mechanism for both the generator and discriminator components. This adaptation enables both the generator and discriminator to selectively switch between two modes of operation, depending on the density difference between the input and output images. This allows our model to achieve a balance between sample-specific detail preservation and global structure restoration. To prevent mode switching during training, we introduce a technique that applies both local and global loss functions, including a new edge-aware loss function that prioritizes structure restoration in low-contrast regions. Compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, our model exhibits superior performance in preserving organ boundaries and restoring missing textures, as evidenced by visual assessment and quantitative metrics. We investigate this intersection by exploring a high-performance neural network system that addresses a complex set of tasks requiring both high model update frequency and a large number of updated models. Our results show that this system features a unique landscape with issues such as catastrophic forgetting and stabilization conflicts. To tackle these challenges, we develop a novel modular multi-task reinforcement learning framework that utilizes multiple interconnected systems, each responsible for a subset of tasks. This framework facilitates frequent model updates in a way that minimizes forgetting and conflicts, and our experiments confirm its effectiveness by achieving the best performance among comparison methods and matching the performance of a non-modular system in our testing suite. Additionally, our research reveals that a simple modular system with minimal connection can already outperform a more complex system without modularization. We also examine the impact of different model update methods, find that a mixture of intramodal and intermodal updates is key to success, and discuss ways to apply this approach to other multi-task learning settings. Research has shown that when only one image is provided, humans can use other cues such as shape and size to estimate depths. With only one training session, we significantly improved performance compared to not having any training. Additionally, our results showed that when no training was involved, a random action was taken about 75% of the time. We also explored the effects of providing two training sessions and gave technical details of the method used.

This article examines the existence of invariant surfaces in fractional order dynamical systems. We first derive a novel approach for identifying the signs of Lyapunov exponents in fractional order systems. We then leverage this method to investigate the presence of invariant surfaces in these systems. Specifically, we show that if the global surface is continuously differentiable and its gradient is non-zero, it cannot be invariant if the fractional order is other than unity. We also introduce an illustrative example of a fractional order Lorenz system to visually demonstrate our findings. The conditions derived in this study provide a framework for analyzing the local stability of specific surfaces in fractional order systems. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. While deep learning techniques have improved significantly in classifying and analyzing medical images, there is still a need for extensively annotated datasets tagged for polyp characterization. To address this, our research presents UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset comprising annotated H&E stained images of colorectal polyps, along with detailed scorecards according to the Vienna classification and the Hamburger classification. This dataset serves as a foundation for developing and evaluating advanced deep learning-based approaches to identify neoplastic foci, characterize their type, and assign a grade according to the Hamburger system. To facilitate further research, UniToPatho is publicly accessible and can be utilized through a user-friendly web interface enabling easy dataset exploration and the generation of custom splits. Notably, this dataset stands out from similar initiatives due to its exhaustive annotations covering the entire cross-sectional area of colorectal polyps. To complement the dataset, our research includes novel state-of-the-art baselines, along with key findings and observations that provide valuable insights for the deep learning community. Specifically, our studies reveal that incisional neoplastic foci are consistently missed by models, whereas focal neoplastic patterns are more challenging to detect. Regarding classification, our results show that models exhibit a well-documented preference for predicting the adenoma category over the carcinoma category. Moreover, our analysis of grade predictions offers qualitative insights, highlighting the importance of further exploring the Hamburger classification system through large-scale evaluations. UniToPatho is publicly available at https://unito.patho.unige.ch/. The code for our research is accessible at https://github.com/unito-eth-unihh/unioto_pathology. Additionally, pre-trained models have been uploaded to https://www.compvis.ethz.ch/research/colorectal/. Our research was conducted in collaboration with pathologists from the University of Zurich and the University of Geneva. For more information on this project, please refer to https://www.compvis.ethz.ch/research/colorectal/. Our analysis of water content in Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites provides the basis for a new argument that suggests the inner Solar System was home to significant water accumulation as a result of planetesimal activity, in contrast to the commonly held view that water was delivered to the inner Solar System via Neptune-Kuiper Belt material transport. This conclusion is derived from the evidence of water-rich secondary minerals found in the meteorites, specifically indicating high temperatures necessary for their formation and subsequent rapid cooling, coupled with evidence of mechanical processing, which together indicate that these meteorites originated from impact melts generated by objects in the 1-10 km in size range that were rich in water. This interpretation challenges the widely accepted theory that water in the Benenitra chondrite ring melt came from partially melted asteroids at higher temperatures. Our data also include new determinations of the H2O content in shock melt inclusions from the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra falls, specifically showing an average water content of 0.789 ± 0.290 wt. % for Chelyabinsk and 2.870 ± 0.570 wt. % for Benenitra. Notably, the water content in Benenitra is significantly higher than in other C-type chondrite meteorites, and can be accounted for by the presence of hydrous primary minerals in the parent asteroid, supporting the hypothesis that the Benenitra asteroid was rich in water. This water would have been released into the gas phase during high-temperature processes within the asteroid, eventually getting trapped in the shock melt, a process that in turn led to the formation of water-rich secondary minerals following rapid cooling. This finding provides evidence that water in the Benenitra fall came from primary hydrous minerals in the parent asteroid, further supporting our initial argument that water was extensively distributed throughout the inner Solar System in the form of hydrous minerals in small asteroids. This interpretation has implications for the ongoing debate regarding the source of water in the early Solar System and has notable effects on models predicting delivery of water to the inner Solar System. This method enables a comprehensive expansion of the electromagnetic field in terms of higher-order multipolar terms, which can be used to accurately assess electromagnetic interactions with small objects. This approach also facilitates the breakdown of optical thrust forces into distinct components driven by different multipolar effects. We validate our method through numerical simulations, first by verifying its ability to surpass the conventional multipolar approximations in treating small objects. Next, we investigate the fundamental properties of optical thrust forces arising from local field enhancements at specific locations within an object, made possible only by considering higher-order multipolar terms. Finally, we explore the potential of optical thrust forces to serve as an efficient means of propelling small dielectric objects in vacuum. This research provides a ground for further study on the interplay between electromagnetic fields and small objects, potentially enabling innovative applications across fields like super-resolution imaging, optical tweezers, and the controlled movement of objects at the nanoscale. To facilitate further investigation, we offer a numerical framework for calculating the precise multipolar expansion of any dielectric object, compatible with multiple finite difference time domain (FDTD) implementations. This framework includes a sample FDTD solver for integrated calculation of multipolar coefficients and optical thrust forces. We anticipate this work to contribute significantly to the advancement of accurate models for the interaction of light with small objects and will provide a reference point for evaluating novel methods for field and flux calculations. This work is a follow-up to our earlier findings on optical thrust forces and we hope it will serve as a foundation for future research on the multidisciplinary aspects of light-object interactions. Additionally, we believe it will provide a valuable reference for the evaluation of new numerical methods for field and flux calculations. To this end, we will continue to maintain and update the accuracy of this work as new methods are developed. In the context of FDTD solvers, we expect this work to contribute to the ongoing evolution of this numerical method.
